A.1 Plan Development Process

Planning Process Overview
The City of Berkeley’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan was originally adopted by the City

Council on June 22, 2004, following a process that built on years of disaster mitigation

activities. An update to the Plan was adopted on December 16, 2014 and again on

December 20, 2019. To create the 2024 LHMP update, Berkeley followed the same multi-

phased, broadly-inclusive process used to update the Plan in 2019.


LHMP Kickoff Meeting and Formation of Core Planning Team
On June 20, 2023 the City of Berkeley kicked off the 2024 LHMP Planning Process by

convening a Core Planning Team made up of City Staff representing the many

departments and divisions most involved in mitigation efforts. The Core Planning Team

met monthly throughout the development process. The Core Planning Team included the

following City Staff:


   •   Jamie Albrecht, Emergency Services Coordinator, Office of Emergency Services

   •   Galadriel Burr, Community Services Specialist, Building and Safety

   •   Zoe Covello, Assistant Planner, Land Use Division

   •   Dan Green, Assistant Fire Chief, Wildland Urban Interface Division

   •   Ashley James, Senior Planner, Land Use Division

       Preparedness

       Preparedness

   •   Sarah Moore, Community Services Specialist, Office of Energy and Sustainable
       Development

   •   Steve Riggs, Fire Marshal, Fire Department

Development of First Draft Plan
Throughout 2023 and in early 2024, the Project Manager collaborated with numerous City

staff, hazard experts, and community partners to update the plan’s hazard analysis,

progress on 2019 actions, and to develop the 2024 mitigation strategy. During this time

City leaders provided guidance to the Project Manager through participation in the Core

Planning Team. As the Project Team developed the First Draft 2024 LHMP, they engaged

key partners and community members to update hazard and risk assessments and

mitigation initiatives in the Plan, including the new section in the hazard analysis on

mitigating individual and household risk for each hazard. The Core Planning Team

worked with key partners to identify opportunities for collaboration on new Actions in the

2024 mitigation strategy.


The list of City Staff and hazard expert representatives as well documentation of their


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         A-2
participation is in the Attachment.


Public Review of First Draft Plan
In May 2024, the City posted the First Draft Plan on the City website for review and

comment by the Berkeley community. All of the City’s commissions were invited to

provide feedback on the Plan. The Project Manager presented the First Draft Plan to the

Disaster and Fire Safety Commission and Planning Commission, offering an opportunity

for feedback from Commissioners and community members. The City also offered to

meet with Council Members one-on-one to discuss the Plan and hear their feedback. In

response to this offer, Council Members suggested a presentation to the Safety

Committee, which staff gave in July 2024.


To support and encourage community members to provide asynchronous feedback, the

City posted created videos introducing Risk Assessment content in an accessible and

short format. These videos are accompanied by an email address where community

members can share their ideas.


The City also held two First Draft Plan Workshops, offering the public an opportunity to

engage in person with staff on the Plan’s content. The Workshops included a short

presentation introducing the Plan and then an opportunity to comment on poster boards

describing each hazard in the First Draft Plan.


This public review process is considered a key step in the City Council’s adoption of the

2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan. See Element F: Plan Adoption for details on the public

review process.

A.2 Stakeholder Engagement
In August 2023, the Core Planning Team invited Community Partners to help develop the

First Draft 2024 LHMP. Community Partners included local and regional agencies,

neighboring communities, representatives from business, academia, and other

organizations, as well as local non-profit and community groups. Each Community

Partner was asked via email to submit their risk assessment information, mitigation

strategy approaches, successes, and ideas for collaboration. The City incorporated this

feedback into the Plan.


The Project Manager collaborated with these agencies to include detailed information

about partners’ hazard and risk assessments and mitigation initiatives in the hazard

analysis section of the Plan. Additionally, Community Partners were invited to review and

provide comment on proposed actions as part of the process to develop the First Draft

2024 LHMP. The list of Community Partner representatives as well documentation of their

invitation to participate is in the Attachment.


Community Partners are also invited to provide feedback on the First Draft Plan as part

of the public process.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                        A-4
A.3 Public Engagement during
Drafting Stage
In order to involve the public early in the mitigation planning process, the City of Berkeley’s

Office of Emergency Services spoke to people about the Plan at community events, like

National Night Out. During National Night Out, staff went to neighborhoods across

Berkeley where residents were hosting free block parties. The block parties were out on

the streets or green space of the neighborhood, blocked off to traffic, making them open

and accessible to anyone who was available to join. Questions focused on top hazards

of concern and how community members can take mitigation and preparedness actions

to reduce risk.


The Office of Emergency Services also hosted three community workshops focused on

offering the public mitigation actions that could easily take as well as collecting input into

the Plan. These workshops included one on all Berkeley’s Hazards in central Berkeley,

one on Tsunamis at the waterfront, and a Winter Weather Workshop held in north

Berkeley. These workshops were held at different times to accommodate a variety of

schedules: one on a weekday evening, one on a Saturday morning, and one on Saturday

morning and afternoon. Locations were all public transit accessible.


For individuals that could not attend in person events, there was always an option to email

staff at mitigation@berkeleyca.gov. This email address was advertised as part of

outreach materials such as newsletters and at community events for people to share.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                              A-5
This public engagement led to the decision to remove climate change as its own

standalone hazard and instead integrate it more thoroughly into each hazard of concern.

Many community members expressed that it didn’t make sense to have it so separate

from the other hazards. Climate change is now more of framing discussion throughout

each hazard section.

Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         A-7
     B.    Risk Assessment
To become disaster resilient, a community must first understand the existing hazards and

their potential impacts. Berkeley is exposed to a number of hazards that vary in their

intensity and impacts on the city. This mitigation plan addresses hazards: earthquake,

wildland-urban interface (WUI) fire, flood, rainfall-triggered landslide, tsunami, extreme

heat, hazardous materials release, poor air quality, sea level rise, infectious disease, high

wind events, and utility interruption. Each of these hazards can occur independently or in

combination, and can also trigger secondary hazards.


Describing Likelihood and Impacts
Using a structure outlined by Saunders, Beban and Kilvington (2013 draft), the table

below summarizes these hazards, their relative likelihoods, and the relative severities of

their potential consequences.


Relative degrees of likelihood are described as:


   •   Likely: The event may occur several times in your lifetime, up to once every 50
       years

   •   Possible: The event might occur once in your life time, once every 51 – 100 years

   •   Unlikely: The event does occur somewhere from time to time, once every 101 –
       1,000 years

   •   Rare: Possible but not expected to occur except in exceptional circumstances,
       once every 1,001 to 2,500 years

   •   Very rare: Conceivable but highly unlikely to occur, once every 2,500+ years

Relative severity of hazard impacts is described using the following terms, which are

defined by matrix of factors, including Social/Cultural, Buildings, Critical Buildings,

Lifelines, Economic and Health and Safety:


   •   Catastrophic

   •   Major

   •   Moderate

   •   Minor

   •   Insignificant

B.1.a   Description of Hazards
Sections B1-B13 describe hazards and how they occur in Berkley. They also describe

how related hazards can trigger or be triggered by the hazard in question.


Natural Hazards
Originally, the natural hazards included in this plan were first identified through a

community-based process during the revision of the Disaster Preparedness and Safety

Element of the City’s General Plan, adopted in 2002. The General Plan is the result of

four drafts, approximately 100 hours of public workshops, meetings, and hearings, almost

1,000 pages of policy suggestions submitted by Berkeley citizens, and the hard work and

dedication of the Berkeley community and Berkeley Planning Commission 1. Specialists

from the California Geological Survey, US Geological Survey, UC Berkeley, the

Earthquake Engineering Research Institute (EERI), the Association of Bay Area

Governments (ABAG) and many others worked with the city on programs and research

that were incorporated in the Disaster Preparedness and Safety Element.


Since then, the natural hazards in the plan included in the Plan have been updated with

each cycle. Updates are based on new science, recent hazard occurrences, and

community feedback during the drafting stage.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                       B-3
   •    In 2014, the LHMP added Climate Change as a hazard of concern.


   •    In 2019, the LHMP added extreme heat as a specific hazard.


   •    In 2024, the LHMP added poor air quality, infectious disease, high wind, sea level

        rise, and utility disruption as specific hazards. The LHMP removed Climate Change

        as its own hazard and integrated into each specific hazard, inspired by community

        feedback during the drafting stage.


Hazards Not Considered in the Plan
Other natural hazards that are extremely rare in Berkeley are not included in this plan;

these include prolonged low temperatures, hail, and small tornados and waterspouts. This

plan does not focus on these hazards because they are not as likely to occur or to create

damage that is as serious as the hazards addressed in detail. California is not generally

exposed to the large tornado events experienced in the Midwest. Berkeley’s geographic

location and moderate climate typically shelters it from prolonged cold. Ocean

temperatures moderate the power of tropical storms, lessening the effects of low

barometric pressure and storm surge. However, these hazards may become more

prevalent in Berkeley with the changing climate.

Vulnerability to Current and Future Assets
Sections B.1.f – B.13.f describe risk to assets including people, structures, systems,

natural, historic, and cultural resources, and activities of value to the Berkeley community.


Access and Functional Needs
This plan also recognizes that there are many individuals that are still disproportionately

impacted during disasters. People with access and functional needs are defined as

community members who may have additional needs before, during and after an incident

in functional areas, including but not limited to: maintaining independence,

communication, transportation, supervision, and medical care. Individuals in need of

additional response assistance may include those who have disabilities, live in

institutionalized settings, are elderly, are children, are from diverse cultures, have limited

English proficiency, or are non-English speaking, or are transportation disadvantaged. An

Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                             B-5
individual with a disability is defined by the ADA as a person who had a physical or mental

impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities, a person who has a

history or record of such an impairment, or a person who is perceived by others as having

such an impairment. The ADA does not specifically name all of the impairments that are

covered.


Underserved Communities and Marginalized Populations
Disasters also disproportionally impact undeserved communities and marginalized

populations. For example, people of color and people with low incomes have been

historically denied access to housing and resources, increasing their vulnerability to these

shocks. In the 2024 LHMP, actions are considered for how they prioritize underserved

communities and marginalized populations. Further, the 2024 LHMP includes a list of

mitigation actions for individuals and households that are designed to be approachable

and accessible to a variety of circumstances.



B.1.g   Risk and Loss Estimates
Sections B.1.g – B.13.g describe the consequences or effects of the hazard on the assets.

Impacts are estimated quantitatively, when possible. Economic losses are described

when possible.


GFOA Analysis
Some hazard sections Risk and Loss Estimates include analysis from the GFOA. In 2023,

the City of Berkeley has been considering the implication that extreme events, like natural

disasters, could have on the City government’s financial condition, particularly its reserve




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           B-6
levels for the general fund. The City engaged the GFOA to produce a recommendation

to help it decide the appropriate reserve level for the general fund, given the risks from

extreme events. GFOA is a non-profit association of more than 23,000 state and local

government finance professionals and elected officials from across North America. A key

part of GFOA’s mission is to promote best practices in public finance, including reserve

policies. The analysis by GFOA also shed light on the potential broader economic losses

to the community from the risks posed by extreme events.


Any “risk” can be thought of as the downside to an uncertain event. The next section

describes GFOA’s approach to uncertainty.



B.1.h   The Approach to Uncertainty
The accomplished forecasting scientist, Spyros Makridakis, suggests a “Triple-A”

approach for dealing with highly uncertain phenomena.


Accept. First, we must accept that we are subject to uncertainty. For example, the

severity and timing of an earthquake is unpredictable. Berkeley could go years without

experiencing a serious earthquake or one could occur next month!


Assess. Next, we must assess the potential impact of the uncertainty, with history

providing a useful reference point. The experiences of other local governments are also

a good reference point. For example, we used the historical experiences of Berkeley and

other relevant municipalities to estimate the potential impact of future extreme events.

However, historical experiences are not perfectly predictive of the future.


Augment. The range of uncertainty we face will almost always be greater than what we



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-7
initially assess it to be. Therefore, we must augment our understanding of risk beyond

what our historical experiences show us. For example, very few people saw the 2008

Great Recession coming or thought it could be as bad as it was. They were unprepared

for this historically unprecedented recession. We can augment our understanding of risk

using a technique called “Probability Management.” 2 Probability Management is an

application of modern information processing technology that allows us to simulate

thousands of potential events (e.g., floods, recessions, etc.) so that we can observe the

probability of events of various magnitudes coming to pass. The statistical technique that

Probability Management is based on is called “Monte Carlo analysis.” This technique was

established in the late 1940s, but until very recently required special computers and

software to use. Modern information technology has made Monte Carlo analysis

accessible to anyone with a personal computer.


In order to use Probability Management, we express any given type of extreme event as

a range of possibilities that the City might experience. This range is called a “distribution.”

A distribution is a shape that signifies how frequently the City might expect to experience

a certain type of event and/or how severe the event might be.


The most common type of distribution is called the “normal distribution,” more popularly

known as the “bell curve.” Many phenomena fit a bell curve. To help us understand how

to read a distribution, we can start with an example that is related to everyday life: the

height of American men.


Exhibit 3.1 shows a bell curve for the height of American men. The horizontal axis of

Exhibit 3.1 represents height. The vertical axis represents frequency. The most common



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                              B-8
height is 5’9”, so it is shown at the top of the curve. Much taller men, like NBA centers,

would be found on the right-hand side of the curve. Very short men would be found on

the left.

Another type of distribution we use in our analysis is an asymmetrical distribution, shown

in Exhibit 3.2. Earthquakes fit an asymmetrical distribution. Exhibit 3.2 shows that tremors

are the most common. Full-fledged earthquakes are relatively rare. The distribution is

“asymmetrical” because the frequency with which we will experience these events are not

evenly distributed around the middle of the distribution. Put another way, there are far

more tremors that are smaller than the “average” earthquake. Yet, there are far fewer

earthquakes (“the big one”) that are larger than the average earthquake.


Expressing Berkeley’s vulnerability as distributions allows us to calculate the probability

that an event of a given magnitude will come to pass. When we associate a dollar amount

with that event, we can estimate the probability or chance that Berkeley will need to have

a given amount of money on-hand to respond.


Exhibit 3.3 is not a distribution but is a type of graphic we use in our work. It is called a



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                            B-10
“cumulative probability chart.” The example in Exhibit 3.3 shows the economic losses to

the entire Berkeley community from earthquakes over the course of 10 years.

Earthquakes are rare events, so over a ten-year period there is a chance that there are

no earthquakes at all. Hence, the red line intersects the vertical axis at about 50% (there

is about a 50% chance of no earthquake). We then see the red line go up and to the right

from the vertical axis. This means that the chance of larger and larger losses become

increasingly remote. To illustrate, the red line intersects 70% at about $300 million. This

means there is a 70% chance that total economic losses are $300 million or less (or a

30% chance that losses will be more). The red line insects 80% at $670 million, which

means there is an 80% chance that losses will be less than that (or a 20% chance that

losses will be more).

Both cumulative probability charts and loss exceedance curves are commonly used when

quantifying risk. In our work with the City we will use loss exceedance curves to show

economic losses to the entire Berkeley community and cumulative probability charts to

show losses to just City government. In this particular report, we will be focusing on

economic losses to the entire community, so we will show loss exceedance curves. GFOA

is working with the City of Berkley on a separate report about financial losses to City

government. Our intent is to make it easier to distinguish between charts that depict

community versus city government losses by giving each type of loss a distinctive chart

(and a different color line), for those readers that will use both reports.

B.2     Earthquakes

B.2.a   Description of Earthquakes and Related Hazards
An earthquake is the ground shaking caused by a sudden slip on a fault. Stresses in the

earth’s outer layer push the sides of the fault together. Stress builds up and the rocks slip

suddenly, releasing energy in waves that travel through the earth's crust and cause the

shaking that we feel during an earthquake.


Shaking and Ground Failure
The most significant physical characteristic of a major earthquake is the ground shaking.

During an earthquake, the ground can shake for a few seconds or up to a minute or more.

The strength and duration of ground shaking is affected by many factors, including the

types of soils underneath, and the distance, size, depth, and direction of the fault rupture

that caused the quake.


The strongest shaking is typically close to the fault where the earthquake occurs.

Horizontal shaking in particular causes most earthquake damage, because structures

often have inadequate resistance to this type of motion.


Earthquakes can cause the ground to fail in several ways, resulting in additional hazards:

surface fault rupture, liquefaction, and seismically-triggered landslides.


Surface fault rupture: Surface fault rupture occurs when movement on a fault deep within

the earth breaks through to the surface. This can severely damage structures that cross

the fault, including buildings, roads, pipelines, and train tracks.


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           B-15
Liquefaction: Liquefaction is a phenomenon that occurs in wet, sandy, or silty soils. When

shaken, the soil grains consolidate, pushing water towards the surface and causing a loss

of strength in the soil. The ground surface may sink or spread laterally.


Seismically-Triggered Landslides: Ground shaking from an earthquake can trigger

landslides. This landslide movement can range from a few inches to tens of feet. Ground

surface displacements as small as a few inches are enough to break typical foundations.


Fire Following Earthquake3
Fires break out following all major earthquakes. Fire following earthquake presents a

significant problem in dense urban environments, where many simultaneous ignitions

lead to a firestorm. In these cases, fire damage is even more severe than damage from

earthquake shaking.


Earthquake shaking can start fires in numerous ways, such as:


   •   Tipping over appliances with pilot lights

   •   Damaging electrical equipment leading to sparks

   •   Exposing materials to open flames from stoves, candles, fireplaces and grills

Post-earthquake fires can also spread quickly when flammable chemicals spill.


Ground failure due to liquefaction, surface fault rupture and landslide can rupture gas

lines (both underground and at the private gas meter). These ruptures can start and fuel

fires, which also spread more quickly after major earthquakes because earthquakes

damage the infrastructure needed to mitigate or respond to fires:




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                          B-16
   •    Within a building, earthquake shaking and ground failure can damage a building’s
        active fire protection systems (e.g., fire alarms and sprinkler systems), as well as
        its passive fire protection systems (construction features designed to slow/stop fire,
        e.g. fire walls, fire-rated floor-ceiling assemblies, and fire doors).

   •    Within a community, fires also spread more quickly after major earthquakes
        because earthquakes damage the infrastructure needed to fight them. Earthquake
        shaking and ground failure due to liquefaction, surface fault rupture and landslide
        can simultaneously break water mains, damage electrical systems necessary to
        provide energy to pump water, damage communication infrastructure, impede
        emergency transportation routes with debris or landslides, and jam firehouse
        doors, preventing apparatus from responding. Fires can occur in the days or
        months following an earthquake due to the to electrical systems, fire protection
        systems, and gas lines.

Connection to sea level rise
The United States Geological Survey predicts that sea level rise will lead to rising water

tables. Higher water tables in turn increases the risk of liquefaction during earthquakes,

as more soils become wet, sandy, or silty. This means as climate change continues and

sea level rise increases, liquefaction will be a concern for more areas in Berkeley.


Connection to utility disruption
All utilities are vulnerable to disruption from earthquake shaking and ground failure. See

the Vulnerabilities and Risk and Loss sections of this Earthquake section for more details.



B.2.b   Locations of Earthquakes and Related Hazards
Map 1 shows the City of Berkeley and its proximity to known active geologic faults in the

San Francisco Bay Region. This map shows most the San Francisco Bay Area, with the

City of Berkeley shaded in dark gray. Many green lines move across the map in a

northwest to southeast direction:


   •    On the western side of the picture, in the Pacific Ocean, multiple green lines move


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                            B-17
       along the coast, starting and stopping. One of these lines begins in Marin,
       stretches through the ocean, and then continues through Daly City and down the
       peninsula, off the picture. This is the San Andreas Fault.

   •   On the right side of the frame, another set of green lines starts and stops, showing
       earthquake faults in the East Bay. One of these lines stretches from the middle of
       San Pablo Bay, crosses directly through the eastern section of Berkeley, and
       continues down the East Bay past Union City. This is the Hayward fault, which
       stretches to Milpitas, and is of particular concern in Berkeley.

A large earthquake on any of the illustrated faults could impact Berkeley. For example,

the 1989 M 6.9 Loma Prieta earthquake was a rupture of the San Andreas fault, and the

2014 M 6.0 South Napa earthquakes occurred along the West Napa fault.

Location of Seismically-Triggered Landslides


The California Geological Survey has identified the areas of Berkeley with potential to

experience earthquake-induced landslide. All areas underlain by known active or dormant

landslides are included in the zone. These areas are identified by combining information

on rock or soil strength, slope gradient (steepness), and anticipated future shaking levels.

In Berkeley, the potential for landslide from seismic activity is high in the hill areas and

along creek banks. Map 4 indicates that significant portions of the Berkeley hills have the

potential to experience earthquake-induced landslide. These areas are shown in light

brown on Map 4 throughout the Berkeley hills.

Location of Fire Following Earthquake
Fire following earthquake is a threat throughout Berkeley making it impossible to map the

potential locations. We do know that seismically vulnerable buildings also likely to be a

key source of earthquake-caused fires when gas or electricity lines break or rupture.

Additionally, Berkeley has many older multi-unit apartment buildings without fire sprinkler

systems. These buildings could both cause and feed fires following an earthquake.

Ultimately, densely-populated neighborhoods with wooden homes, such as most of the

residential areas in Berkeley, are at high risk of fire spread following a major earthquake.


However, even buildings that survive earthquake shaking can succumb to fire, including

those buildings that have been seismically retrofitted.



B.2.c   Extent of Earthquakes and Anticipated Intensities
Magnitude and intensity are the two commonly-used scales to represent different

earthquake characteristics. 4


Magnitude: An earthquake has a single magnitude, which indicates the overall size and

energy released by the earthquake. Magnitude is measured using moment magnitude

(M).


Intensity: In the same earthquake, different locations will experience different amounts of

shaking. The shaking experienced at different locations varies based on:


   •    The earthquake’s overall magnitude

   •    The distance from the fault that ruptured in the earthquake

   •    The ground type: thick valley deposits shake longer and harder than rock.


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                          B-28
Intensity measures the strength of earthquake shaking at a particular location. Intensity

is measured using the Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) scale. Intensity is based on

observed effects. The MMI value assigned to a specific site after an earthquake provides

a more meaningful measure of the earthquake’s severity at that location than the

magnitude, which applies one value to the entire earthquake.


MMI descriptions 5

The MMI scale is composed of twelve increasing levels of intensity that range from

imperceptible shaking to catastrophic destruction. Lower numbers on the intensity scale

generally deal with the manner in which the earthquake is felt by people. Higher numbers

on the scale are based on observed structural damage. Levels are as follows:


   •   MMI Level I (White): Shaking Not Felt: Not felt except by a very few under
       especially favorable conditions.

   •   MMI Level II (Lavender): Weak Shaking: Felt only by a few persons at rest,
       especially on upper floors of buildings.

   •   MMI Level III (Aqua): Weak Shaking: Felt quite noticeably by persons indoors,
       especially on upper floors of buildings. Many people do not recognize it as an
       earthquake. Standing motor cars may rock slightly. Vibrations similar to the
       passing of a truck. Duration estimated.

   •   MMI Level IV (Blue): Light Shaking: Felt indoors by many, outdoors by few during
       the day. At night, some awakened. Dishes, windows, doors disturbed; walls make
       cracking sound. Sensation like heavy truck striking building. Standing motor cars
       rocked noticeably.

   •   MMI Level V (Gray): Moderate Shaking: Felt by nearly everyone; many awakened.
       Some dishes, windows broken. Unstable objects overturned. Pendulum clocks
       may stop.

   •   MMI Level VI (Light Yellow): Strong Shaking: Felt by all, many frightened. Some
       heavy furniture moved; a few instances of fallen plaster. Damage slight.



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                       B-29
   •   MMI Level VII (Medium Yellow): Very Strong Shaking: Damage negligible in
       buildings of good design and construction; slight to moderate in well-built ordinary
       structures; considerable damage in poorly build or badly designed structures;
       some chimneys broken.

   •   MMI Level VIII (Orange): Severe Shaking: Damage slight in specially designed
       structures; considerable damage in ordinary substantial buildings with partial
       collapse. Damage great in poorly built structures. Fall of chimneys, factory stacks,
       columns, monuments, walls. Heavy furniture overturned.

   •   MMI Level IX (Red): Violent Shaking: Damage considerable in specially designed
       structures; well-designed frame structures thrown out of plumb. Damage great in
       substantial buildings, with partial collapse. Buildings shift off foundations.

   •   MMI Level X+ (Dark Red): Extreme Shaking: Some well-built wooden structures
       destroyed; most masonry and frame structures destroyed with foundations. Rails
       bent.


Berkeley could experience earthquakes that span the range of the MMI scale. However,

the most concerning is when the shaking is strong, very strong, violent, or extreme. To

understand what this means for Berkeley, Map 6 shows most of the San Francisco Bay

Area and the different levels of shaking intensity anticipated with a hypothetical magnitude

7.0 earthquake on the Hayward fault. Shaded in colors of yellow, orange, and red, the

map shows that very strong, severe, and violent shaking will be felt all along the East

Bay, stretching from Pinole to south of Hayward.


Berkeley is outlined with a thick black line and is shaded in colors of orange and red,

indicating that in this scenario, the Berkeley flats will experience MMI Level VII (severe

shaking), and eastern Berkeley will experience MMI Level IX (violent shaking).




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                          B-30
Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan   B-31
B.2.d   Previous Earthquakes
The strongest, most recent earthquakes occurred in the Bay Area in 2022. A magnitude

5.1 earthquake struck near San Jose in October and a magnitude 3.6 struck near El

Cerrito in December. Both of these earthquakes had minimal reported damages. There

have been no federally-declared earthquake disasters in Berkeley since the last update.


Destructive earthquakes struck the Bay Area in 1838, 1868, 1898, 1906, 1911, 1989, and

2014. Impacts of the earlier earthquakes in Berkeley are not well documented, but the

damage of the 2014 magnitude 6.0 South Napa Earthquake is fresh in the memory of

many Berkeley residents. It killed two people, injured 300 others, and caused moderate

to severe damage to more than 2,000 structures. 6 Electricity and water services sustained

disruptions and there was minor damage to roads, water and natural gas lines, and

wastewater treatment facilities.


The 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake also informs the Bay Area’s understanding of

earthquakes. Sixty-two people died in the Bay Area as a direct result of this earthquake.

Most of the fatalities, 42, were caused by the collapse of a two-level elevated highway in

Oakland only a few miles from the Berkeley city limits. Damage in the City of Berkeley

was minor in comparison to many of its neighbors. Many residential structures

experienced collapse of unreinforced masonry chimneys, and new cracks were found in

the Martin Luther King, Jr. Civic Center Building. The earthquake epicenter was far from

Berkeley, but region-wide impacts and disruption increased the Berkeley community’s

awareness of the high-risk Berkeley faces from much closer earthquakes.


The 1906 San Francisco Earthquake caused structural damage in Berkeley, including



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                        B-32
chimney cracking and collapse, and considerable damage to some public buildings

including Berkeley High School structures. 7 Other “small” earthquakes in Berkeley over

the years have caused slight damage to and in some buildings.



B.2.e   Probability of Future Events
Earthquakes, especially smaller ones, are a part of life in the San Francisco Bay Area.

Smaller earthquakes happen regularly and sometimes cause damage, especially inside

of homes when furniture or other items move. Although small earthquakes can cause

some damage, they are not as concerning as a catastrophic earthquake with a magnitude

of 6.0 or more.


According to the US Geological Survey, there is a 72% probability of one or more M 6.7

or greater earthquakes from 2014 to 2043 in the San Francisco Bay Region. 8 There is a

33% chance that a 6.7 or greater will occur on the Hayward fault system between 2014

and 2043. 9 This means that it is likely that many Berkeley residents will experience a

severe earthquake in their lifetimes.


Researchers are still trying to understand how climate change is impacting the probability

of future earthquakes. According to the United States Geological Survey, there is

currently no pattern of earthquakes occurring more frequently during periods of heavy

precipitation or drought. 10



B.2.f   Vulnerabilities

People
People with disabilities and people with access and functional needs, students, and low-


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                        B-33
income individuals may live in older housing units that are more vulnerable to collapse or

damage from earthquakes. These groups may also have less socioeconomic means to

prepare for and recover from an earthquake that damages their home. Earthquakes

cause power outages, and people who are dependent on medical or other assistive

devices that use electricity are especially vulnerable. Significant damage to streets, curbs,

and transportation systems may prevent people with disabilities and people with access

and functional needs from navigating to their destinations. Earthquake damage to and

reduced functionality of communication systems may create additional challenges for

people to get assistance from their families, friends, and caregivers.


Structures
Several types of seismically vulnerable buildings are located throughout Berkeley,

including wood-framed buildings with soft, weak or open front conditions (SWOF),

unreinforced masonry (URM) buildings, tilt-up and other rigid wall-flexible diaphragm

(RWFD) buildings, and non-ductile concrete buildings. Other wood-framed buildings with

seismic deficiencies include those with inadequate anchorage to foundation and/or

inadequate cripple wall bracing, multi-family “weak story” buildings, one-story open-front

buildings, and buildings with unique configurations.


Map 7 shows Berkeley’s Inventory of Potentially Seismically Vulnerable buildings,

developed in 2023. Potentially soft, weak or open front (SWOF) buildings are somewhat

evenly spread throughout the City. Potentially non-ductile concrete buildings and rigid

wall-flexible diaphragm buildings are more heavily concentrated along commercial

corridors and west of San Pablo Avenue. Non-ductile concrete buildings are also



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           B-34
clustered in central Berkeley, and near the UC Berkeley Campus. Soft story buildings are

depicted in blue, non-ductile concrete buildings in orange, rigid wall-flexible diaphragm

buildings in purple, and unreinforced masonry buildings in red.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                       B-35
Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan   B-36
Soft, Weak or Open Front (SWOF) Buildings

Soft story buildings are characterized as multi-story wood-frame buildings with extensive

ground story openings such as windows, storefronts, garage openings, or open-air

spaces such as parking. These buildings may have few perimeter or interior walls at the

ground level, leading to a relatively soft or weak lateral load resisting system in this lower

story.


Exhibit 6. Example soft story construction




Unreinforced Masonry (URM) Buildings

Unreinforced masonry (URM) buildings are generally constructed of brick, block, tile,

stone, or other types of masonry, and were built prior to modern earthquake-resistant

design. During an earthquake, unreinforced masonry walls that were originally built

without adequate reinforcement (from embedded steel bars) are susceptible to collapse.

In addition, URM buildings often include unreinforced masonry parapets, chimneys, and

high brick veneers that tend to disconnect from the building and fall outward, creating a

hazard for people below, and in some instances causing the building to collapse. Weak

or nonexistent connections between the masonry walls and the floors and roofs place



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                            B-37
occupants, pedestrians, and adjacent buildings in harm’s way.


Exhibit 7. Example of unreinforced masonry construction




Rigid Wall-Flexible Diaphragm (RWFD) Buildings, Including Tilt-Up Buildings

Tilt-up or other rigid wall-flexible diaphragm building types are typically one- or two-story

commercial buildings with reinforced concrete or reinforced masonry (brick or concrete

block) walls. A “tilt-up” building is distinguished by its method of construction, using

precast concrete walls. RWFD have “flexible” roof diaphragms that consist of wood or

steel beams, trusses, or rafters with wood sheathing or metal decking above. They may

also have flexible diaphragms at intermediate floor levels. These buildings commonly

include warehouses, manufacturing facilities, large retail stores, and other similar

structures. The most common deficiency is an inadequate connection between the rigid

walls and the roof (and floors), leading walls to pull away and collapse during ground

shaking.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           B-38
Exhibit 8. Example of Rigid Wall-Flexible Diaphragm Construction




Non-Ductile Concrete Buildings

Non-ductile concrete buildings built prior to the mid-1970’s and modern seismic code

standards have performed very poorly in recent earthquakes, and have resulted in

catastrophic collapses. In older concrete buildings, the detailing and construction of the

reinforcing steel may be inadequate to safely resist large seismic forces caused by ground

motions on these heavy structures. The most vulnerable buildings contain elements like

columns, wall piers, and joints of beams and slabs that can fail in an earthquake. These

buildings are considered “non-ductile” (i.e. brittle) concrete buildings and pose a high risk

during a major earthquake. Retrofits of these buildings can vary widely in terms of scope

and level of difficulty, and are often expensive to retrofit or rebuild.


Other Wood-Framed Buildings with Seismic Deficiencies

Throughout Berkeley, the most prevalent group of wood-framed buildings vulnerable to

significant damage from an earthquake are those constructed prior to 1960 with

inadequate cripple wall bracing and/or anchorage to the foundation, which can result in

buildings sliding off supporting foundations and cripple wall collapses. These include

hillside houses with increased risks of failure to cripple walls and poorly braced extra-tall


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           B-39
walls along the sloping sides.


Multi-family Weak-Story Buildings

In Multifamily Weak-Story buildings (3+ stories), the lowest story of the building may be

vulnerable to significant damage due to high demand to-capacity ratios. Multi-family Weak

Story buildings are primarily found among the areas of multi-family residential buildings

to the south of UC Berkeley (Southside) and extending along College Avenue and nearby

streets.


One-Story Open-Front Buildings

One-story open-front buildings, while having less mass to drive seismic response than

multi-story buildings, are still anticipated to have very significant torsional response and

to have potential concerns of partial or complete collapse. Single-story Open Front

buildings can be found along the major commercial corridors, such as Telegraph Avenue,

University Avenue, College Avenue, and similar locations.


Buildings with Unique Configurations

Buildings with unique configurations are also potentially vulnerable to an earthquake and

are anticipated to be of an age that engineering for seismic loading would not have been

provided at the time of construction. These buildings have been observed throughout the

City’s building stock.


Homes

Berkeley has about 50,046 housing units11, serving the city’s population of 124,321 12.

Most were built before 1980, meaning that few of Berkeley’s homes were constructed to

modern building code standards, which require earthquake-resistant structural measures,


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                          B-40
fire-resistant materials, and landslide-resistant siting and landscaping. As described

above, many people throughout Berkeley live in buildings with seismic vulnerabilities.


City-Owned Buildings

The City of Berkeley owns or leases approximately 221 buildings and structures. These

facilities have multiple uses, including running City government, providing emergency

services, low- income housing, and recreation. In recent years, the City has been

seriously examining the risk to its buildings from disasters, particularly earthquakes. Many

important City buildings have been assessed for seismic safety and, when possible,

strengthened or replaced. However, additional assessments of City buildings are needed

to further determine their level of vulnerability to seismic events. Some buildings’

earthquake vulnerabilities may pose risks to life and/or emergency operations, including

Old City Hall (2134 Martin Luther King, Jr Way) and Veterans’ Memorial Building (1931

Center Street).


City-Owned Critical Response Facilities

Most of the City’s critical response facilities have been strengthened or retrofitted because

of their importance to continuing emergency services, as well as day-to-day operations.


The Civic Center Building’s isolation system and retrofit elements were designed to

provide life safety and limited repairable damage in a Design Basis Earthquake (DBE),

and life safety and repairable damage in the Maximum Considered Earthquake (MCE).

Although the building’s base isolation system would meet the essential services standard

of the 2010 California Administrative Code, the building was not built to essential services

standards. The nonstructural systems and equipment in the Civic Center Building would



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           B-41
need to be evaluated to ensure that their support and bracing systems also meet essential

services requirements. Nonstructural elements along the access path to the essential

services area should also be evaluated to ensure unobstructed access to these areas in

the aftermath of an earthquake.


Hospitals

There is one acute care hospital in Berkeley, Alta Bates Summit Medical Center, owned

and operated by the Sutter East Bay Hospitals. The hospital has two campuses in

Berkeley: Alta Bates and Herrick.


The Alta Bates campus is a full-service acute care hospital, while the Herrick campus

provides acute care limited to mental health and cancer care services. Alta Bates is

comprised of eight buildings used to provide acute patient care, five of which were built

to pre-1973 seismic standards. These buildings are not considered a threat to life safety,

but may not be functional or repairable after an earthquake. 13 The Hospital Seismic Safety

Act requires these buildings to be retrofitted or replaced by 2030 to meet standards to be

repairable or functional following an earthquake. Three additional buildings at Alta Bates

and three at Herrick have already met this standard. 14 Four buildings at the Herrick

Campus are considered to be a significant risk to life safety. 15 Acute care functions

formerly housed in these buildings have been relocated into seismically compliant portion

of the Herrick campus and/or to the Summit Campus.


Businesses

Businesses are vital to the economy of the city and provide jobs to city residents. Damage

to commercial buildings could adversely impact business operations, increase economic



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-42
losses, disrupt supply distribution, disproportionately harm small businesses, reduce

affordable commercial spaces, and slow recovery after a major earthquake. Ensuring that

businesses and employers can return to normal function quickly will in turn ensure that

the city recovers quickly from a disaster.


As described above, many Berkeley businesses operate from buildings with seismic

vulnerabilities. Buildings of potentially non-ductile concrete construction or rigid wall-

flexible diaphragm buildings have been observed along numerous commercial corridors

within the city.


Systems
Berkeley’s electrical, natural gas, aviation fuel, telecommunications, and potable water

supply systems are not under the City’s control, and are owned and managed by other

quasi-governmental, private, or special district entities. Berkeley’s transportation systems

are managed by the City and other public entities.


All of these systems have earthquake exposure and vulnerabilities:


Electricity

Electricity is managed by Pacific Gas and Electric (PG&E). Berkeley’s electricity system

is almost entirely aboveground. Earthquakes can topple or break utility poles, and falling

trees or collapsing structures can damage utility lines. Earthquakes can damage electrical

switches and transformers in the distribution system, along with equipment at substations

and transmission lines, possibly leading to systemwide loss of these utilities.


Because electrical system infrastructure exists throughout Berkeley, earthquake shaking,



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                          B-43
liquefaction, fault rupture and earthquake-induced landslides can all damage this

infrastructure both above and below the ground. This means that a major earthquake will

cause significant power loss to Berkeley.


Natural gas

Natural gas is managed by PG&E. A natural gas transmission line runs the length of

Berkeley (north-south direction) under Seventh Street, the area of Berkeley that is more

susceptible to liquefaction. In an earthquake, if soils are shaken hard and long enough,

liquefaction can occur, causing pipelines in liquefiable soils to tear apart. Underground

systems are particularly prone to damage from ground failure in earthquakes and

landslides. Underground damage is harder to detect and repair, and the length of service

losses may be greater than for aboveground systems. Additionally, rupture compromises

this lifeline unless redundant connections unaffected by the earthquake are available.


Natural gas line rupture is one of the chief causes of post-earthquake fires. Additionally,

natural gas line rupture has climate implications. The main component of natural gas is

methane, which is a potent greenhouse gas that is 25 times more harmful to the

atmosphere over a 100-year period than carbon dioxide. 16


Potable water

Potable water is managed by East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD). EBMUD

provides drinking water to approximately 1.4 million people and sewer services to 640,000

in the East Bay. EBMUD was created in 1923, and the age and extent of its system makes

it particularly vulnerable to damage in earthquakes. Because the potable water system

exists throughout Berkeley, its infrastructure will be subject to shaking and ground failure,



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           B-44
including liquefaction, surface-fault rupture, and landslide, leading to many pipeline

breaks.


Sanitary sewer system

The City of Berkeley’s sanitary sewer system is made up of pipelines with large diameter

(six inches to 120 inches). Of the 260 miles of pipelines in the sanitary sewer system:


   •   50 miles or 19% is in the Earthquake-Induced Landslide Planning Zone

   •   29 miles or 11% is in the Fault Rupture Planning Zone.

   •   101 miles or 39% is in the Very High, High or Moderate Liquefaction Zone.

Because the sanitary sewer system exists throughout Berkeley, its infrastructure will be

subject to shaking and ground failure, including liquefaction, surface-fault rupture, and

landslide.


Storm Drainage System

Areas of the city’s storm drainage system are known to be extremely weak and at risk of

collapse. Ground shaking, liquefaction, fault rupture and landslides as a result of an

earthquake would cause significant damage to this system. If the next earthquake occurs

during or shortly before a rainstorm, the city could experience significant flooding in areas

that have not seen floodwaters previously.


Of the 94 miles of the storm drain system:


   •   13 miles or 14% is in the Earthquake-Induced Landslide Planning Zone.

   •   8 miles or 9% is in the Fault Rupture Planning Zone.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           B-45
   •   48 miles or 48% is in the Very High, High, or Moderate Liquefaction Zone.

Transportation systems

Transportation systems are managed by the City and other public entities, including

Caltrans, Amtrak, Bay Area Rapid Transit, and Union Pacific.


   •   Nearly half of all City streets are have a moderate or greater exposure to
       liquefaction, meaning that vehicle movement throughout the city is likely to be
       impacted. This movement will also affect aboveground infrastructure (streets,
       curbs and sidewalks.)

   •   To Berkeley’s east, 17 percent of City streets are situated in the earthquake-
       induced landslide planning zone. Landslides in this area could distort major and
       minor roads. This would make access difficult or impossible for firefighters and
       other emergency responders. It would also complicate evacuation for residents in
       the Berkeley hills.

   •   Fault rupture, if it occurs, could damage important east-west streets along the fault,
       making travel between the hills and flatland areas difficult where displacements
       are large. Interstate 80 is highly susceptible to earthquake-induced liquefaction
       and is main thoroughfare for Berkeley and the Bay Area.

Bay Area Rapid Transit District (BART) provides an important public transportation link

between Berkeley, San Francisco, and other Bay Area locations to 172,000 riders daily,

as of September 2023. In the 1960s, Berkeley taxpayers issued a separate tax to have

the BART facilities in Berkeley (three stations and over four miles of tunnel) put

underground. These tunnels are generally considered low risk by BART engineers. While

the BART system is not exposed to landslide or surface-fault rupture from earthquakes,

BART infrastructure in Berkeley will be subject to severe shaking and possibly to

liquefaction in a catastrophic earthquake.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           B-46
Telecommunications

Telecommunications are managed by a variety of private partners, including Verizon,

AT&T, and Comcast, among others. Communications infrastructure is spread throughout

Berkeley, and thus is exposed to all earthquake ground failure hazards.


Hazardous Materials

Hazardous materials are managed by private and public entities. The shaking and ground

failure that can accompany earthquakes could cause hazardous materials release.


Following an earthquake, building structural failures, dislodging of asbestos or

encapsulated asbestos, laboratory spills, transportation accidents, pipeline breaks,

storage tank failures, and industrial equipment problems will be the major sources of

hazardous materials release.


The City carefully tracks and regulates hazardous materials in both public and private

structures through its Toxics Management Division. See the section on Hazardous

Materials Release for details.


Aviation fuel

Aviation fuel is managed by Kinder Morgan, Inc. Two aviation and multipurpose pipelines

run along the railroad tracks from Richmond to the Oakland Airport, through western

Berkeley. These pipelines run along the Union Pacific railroad right-of-way in the western

part of the city. Soils in this area are potentially susceptible to liquefaction. Rupture of

these aviation fuel lines during an earthquake could spark and feed a dangerous fire.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                          B-47
Natural, historic, and cultural resources
Natural Resources

Parks and natural spaces are situated throughout Berkeley and may be damaged from

shaking and ground failure based on their locations. Berkeley watersheds (see Floods

section) and the San Francisco Bay Shoreline are vulnerable to hazardous materials

release. All natural resources are vulnerable to and post-quake fire.


Historic Resources

Because historic structures were not built to meet current building and fire codes, they

are especially vulnerable in earthquakes. Historic structures throughout Berkeley are

vulnerable to earthquake shaking and ground failure based on their locations. All locations

could be subject to hazardous materials release and post-quake fire.


Cultural Resources

Berkeley’s culture comes from the people who make up the Berkeley community.

Residents, businesses, and the UC Berkeley community are critical parts of Berkeley’s

culture and will all be impacted in a catastrophic earthquake. The Risk and Loss section

below also describes impacts to natural and historical resources.


   •   Berkeley Resident Community: Based on experiences in large urban areas being
       rebuilt following disaster, planners expect that rebuilding activities will begin
       quickly, but will prove expensive as construction professionals around the Bay
       Area are overloaded with work. Owners of damaged multi-unit rental housing may
       not be able to rebuild affordable housing, and may choose to build condominiums
       or other higher-profit housing to replace the damaged structures. Many residents
       will discover they are underinsured for earthquake and fire damage, making it
       difficult or impossible for them to rebuild. Rebuilt homes, meeting modern codes
       and style considerations, will change the look of the city.

   •   Although much harder to predict, demographic shifts may also follow an upended
       housing market. Older homeowners may be unable or unwilling to rebuild, for

Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-48
       example, and young families may need to relocate, at least temporarily, to ensure
       the continuity of their children’s education. The likely loss of older, more affordable
       housing stock will also change Berkeley’s economic profile, creating displacement
       of thousands of households.

   •   Businesses may rebuild or may move to new, cheaper locations. Many local,
       independent businesses will need to make the tough decision to rebuild or close
       shop. Retail businesses will be affected by demographic changes after an
       earthquake. Businesses located in neighborhoods with significant damage will
       suffer as customer demand changes, even if the businesses themselves are
       undamaged by the earthquake.

   •   After a catastrophic earthquake, enrollment at UC Berkeley may slow for a few
       years, depending on the level of damage experienced on campus. In the unlikely
       but possible event of a catastrophic incident, such as significant loss of life in a
       residence hall or classroom building, declines in enrollment will be significant.
       Remaining students, currently about 30 percent of the city’s population, may
       struggle to find affordable housing.

B.2.g Risk and Loss Estimates
No one knows what the characteristics of the next damaging quake to strike Berkeley will

be. A quake could occur on any of the regional faults, be deep or shallow under the

ground, and shake for a few seconds or up to nearly a minute. The degree of shaking and

resulting damages will vary greatly depending on these characteristics.


Currently, there is not sufficient data or understanding of how climate change is impacting

earthquakes. However, the cascading impacts from an earthquake might be more severe

due to climate change. For example, areas in Berkeley might be even more susceptible

to liquefaction due to sea level rise and shallow ground water rise.


Berkeley’s population is expected to keep growing steadily. With more people in Berkeley,

the more people are exposed to the catastrophic earthquake risk and the greater potential

for impacts and losses. With population and housing demands, Berkeley has regular new

development. Current building standards are high, resulting in safer structures that will


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                            B-49
suffer minimal damage. High housing costs and insufficient supply of low-income housing

today means that after a catastrophic earthquake, there will be even greater levels of

homelessness and displacement.


FEMA developed the Hazards US (HAZUS) software to help estimate the consequences

of different earthquake scenarios. HAZUS runs a computer model of a hypothetical

earthquake, defining the earthquake’s magnitude, epicenter location, rupture mechanism

and time of day. Using this information, HAZUS estimates losses for that particular

earthquake. These theoretical losses will not exactly predict the actual damage of

the scenario earthquake. Instead, they provide reasonable data to help guide

earthquake readiness activities.


Scenario Predictions
This section references three different HAZUS analyses:


   •   For the 2004 version of this plan, a magnitude 6.9 scenario earthquake on the
       Hayward fault underneath Berkeley was simulated using HAZUS. 17 In 2014, these
       loss estimates were combined with impact descriptions from newer HAZUS
       scenarios for a larger earthquake. 18 Because Berkeley’s increased population and
       density since 2004, it is likely that these predictions underestimate the impacts and
       associated costs of such an event.

   •   For the HayWired Earthquake Scenario, a magnitude 7.0 scenario earthquake on
       the Hayward fault epicenter in Oakland was simulated using HAZUS. Predictions
       from this scenario consider all losses across the Bay Area, not just those in
       Berkeley specifically.

   •   Together, these HAZUS analyses create a broad picture of the impact to Berkeley
       and the Bay Area overall from a catastrophic earthquake:

People

To address earthquakes, we obtained a data set of simulated earthquakes from Aon for

share of total property value to the rest of the two-county area. Berkeley comprises about

4% of the total property value, so we assumed Berkeley would experience about 4% of

describes the potential damage of a 6.0 quake as “light” so earthquakes below that might

not cause a material amount of economic loss. That said, our model does provide the

B.3     Wildland Urban Interface Fire

B.3.a   Description of Wildland Urban Interface Fire and Related Hazards
Fire has always been a natural part of the California and East Bay wildland ecosystem.

Fire has historically been a way to maintain forest health, control invasive species, and to

provide a rich habitat for wildlife. In Berkeley, densely-built homes and vegetation have

been introduced to hillside areas that otherwise required burning to maintain ecological

balance. For many years people have tried to prevent fire in forests and developed areas,

disrupting this balance. As a result, catastrophic fires are now occurring throughout the

Bay Area and the world.


There are two primary types of wildfire: “wildland” fire and “wildland-urban interface”

(WUI) fire. WUI fires, the primary concern in Berkeley, occur where the natural landscape

and urban-built environment meet or intermix. It is especially difficult to control a fire in

the wildland-urban interface, where homes and other infrastructure are close to and within

wildland areas.


Ignition
WUI fires can be sparked by both human activity and natural causes. Human activity

examples include power lines, sparks from campfires, fireworks, cigarettes, and arson.

The only natural cause of wildfire is lightning strikes. In a study of wildfires of the United

States from 1992 to 2015, human-caused wildfires accounted for 97% of the residential

homes threatened (within 1 km of a wildfire) and nearly a third of suppression costs.26

This study also shows that the WUI, which accounts for only a small portion of U.S. land


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                            B-56
area (10%), hosts a major portion of fires, as these fires are almost exclusively human-

started.


Spread
Low humidity and high sustained winds create the most dangerous conditions for wildfire

spread. While WUI fires can occur at any time of the year, they are especially dangerous

in fall when the landscape and vegetation are dry, and strong, hot, dry offshore winds

further desiccate vegetation and can push a fire down or up a slope with amazing speed.

Under these conditions, traditional firefighting becomes far more difficult.


Connection to climate change
Climate change is resulting in longer and drier summer conditions leading to wildfires of

greater frequency and duration. Increased drought conditions cause fuels to become

extremely dry and more fire prone. Additionally, climate change causes more frequent

bouts of extreme weather, including low humidity and high winds associated with fire

weather.


Connection to earthquakes
Earthquakes often spark fires, fueled by damaged gas or power lines. Damage to water

pipes from earthquake shaking or ground failure can limit fire suppression. This sequence

of events could grow into a firestorm, threatening neighboring jurisdictions. For

information on Fire Following Earthquakes, see the Earthquake Section.


Connection to poor air quality
Air pollution from fires both in Berkeley and throughout the region can cause eye and


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                       B-57
respiratory illnesses, and can exacerbate asthma, allergies, chronic obstructive

pulmonary disease, and other cardiovascular diseases. For more information see the

Poor Air Quality Section.


Connection to landslides and flooding
WUI fires can increase an area’s risk of landslide. When all supporting vegetation is

burned away, hillsides become destabilized and prone to erosion. The charred surface of

the earth is hard and absorbs less water. Winter rains in burned areas lead to increased

runoff, erosion and landslides in hilly areas. Erosion and land slippage subsequent to fires

can lead to temporary or permanent displacement and property damage or loss, 27 28

making erosion a secondary hazard that must be mitigated immediately after a fire.


Connection to power outage
Fire is related to power outage in two ways: preemptive power shutoff by utilities, or event-

caused outages when fires damage power infrastructure.


Pacific Gas & Electric, Berkeley’s electric utility, uses two approaches to preemptively cut

power to reduce the likelihood of fire ignition. The first, Public Safety Power Shutoffs,

involves preemptive cuts to power on specific power lines during times of high fire threat.

See the Utility Outage section to learn more. Another PG&E approach is Enhanced

Powerline Safety Settings (EPSS), which allow power lines to automatically turn off power

within one-tenth of a second when there is a hazard, such as a tree branch falling into a

power line. Some PG&E equipment in the Berkeley Hills areas have EPSS protection.

According to PG&E, in 2022 there was a 68% reduction in ignitions on EPSS-enabled

powerlines.


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           B-58
Loss of power can lead to many cascading and significant consequences, such as

impacts to vulnerable infrastructure, inability to operate fuel and water systems that

require electricity, communication and service disruptions, loss of heating or cooling, and

loss of critical functions for people who rely on power for survival. Locations of Wildland

Urban Interface Fire


Berkeley is most vulnerable to a wind-driven fire incident originating in an area adjacent

to the City’s eastern border, in land owned by UC Berkeley, the Lawrence Berkeley

National Lab, the East Bay Regional Park District, the City of Oakland, or Contra Costa

County.



B.3.b   Locations of WUI Fires and Related Hazards

Fire Hazard Severity Zones
Map 9 presents the State’s Very High and High Fire Hazard Severity Zones. The State

Fire Marshal is mandated to classify lands within State Responsibility Areas into Fire

Hazard Severity Zones (FHSZ). Fire Hazard Severity Zones fall into one of the following

classifications: Moderate, High, and Very High.


As shown in Map 9, the lands to Berkeley’s east are almost uniformly the highest hazard

classification, shown in in red and orange to the east of Berkley’s border.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-59
Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan   B-60
The WUI fire risk facing Berkeley’s wildland-urban interface area is compounded by the

area’s mountainous topography, dense fuel loads, constrained access and egress routes,

and its location, overlaid upon the Hayward Fault.


Since before the 1920s, the City of Berkeley has established and adjusted fire zones in

Berkeley. While the zones were initially established to address urban fire issues, they

have evolved to designate the City’s WUI fire hazard. These maps are now linked to the

State Fire Marshal’s work to classify fire hazards. In addition to the fire hazard map of

State lands, shown in Map 9, the State Fire Marshal is also mandated to recommend

maps of Very High Fire Hazard Severity Zones in Local Responsibility Areas, including

the City of Berkeley.


Following receipt of the State recommendation of very high fire hazard severity zones,

the City of Berkeley further interprets the hazard and has divided the city into Fire Zones

1, 2, and 3, designated in order of ascending fire risk. These zone boundaries are adopted

by the City Council, along with the Fire Code. These zones are shown in Map 10.


Map 10 shows Fire Zone 3, the Panoramic Hill area, colored in dark red. Fire Zone 2,

colored in bright red, covers the remainder of the city’s eastern hills up to the northern

border. Fire Zone 1, with yellow coloring, covers the rest of Berkeley west of the hills.


Fire Zones 2 and 3 currently include 8,603 parcels with 32,109 residents. These zones

have the strictest fire prevention standards in the City for issues such as building materials

for new structures. The City also enforces vegetation management measures in these

areas to create defensible space around homes.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                            B-61
Fire Zone 3, known as Panoramic Hill, has the greatest WUI fire vulnerability. Panoramic

Hill includes areas in both Berkeley and Oakland. In the Berkeley part, there are about

277 parcels, with 989 units in 261 buildings and 2,591 residents. The Hill’s minimal access

and egress routes, and its exposure to fault rupture further exacerbate the area’s WUI fire

risk above that of Fire Zone 2.


While much of the concern for fire is placed on the Berkeley hills (Fire Zone 2 and 3),

Berkeley’s flatlands (Fire Zone 1) are at risk as well. The flatlands are densely covered

with old wooden buildings, most not built to modern fire-resistant code. They also have a

high risk of damage in an earthquake, which could spark multiple fire ignitions, for

example, by damaging gas or electric lines.

Wildfire Hazard Ratings
New data and modeling from Tukman Geospatial prepared for East Bay Regional Parks

have characterized the relative wildfire hazard for Alameda and Contra Costa counties, 29

considering estimates from 2017-2022 for conditions including extreme fire weather

potential, ember load, suppression difficulty, vegetation (or lack thereof), past fire

ignitions, and proximity to human development and power lines.


Map 11 shows this data for Berkeley: the highest relative wildfire hazard (classes 4, 5,

and 6) is in the eastern part of the city in yellow, orange, and red. Lower relative wildfire

hazard is show in light and darker greens (classes 1, 2, and 3) in the flatlands and along

the Bay.


Although the Berkeley flatlands are presented as having the lowest wildfire hazard,

researchers were careful to classify this hazard levels as “relative.” An area with lower

relative wildfire hazard does not have no risk, it simply means that it has less risk than

other areas. Researchers also noted that this data does not account for home-to-home

ignitions common in dense urban areas. This means the analysis likely underrepresents

the wildfire hazard in Berkeley.

Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan   B-65
Structure Density
Increased structure density exacerbates wildland-urban interface fire risk. The rate of

structure-to-structure ignitions increases when there are more structures per acre.


The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) characterizes high structural

density of wildland urban interface areas as more than 2 structures per acre. 30 Map 12

shows that most areas of the Berkeley hills have at least 2 structures per acre, considered

high density and shown in dark orange. Further, areas in red, concentrated in the north

Berkeley hills and a bit around Panoramic Hill, are the highest housing density in Berkeley

with more than four structures per acre. Areas in orange have high housing density in the

Berkeley hills with greater than two structures per acre. Areas in light orange have

medium housing density with one or fewer structures per acre.


Map 12 demonstrates that the density of Berkeley’s hills areas will be a critical factor in

fire spread.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-66
Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan   B-67
Structure Separation
Another critical element that helps characterize wildland-urban interface fire risk in

Berkeley is the minimal separation between structures. Structures that are less than 25

feet apart are at extreme risk of directly spreading fire to one another, in a process called

“structure-to-structure ignition.” Fires in denser areas will have high rates of structure-to-

structure ignition and high risk of losses.


Map 13 shows the distances between structures in Fire Zones 2 and 3. Structures with a

separation distance of less than 25 feet are in red. Structures with a separation distance

of 25 to 50 feet are in orange. Structures with a separation distance of greater than 50

feet are in yellow. In Berkeley many structures are less than 25 feet apart, which places

the community in the highest risk category. 31 Map 13 demonstrates this risk with the

predominantly red coloring in Fire Zones 2 and 3. There are some orange and yellow

structures sprinkled throughout Fire Zones 2 and 3, most often on the edges of the

boundaries. The greatest patch of yellow structures is near the Claremont Canyon

Regional Preserve on the Clark Kerr Campus of the University of California – Berkeley.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                            B-68
Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan   B-69
Hazardous Vegetation
Certain plant species, including native and non-native species, have characteristics that

make them ignite readily and burn intensely contributing to wildfire risk. Characteristics

may include being biologically prone to burn due to chemical composition, being difficult

to maintain in a fire-resistant state, presenting challenges to routine maintenance, having

high surface area to volume ratio, or being prone to rapid changes in moisture content in

response to environmental conditions. While these characteristics make some plants

more fire-hazardous, all plants can burn if they are dead, poorly maintained, or drought

stressed. 32


Historically, the East Bay Hills ecosystem burned regularly. Researchers have proposed

that under indigenous land management, fires due to both natural and anthropogenic

ignitions occurred every 5-15 years. 33 Fire is this ecosystem’s natural way of clearing

dead vegetation and maintaining forest health. Many California native plant species

present in the East Bay Hills also need fire in order to reproduce.


Living in a fire-prone area means taking steps to mitigate risks while also recognizing that

it’s infeasible to remove all of our vegetation. The mere presence of a certain fire

hazardous species does not always mean it must be removed. Other factors, such as

maintenance and placement, are more important than the plant itself. For property owners

thinking about their own landscaping, it’s great to focus on California native or other

pollinator friendly plants that require little water and are easy to maintain. However, “There

are no published fire-wise or fire-resistant plant lists that are science based or peer

reviewed. Design and maintenance are more important than plant selection.” 34




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                            B-70
To protect life and property, the Berkeley Fire Department inspects all properties in the

Very High Fire Danger Severity Zone for Defensible Space, which is the buffer created

between a structure on your property and the grass, trees, shrubs, or other vegetation

that surrounds it. This may include the removal of certain vegetation within 100 feet from

any structure. These mitigation measures, along with home hardening, are the

scientifically validated actions that have the most impact on reducing the ignition potential

of homes. Failure to comply with recommendations results in citations and fines.


The City, often in collaboration with regional partners, works to remove and or clean up

the understory of hazardous trees that are likely to burn and potentially impact people

and infrastructure. For more information on these programs, review Element C: Mitigation

Strategy.


Berkeley Overnight Camps
Since the 1920s, the City of Berkeley has operated three resident camps outside of the

city limits: Echo Lake Camp, Berkeley Tuolumne Camp, and Cazadero Camp. The City

owns the property at Cazadero and holds 30-year lease agreements with the United

States Forest Service at Echo Lake Camp and Berkeley Tuolumne Camp. All three camps

face significant wildfire risk because of their locations, topography, and dense fuel loads.

Two of the three camps have experienced federally-declared fires in the last 12 years.

See the section “Fires at Berkeley’s offsite overnight camps” for details.

Cazadero Camp
