B.3.c   Extent of Wildland Urban Interface Fire and Anticipated Intensities
The extent and intensity of a WUI fire is closely tied to weather conditions and fuel

moisture. Fires that ignite under periodic conditions of “Red Flag Warning” or “Extreme

Fire Weather” may result in uncontrollable firestorms.


Red Flag Warning
The National Weather Service declares a “Red Flag Warning” when low humidity and

high winds combine to elevate fire risk. In Berkeley, “Red Flag” weather generally

presents as strong, hot, dry offshore winds (technically called “foehn” winds). These winds

are known locally as “Diablo Winds” since they come from the north or northeast in the

direction of Mount Diablo. “Diablo Winds” carry extremely dry air at high velocity, so they

can quickly desiccate vegetation and other flammable materials and can push a fire down

or up a slope with impressive speed.


Extreme Fire Weather

The Berkeley Fire Department has introduced the “Extreme Fire Weather” designation for


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-73
extremely windy and dry conditions, under which many catastrophic California wildfires

have occurred. Under Extreme Fire Weather, fires spread at extraordinary speeds and

ember storms can ignite spot fires far ahead of the main flame front. These ember storms

are also the primary cause of home ignitions.


Extreme Fire Weather forecasts are far more rare than Red Flag Warnings. Berkeley’s

last forecasted Extreme Fire Weather was for two days in 2020. In the same year,

Berkeley was forecast to have 25 days under Red Flag Warning.


Although Extreme Fire Weather is still relatively rare, these weather conditions are

associated with catastrophic fires. Exhibit 1 shows Red Flag conditions and Extreme Fire

Weather conditions. Relative humidity is on the Y axis. Sustained winds are on the X axis.

As wind speeds increase and humidity decreases, conditions change first to Red Flag

Weather and next to Extreme Fire Weather. The chart identifies five catastrophic fires

that ignited under extreme fire weather conditions (all with very low relative humidity and

most with sustained winds of 30+ mph). These fires are: the 2017 Atlas Peak Fire, the

2018 Camp (Paradise) Fire, the 2017 Thomas Fire, the 2017 Tubbs Fire, and the 1991

Tunnel Fire, which impacted Oakland and Berkeley. Based on reported conditions it is

likely that the 2023 Maui Wildfire also started under Extreme Fire Weather conditions.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-74
Exhibit 10. Graphic X: Red Flag Weather, Extreme Fire Weather, and Catastrophic
          Fires




Fires that ignite during Red Flag Weather or Extreme Fire Weather can be difficult to

contain. A WUI fire can move with devastating speed. In the 2018 North Bay Fires, the

fire burned the equivalent of a football field every second. 35


During Extreme Fire Weather, when a fire builds to this magnitude and travels with such

extreme speed and force, firefighters’ primary focus often shifts from firefighting to

supporting evacuations. This is because during this type of weather, some normally-

available firefighting tools can be ineffective or even unusable – like planes and

helicopters, which need to be grounded during high winds.


The Berkeley Hills have narrow, windy roads that make evacuation difficult, which is why

the Berkeley Fire Department recommends that people leave the hills during Extreme

Fire Weather.



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                      B-75
While the ignition risk is highest in the Berkeley Hills, a wind-driven fire under Extreme

Fire Weather can blow through the Berkeley flats, all the way to the Bay.



B.3.d   Previous Wildland Urban Interface Fire Events
Catastrophic fires have occurred in the greater Bay Area in 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021,

and 2022. Berkeley itself has significant WUI fire history, including the 2017 Grizzly Fire,

the 1991 Tunnel Fire, and the 1923 Berkeley Fire. However, there have been no federally-

declared wildfire disasters in Berkeley since the last update.


2017 Grizzly Fire
On August 5, 2017 a fire burned approximately 20 acres in the Berkeley and Oakland hills

along Grizzly Peak Boulevard just north of South Park Drive. Nine agencies responded

to the fire, with 150-200 firefighters working many hours to extinguish it. The suspected

cause of this fire was arson. 36


1991 Tunnel Fire
This fire in the Oakland/Berkeley hills started the day before as a vegetation fire in the

drought-dried hills east of Oakland. It reignited and was whipped into firestorm proportions

by 20-30 mph winds, gusting to 60 mph. In minutes, the fire spread to residential

structures. While the fire burned a greater area in Oakland, it raged across city boundaries

between Oakland and Berkeley, destroying entire neighborhoods in both cities and

remaining out of control for more than 48 hours. 25 people died in this fire, most of them

while trying to evacuate. This fire received a federal Major Disaster Declaration on

October 22, 1991.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                          B-76
1923 Berkeley Fire
The Berkeley Fire of 1923 began in the open lands of Wildcat Canyon to the northeast

and, swept by hot September Diablo winds, penetrated residential north Berkeley. The

fire burned downhill all the way to Shattuck Avenue in central Berkeley. A total of 130

built-up acres were burned, and about 4,000 people were made homeless. After this

devastating fire, officials stated that the only reason that the fire stopped spreading was

because the northeast wind stopped and the damp western wind took over. Fire officials

at the time were certain that if the northeast wind had not stopped, the buildings would

have burned all the way to the bay in Berkeley, and the fire would have devastated

Emeryville and moved south and west into Oakland. 37


The fire destroyed 584 structures, including homes, apartments, fraternities and

sororities, a church, a fire station and a library. Wood shake roofs are cited as a large

contributing factor in the spread of this fire.


Map 14 depicts in red the area burned by the 1923 fire, which stretches from East Bay

Regional Parks to Shattuck Avenue. It also overlays the Diablo wind pattern indicated by

black arrows to demonstrate how the fire could have spread into the Berkeley flatlands

even more, if the wind direction had not changed. According to San Francisco Fire

Department records, San Francisco sent engine companies to respond, reporting that

one of the San Francisco engine companies “helped control a fire at the municipal dumps

at the foot of Cedar Street.”38 This indicates that there was a fire on the western edge of

the City, where Cedar meets the waterfront (shown with a dot on Map 14). It is possible

that this dump fire was a concurrent but entirely unrelated event. However, there is a

considerable likelihood that the fire at the Berkeley dump was ignited by embercast

Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-77
traveling from the main fire front, which was approximately 2 miles away. This

phenomenon has precedent in more recent fires, such as the 2017 Tubbs Fire, during

which embers traveled over a mile from the main front. Although wildfire is generally

thought of as a problem limited to the Berkeley hills, this historical anecdote, alongside

these more recent experiences, indicate the wildfire vulnerability of Berkeley’s flats.

Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan   B-79
Fires at Berkeley’s offsite overnight camps
   •    Berkeley Tuolumne Camp, located in Tuolumne County just outside of Yosemite
        National Park, was destroyed by the Rim Fire in August 2013. Since that time, the
        City has reconstructed the Camp. The Berkeley Fire Department WUI Division
        visited the Camp in 2023, mapping the area in order to plan future mitigation
        projects. Efforts like this will help to make the Camp more protected and defensible
        in the event of another wildfire.

   •    The Caldor Fire in August 2021 started 32 miles away from Echo Lake Camp, in
        El Dorado County in the El Dorado National Forest. On August 30, the front lines
        of the Caldor Fire reached Camp. The Berkeley Fire Department deployed its
        firefighters to defend the camp. For several days they engaged in active
        firefighting, at one point being forced to retreat from Camp due to the intensity of
        the fire approaching the property. Thankfully, firefighters were able to return to
        defend Camp and continued to engage in active firefighting until the threat had
        passed. While no Camp structures were significantly damaged, several
        neighboring private cabins less than 100 yards away were destroyed, and areas
        of the surrounding forest were burned. The fire burned on all sides of Camp, up to
        within feet of the Ridge Cabins, Recreation Lodge, and Camp Office, but when
        standing in the center of Camp, one might not know that a fire had threatened the
        property. Since the fire, City staff have assessed the status of trees and structures
        on the 15-acre property.

B.3.e   Probability of Future Events
Fire is a natural part of the California and East Bay wildland ecosystem, and they will

continue to occur in the future. Calculating the probability of a future needs to consider

both the likelihood of ignition and the likelihood of spread.


Likelihood of ignition
Historically and more recently, most fire ignitions have been due to human activity and

electrical equipment. According to Cal Fire, of the top 20 most destructive California

wildfires, three had “human related” causes, five were caused by powerlines, and three

had electrical causes. 39




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           B-80
Likelihood of spread
A significant WUI fire is one that will spread out of control. The likelihood of fire spread

primarily relates to three factors: weather, fuel moisture, and the built environment.


Weather

A significant WUI fire is most likely to occur in Berkeley under Extreme Fire Weather

conditions. In 2020, Berkeley was forecast to have 25 days under Red Flag Warning, with

the Berkeley Fire Department declaring two of those forecasted days to qualify as

Extreme Fire Weather. 2021, 2022, and 2023 were uncharacteristically mild, with one or

zero Red Flag Warning days. Despite these mild years, we know that Berkeley will

experience more fire weather in the years to come.


Climate change also creates more volatile weather patterns, extending fire season and

with it the number of days Berkeley is in Red Flag Warning or Extreme Fire Weather

status.


Vegetative Fuel Moisture

The moisture content of live and dead vegetation is not in itself a weather element. It is a

product, however, of the cumulative effects of past and present weather events and must

be considered in evaluating the effects of current or future weather on fire potential. Fuel

moisture content limits fire propagation. When moisture content is high, fires are difficult

to ignite, and burn poorly if at all. With little moisture in the fuel, fires start easily, and wind

and other driving forces may cause rapid and intense fire spread.


Climate change, which is ongoing, increases drought, reducing the moisture of vegetation

and increasing its flammability.


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                                  B-81
Built Environment

Fire spreads through manmade structures as well as vegetation. According to NIST,

“structures represent a significant density of fuels that impact fire spread and, in many

cases, directly contribute to the ignition of additional structures, propagating fire

throughout the community.” The two primary fuel loads in the Berkeley hills are vegetation

and the homes themselves. The “Locations of Wildland Urban Interface Fire” section

above outlines how the density and close proximity of structures in the WUI area increase

the likelihood of fire spread.


Most Berkeley homes were constructed prior to modern home hardening (fire resistive)

codes were put in place, leaving homes in this area vulnerable to ignition from embers,

direct flame impingement, or radiant or convective heat. Additionally, the structures’

density and minimal separation distance, and proximity to dense vegetation and wooden

fences will increase the rate of fire spread through the area. See “Location of Wildland

Urban Interface Fire” for details.



B.3.f   Vulnerabilities
The entire City is vulnerable to WUI fires, as described in the historical outline of the 1923

fire. This section focuses on Berkeley’s areas of highest fire risk: Fire Zones 2 and 3, the

hills areas.


People
32,109 number of people live in Berkeley Fire Zones 2 and 3. Wind driven, fast-moving

fires are particularly dangerous for people, resulting in injuries and deaths from burns and

smoke inhalation.


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                            B-82
Fires also contribute to poor air quality, which can impact people locally and far away,

especially sensitive groups, including infants, young children, people with respiratory

illnesses, and people who live or work outside.


Evacuation

All of the Berkeley Hills are marked by windy, narrow roads, which makes evacuation

difficult. History demonstrates that residents in the path of a major fire will attempt to leave

the area via private vehicles crammed with personal belongings. When there is a

catastrophic fire or earthquake, emergency access and egress on overwhelmed

residential roadways will be highly constrained. People trying to leave a dangerous

condition will hinder emergency personnel trying to address it or trying to reach others

who need help to leave.


Because of these challenges, the Berkeley Fire Department recommends that people

leave the hills ahead of Extreme Fire Weather. Evacuation is particularly challenging for

people with disabilities, people with access and functional needs, and seniors.


Of particular concern is Panoramic Hill. Panoramic Way is the only paved road into and

out of this neighborhood. It forms a single loop, 12-18’ wide, that begins and ends just

south of Memorial Stadium. The street’s narrow width and hairpin turns make it barely

accessible to fire apparatus, which are required to perform three-point-turns to ascend

the Hill. Panoramic Way’s narrow width also means that at many points the road is not

wide enough to allow vehicles to pass one another. Under normal conditions, vehicles

responding to medical emergencies have been impeded by commercial vehicles, trash

collection trucks, and illegally-parked personal vehicles. Further, an earthquake-induced



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                              B-83
landslide impacting Panoramic Way could also block any vehicles from entering or leaving

the area. Panoramic Way could also block any vehicles from entering or leaving the area.


Structures
There are 8,603 parcels in Berkeley Fire Zones 2 and 3. A wildfire will quickly threaten

homes and burn infrastructure. The intense heat associated with a firestorm can also

deteriorate concrete and asphalt pavement, curbs, sidewalks, and drainage structures.


The “Locations of Wildland Urban Interface Fire” section above outlines how the density

and close proximity of structures in the WUI area increase the vulnerability of structures

in the area.


Map 15 presents the wildfire risk to structures in the Berkeley hills. It divides the area into

10-acre hexagon shapes, and ranks the risk to structures for each shape. Areas with high

Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan   B-85
Systems
Many of the systems that Berkeley residents, visitors, businesses, institutions, and other

partners rely on for day-to-day life are vulnerable to fire. The heat associated with fire can

destroy or damage infrastructure that our utility, transportation, and communication

systems rely on to operate. This includes aboveground wiring for electricity, telephone

and cable lines that allow for communications, and poles for lights and street signals.


Fire can also damage and contaminate water systems, threatening public health and

drinking water supplies.


Natural, historical, and culture assets
The City of Berkeley has a variety of natural, historical, and cultural assets spread

throughout all Fire Zones. Fire Zone 1 has restaurants, arts and culture and organizations,

community organizations, and other businesses that serve the Berkeley community. Fire

Zone 3, the Panoramic Hill area, includes one of Berkeley’s most architecturally-

significant residential districts, which is listed in the National Register of Historic Places

because of its association with the Arts and Crafts movement.


Fire Zone 3 includes a number of City parks, playgrounds and recreational facilities. The

East Bay Regional Parks immediately to Berkeley’s east provide a variety of recreational

activities for residents and visitors to enjoy.


Situated outside the City of Berkeley boundaries, the City’s overnight camps also provide

the Berkeley community with a wide breadth of outdoor opportunities in some of

California’s most beautiful natural settings.

B.3.g   Potential Impacts and Losses
Climate change is expected to increase the potential impacts and losses associated with

wildland-urban interface fire. Expected changes in population patterns potentially

increase impacts and losses associated with wildland-urban interface fire. As the

population steadily increases, more people are exposed to the wildfire risk and the

demands on the evacuation infrastructure. Changes in land use and development may

potentially increase impacts and losses. New state laws are mandating increased density

throughout the city, including in the eastern hills, which are more exposed to wildland-

urban interface fire.


Previous wildfires in Berkeley provide some lessons on what the potential impacts and

losses might be from a future event.


Impacts to human life
Twenty-five people died in the 1991 Tunnel Fire. Fortunately, there were no deaths in the

1923 Fire, Grizzly Fire, or at the Berkeley overnight camps during the Caldor Fire and

Rim Fire. However, a catastrophic WUI fire occurring in Berkeley in the present day,

considering Berkeley’s density of structures and considerable evacuation challenges, is

more likely to see death tolls comparable to catastrophic fires like the 2018 Camp Fire,

with 85 civilian deaths, and the 2023 Maui Fire, during which 101 people died.


Fires also have other devastating human impacts. For example, the 1923 Berkeley Fire

made over 4,000 people homeless. Berkeley’s population has more than doubled since

1923, and the Bay Area is now in a housing crisis. This means that a repeat of the 1923

fire in the present day would destroy the homes of many more people, and also leave


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                       B-87
them without alternate local housing options.


Impacts to infrastructure
The 1923 fire was the most extensive WUI fire to impact Berkeley in recent history. This

plan calculates losses that would occur if that fire were to recur today. A repeat of this fire

would cause significantly more damage in Berkeley than the 1991 Tunnel fire.


The 1923 Berkeley Fire started in Wildcat Canyon to the northeast of the city and burned

south and west down to Shattuck Avenue, stopping at the edge of UC Berkeley. Map 15

shows the area burned by this fire. The California Railroad Commission documented the

burned area in 1923, three months after the fire. By superimposing this historical map

onto the current day building data in Berkeley using the City’s Geographic Information

System, we find that, today, there are 1,858 buildings located in the footprint of the 1923

fire. These structures include single-family homes, multi-family residences (many of which

house UC Berkeley students), stores, restaurants, and offices central to downtown

Berkeley.


If a fire occurred today that burned the same area, the loss to structures would be in the

billions of dollars. 41 Efforts to stabilize hillsides after the fire to prevent massive landslides

would also add costs.


While the financial losses from this scenario are staggering, the social impacts of such a

fire would be devastating as well. Thousands of families would be homeless following

such an event, losing all of their possessions. Many more would need short-term shelter

while the fire was burning, and in the immediate aftermath. Residents and firefighters




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                                 B-88
could be killed, especially in difficult-to-access areas. Local, independent businesses

might disappear forever. A large portion of the city would need to be entirely rebuilt. In

short, the entire face of Berkeley would be completely changed.

B.4     Extreme Heat

B.4.a   Description of Extreme Heat and Connection to Other Hazards
According to Cal-Adapt, California’s database of climate information, multiple factors

contribute to the extreme heat hazard:


Extreme heat days: An extreme heat day is when temperatures reach the 98th percentile

of historic maximum temperature. In Berkeley, an extreme heat day is a day above 88.3

degrees Fahrenheit (F).


Warm nights: A warm night in Berkeley is considered to be one that does not cool below

61.7 degrees F. Warm nights can increase health risks significantly, as people do not

have the ability to cool down and recover.


Heat wave: When there are five or more days of extreme heat.


Duration of heat wave: Longer heat waves have proportionally more negative impacts


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-91
than shorter heat waves.


Extreme heat during unexpected times of year: When extreme heat occurs outside of

historically hotter months.


Urban heat island effect
Extreme heat events can be further exacerbated by the urban heat island (UHI) effect,

through which densely-built cities like Berkeley experience higher temperatures in

comparison to surrounding more rural areas.


Factors contributing to the UHI effect include:


   •   A relative lack of vegetation;

   •   Reduced air flow;

   •   An abundance of hard, dark surfaces—such as buildings, streets, cars and
       sidewalks— which absorb heat rather than reflect it. These surfaces also slowly
       release that absorbed heat throughout the night, contributing to warmer nighttime
       temperatures.

The UHI effect can also worsen air quality (particularly ground-level ozone) in urban

environments. 42 The UHI effect increases heat-related illnesses and fatalities, particularly

after two to three days of extreme heat. 43


Vegetation helps mitigate the UHI effect through evaporative cooling. This makes urban

tree cover, parks, and green roofs essential tools to combatting the UHI effect. Green

roofs, cool roofs, and cool pavements (light-colored materials that reflect, rather than

absorb, solar energy) reduce the UHI effect, and can also lower cooling loads in buildings.

Urban vegetation and increased urban tree cover reduce temperatures and provide


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           B-92
benefits such as improved air quality and needed shade (for buildings and people) during

heat events.


Connection to climate change
Due to climate change, projections indicate that the number of extreme heat days, warm

nights, and heat waves will increase exponentially in the next few decades. In addition to

this increased frequency and duration, heat waves are also expected to occur in months

not typically associated with extreme heat.


Connection to wildland-urban interface fire
While hot temperatures do not specifically start fires, they are associated with decreased

moisture in vegetation, increasing its flammability and the length and severity of fire

season. 44 Warming temperatures combined with increased development in the wildland-

urban interface are projected to increase fire risk in most of the Bay Area.


Connection to poor air quality
While naturally-occurring ozone that exists higher in the Earth’s atmosphere is beneficial

to the climate, ground-level ozone can be extremely harmful to human health. Extreme

heat can lead to the formation of ground-level ozone when emissions from industrial

facilities, power utilities, cars, trucks and other sources chemically react in the presence

of heat and sunlight. Ground-level ozone contributes to smog and other secondary air

pollutants.


Extreme heat can also cause stagnant air conditions, causing the smog to stay low longer,

and increase community exposure. 45 Community reactions to extreme heat – including


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                          B-93
use of cars for transport and use of cooling systems in buildings – can compound the

already heightened creation of ozone. For this reason, the availability of non-polluting

modes of transportation and ultra-efficient building systems can mitigate both the direct

impacts of the heat on the community and the worsened air quality.


Exposure to increased ozone concentrations is associated with pneumonia, asthma,

allergic rhinitis, and other respiratory diseases, as well as premature death. Elderly

people, infants, and children are particularly susceptible. 46


Connection to utility disruption
Increased power demand during hot weather and extreme heat events can overload

electrical equipment, causing power outages. The local utility company, PG&E may also

initiate a public safety power shutoff during these high heat events in areas that have high

fire risk to prevent wildfires. Outages can also occur when circuit breakers or other

protective equipment shuts off the flow of power in order to prevent damage to the

electrical system.



B.4.b   Location of extreme heat
Two important factors influence how hot it is in certain parts of Berkeley: the urban heat

island effect and thermal belting.


Urban heat island effect
The urban heat island effect often makes temperatures hotter in the urban, more dense

parts of a city. To visualize what parts of Berkeley might more likely suffer from the urban

heat island effect, Map 16 shows the tree coverage throughout Berkeley. Urban tree



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                          B-94
canopy directly reduces surface and air temperatures through shading and absorption,

combating the urban heat island effect. In addition, this shading can reduce cooling loads

in buildings and provide shade for individuals as well. Trees also improve air quality that

often worsens during extreme heat. A dense tree canopy can result in fewer heat-related

emergencies. 47


In Berkeley, census tracts have between 4% and 48% tree coverage. Map 16 shows the

current percentage of tree coverage for each census tract in Berkeley. Table 3 below

Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                            B-95
Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan   B-96
Thermal belting
Although the Berkeley hills have a greater tree canopy, temperatures are often higher

there than in the rest of the city, due to a phenomenon known as thermal belting. Thermal

belting occurs in areas where there is a hillside and a valley below. Heat is absorbed by

the ground during the day, and the heat energy radiates up from the soil at night. As the

warm air rises, the radiation of the heat causes the air closest to the ground to cool. Since

cold air is heavier than warm air, cooler air sinks down the hillside into the valley. As the

cooler air fills the valley, the warm air heads upwards. This warm air becomes trapped on

the hilltop and is referred to as a thermal belt. For Berkeley, this means that during

extreme heat events, the Berkeley hills are likely to be hotter at night than the rest of the

city.


Map 17 illustrates the thermal belting phenomenon in Berkeley during a heat wave in

September 2022. The graphic is taken from Weather Underground website’s

Wundermap, which displays temperatures and wind directions at citizen weather

monitoring stations throughout Berkeley.


Map 17 shows temperature differentials between the Berkeley hills, flats, and coast at

11:30 pm at night on Monday, September 5, 2022. The Berkeley hills have temperature

readings in the upper 80s and 90s while the flats and waterfront have temperatures in the

60s and 70s F. In some cases, temperature differentials are more than 20 degrees F in a

distance of ten city blocks.

Forecasting Heat Risk
The National Weather Service HeatRisk Prototype is a new tool that forecasts risk of heat-

related impacts in a given day for a given area. In forecasting risk, the HeatRisk tool

considers temperature, how unusual the heat is for the time of year, and the duration of

the heat, including daytime and nighttime temperatures. The index supplements official

National Weather Service heat information to provide risk guidance for decision-makers

and heat sensitive populations who needs to take actions at lower levels.

B.4.d     Previous Extreme Heat Events
Berkeley has experienced extreme heat events regularly, and has experienced extreme

heat each year from 2019 through 2023. However, there have been no federally-declared

extreme heat disasters in Berkeley since the last update. The National Oceanic

Atmospheric Administration Storm Database describes some of the most notable events:


      •   In July 2006, there were five consecutive days with temperatures above 110 F in
          the Bay Area, and approximately 75 heat-related deaths during this period. The
          last comparable extreme heat event prior to this 2006 event occurred for two days
          in 1972. 48

      •   In August 2017, the Bay Area experienced record-setting high temperatures. 49 A
          Berkeley weather station on the University of California, Berkeley campus near
          Hearst and Euclid Avenues reported a temperature of 108.5 F. 50 The National
          Weather Service issued an excessive heat warning that lasted five days for the
          Bay Area. During this time there were six heat-related deaths in nearby San
          Francisco and San Mateo Counties.

Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                             B-101
   •    In June 2019, a combination of high pressure and strong offshore flow resulted in
        an early season heat wave across the Bay Area. Multiple daily records were
        broken across the region and multiple power outages were reported due to the
        heat. Approximately 26,000 people across the region lost power, followed by an
        additional 30,000 on the following day. Three fatalities were reported in the region.

   •    From August 14-19, 2020, a prolonged and oppressive heat wave swept the
        Central Coast and Bay Area for almost a week, with widespread record-breaking
        temperatures observed across the region. Multiple days of triple-digit afternoon
        highs were recorded inland with some coastal locations even reaching the mid-
        90s. Several days of hot and dry weather further dried vegetation in the area,
        increasing fire danger. During this event, a surge of monsoonal and tropical
        moisture from a former Tropical Storm moved northward with sufficient instability
        to generate multiple high-based and dry thunderstorms that produced several
        thousand lightning strikes over the Greater Bay Area. Many locations saw wind
        gusts of 40-50 miles per hour (mph) with isolated areas seeing gusts of 60-75 mph.
        This prompted the San Francisco Bay Area forecast office to issue a rare severe
        thunderstorm warning. At the same time, all of the wildfires burning simultaneously
        across the state gave the Bay Area the worst air quality in the world.

   •    In September 2020, a large area of high pressure over the west brought excessive
        heat and dry conditions to the region. Numerous record high temperatures were
        broken, including 13 broken records on Sunday September 6th alone.
        Temperatures reached 110 degrees F across the interior, with 90s along the coast
        to start the weekend, and even reaching 100 degrees in San Francisco on Sunday.
        Once the ridge began to break down towards the end of the weekend, offshore
        winds increased flaring up some of the wildfires that were ignited during August's
        lightning storm. These winds also enabled smoke from various wildfires across the
        state to blanket much of the Bay Area. The skies were tinted orange and red with
        ash accumulating for many locations.

   •    In July 2021, strong high pressure building over the region in early to mid-July
        brought warm to hot temperatures across the interior. Daytime highs rose into the
        100s with locations across the East Bay up to 110 degrees between July 9-11.
        Overnight lows remained warm, particularly across higher elevations where
        temperatures were still in the 70s and 80s in the early mornings. Additionally,
        prolonged dry conditions resulted in near record dry fuels for July. This along with
        breezy afternoon winds prompted the Diablo Fire in Contra Costa County.

B.4.f   Vulnerabilities

People
Across California, the highest risk of heat-related illness occurs in the typically cooler

regions found in coastal areas like Berkeley. Vulnerability is increased for these

communities as they are relatively unaccustomed to extreme heat. As a result, they are

less acclimatized or potentially less aware of preventative behavior and are less likely to

have air conditioning or cooling in their homes. 52


Public health impacts associated with extreme heat events include premature death,

cardiovascular stress and failure, and heat-related illnesses such as heat stroke, heat

exhaustion, and kidney stones. 53 Studies have also found links between rising

temperatures and a range of mental health issues including mental fatigue, aggression,



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                          B-103
and even higher rates of suicide. 54


People with disabilities, people with access and functional needs, people with chronic

diseases, the elderly, and children under five years old are the most at risk to heat-related

illnesses. 55 People working outdoors and unhoused populations are also more exposed

and at risk. Research also indicates that communities of color, and the poor suffer more

during extreme heat events because of lack of access to common heat adaptation

strategies, such as tree canopy for shading, air conditioning and insulation in buildings,

or car ownership to travel to public cooling centers that allow them to escape the heat. 56


These increased vulnerabilities to heat events among lower-income communities are

illustrated using the University of California, Los Angeles Heat Maps Tool57. The tool

examines excess emergency room visits during heat events based on location.

As extreme heat becomes more frequent and severe, Berkeley buildings, including City

facilities, will need to add cooling capacity. This effort will need to be done strategically

over the coming decades to find building upgrade solutions that are clean, efficient, and

functional during electrical grid outages. For existing buildings and new construction,

consideration will be given to heat pump technology, a highly-efficient electric HVAC

system (up to 400% efficient 58 in energy efficient buildings) with both heating and cooling



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                          B-108
capabilities. Cooling approaches will also include natural ventilation and passive cooling

techniques whenever possible, such as shading, orientation, and building envelope.


Strategic planning is also needed to ensure the readiness of critical City facilities during

grid failure. The ability for these facilities to island off of the grid and rely on clean backup

energy during a power outage would improve the City’s energy assurance during extreme

heat events. The City is currently partnering with Ava Community Energy (its local

community choice aggregator and electricity provider) to design and install solar panels

and backup batteries at some critical municipal facilities to advance this energy assurance

goal.


Systems
High temperatures can damage critical infrastructure, including transportation systems.

During a Fall 2017 extreme heat event, BART and Caltrain operated trains at reduced

speeds in order to avoid damage to the tracks. 59 Unreliable public transit during extreme

heat could cause more people to drive, adding to the heat and worsening air quality.

Extreme heat events also create needs for additional infrastructure maintenance,

particularly for roadways where heat can contribute to deformation or premature failure. 60


Extreme heat can also lead to power outages. Due to Berkeley’s historically mild climate,

many buildings are not equipped with efficient cooling systems, and therefore rely on

inefficient and sometimes ineffective methods of indoor cooling, such as window air

conditioning units. This increases electricity demands which in turn can overwhelm the

power grid, causing power outages when people need their cooling devices the most.

Power outages can lead to many cascading and significant consequences including


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                              B-109
impacts to electrically powered fuel and water systems as well as communication

infrastructure. The loss of power can also be devastating for people with disabilities who

rely on electricity to power medical devices.” The Utility Disruption section of this plan has

more information about the impacts of power outages.


Natural, historic, and cultural resources
Berkeley’s tree canopy provides some measure of protection during extreme heat events

but also is vulnerable to extreme heat. Sudden limb failure is a commonly-noted

phenomenon in trees during extreme heat events. The precise mechanism leading to limb

failure is not well understood, but poses hazards to trees, as well as people trying to

escape the heat by sitting in their shade.


Berkeley and its immediate surrounding cities have bodies of water that are usually places

to cool down and seek relief from the heat. Locations such as Lake Anza or the Bay are

prime examples. However, extreme heat can cause harmful algae to bloom when water

temperature is warmer than usual. When this kind of algae is present, community

members cannot enjoy or seek relief in the water.


Activities that have value
As noted earlier, studies have shown that extreme heat causes mental fatigue and

aggression. These feelings and behaviors can impact family and social dynamics, work

productivity, and participation in community events and outdoor activities. Researchers

have also linked high heat to decreased academic performance, with lower-income, older,

and other marginalized populations being disproportionately impacted. 61




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           B-110
B.4.g   Potential Impacts and Losses
According to California Climate Change Center, by mid-century with climate change,

extreme heat in urban centers could cause two to three times more heat-related deaths

than occur today. 62 Population patterns in Berkeley could also increase the potential

impacts. The senior population has grown steadily in Berkeley as well as the population

experiencing homelessness. These groups suffer greater impacts of extreme heat.

Development has the potential to decrease the impacts of extreme heat, as new buildings

are designed to mitigate heat and energy use.


A study of the 2006 heat wave in California estimated excess statewide healthcare costs

of $120 - $175 million, lost productivity costs nearing $10 million, and the societal cost of

over 650 premature deaths, which exceeded $5 billion. 63 Unfortunately, little useful

research exists on economic impacts of high heat at the local level – research focuses on

aggregated losses at the national or international level.

B.5     Poor Air Quality

B.5.a   Description of Poor Air Quality and Related Hazards
Poor air quality is a growing concern in Berkeley and in California. According to the

California Air Resources Board, 90% of Californians breathe unhealthy levels of outdoor

air during some parts of the year. The Bay Area Air Quality Management District

(BAAQMD) offers continuous monitoring for 11 pollutants, set by state and federal

standards to protect the health and climate. More information about those 11 pollutants

and how they compare to federal or state standards is available on the BAAQMD website.


In the Bay Area, the air pollutants of greatest concern include ozone, particulate matter,

and toxic air contaminants.


   •    Ozone is formed in the atmosphere through chemical reactions between pollutants
        emitted from vehicles, factories and other industrial sources, fossil fuels,
        combustion, consumer products, evaporation of paints, and many other sources.
        Ozone is the main ingredient in summertime smog.

   •    Particulate matter is composed of an assortment of tiny airborne particles that vary
        in size and mass (ultrafine, fine, and coarse), physical state (solid or liquid),
        chemical composition, toxicity, and how they behave in the atmosphere. These
        particles originate from a variety of manmade and natural sources, including fossil
        fuel combustion, refining crude oil, residential wood burning and cooking, wildfires,
        volcanoes, sea salt, and dust. Residential wood burning is the largest source of
        particulate matter in the Bay Area during the winter.

   •    Toxic Air Contaminants are generally present in very small amounts in the air, but
        are extremely hazardous to human health. In the Bay Area, the toxic air
        contaminant of greatest overall concern is exhaust from diesel engines.


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                          B-114
Poor air quality is a major public health concern. Poor air quality can irritate the eyes,

nose, and throat, cause shortness of breath, aggravate asthma and other respiratory

conditions, and affect the heart and cardiovascular system. Poor air quality can last for a

few hours or a few weeks, depending on its source. It can also be a chronic issue, for

example in places near industry or highways. The air quality can also change quickly due

to weather conditions, such as rain or wind.


Connection to climate change
According to the National Climate Assessment, the global warming observed over the

industrial era is unequivocally caused by greenhouse gas emissions from human

activities—primarily burning fossil fuels. Climate change will affect human health by

increasing air pollution, affecting ozone and/or particulate matter. Scientists are also

predicting that climate change will contribute to longer, hotter, and drier fire seasons,

which will increase the risk of severe wildfires and exposures to wildfire smoke. While

climate change can harm everyone’s health, its impacts exacerbate long-standing

disparities that result in inequitable health outcomes for historically marginalized people,

including people of color, Indigenous Peoples, low-income communities, and sexual and

gender minorities, as well as older adults, people with disabilities or chronic diseases,

outdoor workers, and children.


Connection to extreme heat
As the world’s climate has shifted toward warmer conditions, the frequency and intensity

of extreme cold events have declined over much of the US, while the frequency, intensity,

and duration of extreme heat have increased. Extreme heat can lead to negative health



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-115
risks including heat-related illness and death. People who regularly struggle to afford

energy bills—such as low-income, and older fixed-income households and communities

of color—are especially vulnerable to more intense extreme heat events and associated

health risks, particularly if they live in homes with poor insulation and inefficient cooling

systems.



B.5.b   Location of Poor Air Quality
Poor air quality can impact all of Berkeley, for those both indoors and outdoors. South

and west Berkeley are generally more exposed to everyday poor air quality from outdoor

pollutants due to the areas’ proximity to the train, highways, and industrial facilities.


The California Communities Environmental Health Screening Tool CalEnviroScreen is a

screening methodology that can be used to help identify California communities that are

disproportionately burdened by multiple sources of pollution. Map 20 shows the

CalEnviroScreen percentile for Berkeley. Higher percentiles indicate that an area

experiences more pollution burden. Generally, the everyday pollution is higher in west

Berkeley and lower in the eastern areas of the city. Areas in west and south Berkeley

carry higher pollution burdens with percentiles in the 50s, 60s, and 70s, shown in the

shades of orange color. The Berkeley hills show percentiles of 10s, 20s, and 30s. The

eastern portion of the Berkeley flats shows percentiles in the 40s.

consumer products, gas appliances, building materials, smoking, furniture, and other

household materials. Given that most people spend more time indoors than outside, the

quality of indoor air is important. Indoor air quality monitors and air filtration systems are

on the market, but are expensive.

B.5.d   Previous Poor Air Quality Events
Everyone in Berkeley can be impacted by poor air quality – some neighborhoods

experience moderate or unhealthy air quality on a regular basis due to proximity to various

sources of pollutants like highways and industry, and there have also been several

extreme examples of poor air quality that impacted the entire City due to nearby wildfires.


In September and October of 2017, the wildfires in North Bay sent smoke to Berkeley,

causing unhealthy air for sensitive groups. In November 2018, smoke from the Camp Fire

brought very unhealthy air quality. Schools were cancelled, and there were calls for the

entire population to avoid outdoor activities for multiple days. In October 2019, smoke

from the Kincade Fire brought unhealthy air to Berkeley for a few days. In September and

Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                               B-121
October of 2020, multiple northern California wildfires brought very unhealthy air to the

Bay Area for over twenty consecutive days. In August and September 2021, smoke from

northern California wildfires created moderate air quality in the Bay Area for a few days.

In December 2022, the Bay Area had unhealthy air mostly due to local residential wood

burning and active wildfires in the state.


There have been no federally-declared poor air quality disasters in Berkeley since the last

update.

forecasted to be unhealthy and to share information on ways to reduce air pollution. Since

B.5.f   Vulnerabilities

People
Poor air quality creates negative health impacts for everyone, including irritation of the

eyes, nose, and throat, coughing, chest tightness, shortness of breath, fatigue, and

headaches. Poor air quality can also exacerbate other respiratory problems like asthma.

According to the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), some studies

have shown a link between poor air quality and severe cardiovascular issues. Groups

most at risk during poor air quality events include the elderly, children, infants, pregnant

women, people with preexisting conditions, people who work or live outdoors, and people

who live in neighborhoods that have been historically overburdened by pollution and other

environmental contaminants, such as west and south Berkeley.


Structures
The effect of air pollution on physical structures may be seen in terms of discoloration,

material loss, structural failing and soiling. The smell and residue of smoke can also

permeate homes, which may cause a financial burden to clean or replace items.


Natural, historic, and cultural resources
According to the EPA, there is a robust body of research that links the negative impacts

that air pollution can have on natural ecosystems. Pollutants can put excess levels of

acids into bodies of water, damage soils, and harm plants, trees, and other wildlife.


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           B-123
Berkeley is lucky to be in an area of rich environmental diversity, including close proximity

to regional parks. All of these natural resources can suffer due to poor air quality.


Activities that have value to the community
Berkeley provides great access to a wide variety of outdoor activities, including parks,

recreation facilities, commerce, outdoor dining, and other unique experiences. These

activities can be unsafe during poor air quality events, causing residents and visitors to

miss out on the opportunity to visit and enjoy these special parts of Berkeley. The Parks,

Recreation, and Waterfront Department hosts a number of activities for children and

families throughout the year. During the COVID-19 emergency, when there were poor air

quality days, activities had to be cancelled as it was unsafe to have children indoors or

outdoors. Additionally, businesses that rely on outdoor activities experience financial

losses during these events.



B.5.g   Potential Impacts and Losses
The biggest impacts related to poor air quality are those on human health. Southerland

et al., published a study in 2021 66 on the harmful impacts of pollution in the Bay Area.

According to these estimates, more than 2,500 people die and 5,200 children develop

asthma every year due to traffic-related air pollution exposure in the Bay Area.


Map 22 from the Environmental Defense Fund shows the percentage of new childhood

asthma caused by air pollution in the East Bay. Most of Berkeley is in dark orange

category, meaning over 40 percent of new asthma cases in Berkeley are attributable to

air pollution. Some pockets of the Berkeley flats near major intersections rise to fifty

percent. The eastern edges of Berkeley in the peaks of the hills drop to thirty percent.


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           B-124
Until recently, most of the research on the health impacts of air pollution were not wildfire-

specific. Increased fire activity has led to an uptick in published research on health

outcomes. A growing body of scientific evidence links wildfire smoke exposure to various

adverse health effects. It is often assumed that while most healthy people will recover

from short-term exposure to wildfire smoke, others might experience more severe

symptoms, especially people with preexisting medical conditions or other factors, like

inadequate housing or lack of access to health care. 67




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           B-125
B.6     High Wind

B.6.a   Description of High Wind
According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), wind is air in

motion, traveling between areas of high pressure to areas of low pressure. Bigger

differences in air pressure create strong winds. High- and low-pressure systems are

created by ascending and descending air, caused most often by differences in

temperature. Wind is described using its horizontal speed and the direction it is coming

from.


National Weather Service Definitions
The National Weather Service (NWS) defines “high winds” as:


   •    Sustained wind speeds of 40 miles per hour (mph) or greater lasting for one hour
        or longer, or

   •    Wind gusts of 58 mph or greater for any duration.

Sustained wind speed is different than a wind gust. A wind gust is a brief increase in the

wind speed typically around 20-30 seconds.


The NWS issues a wind advisory when there are sustained winds of 31 to 39 mph, or

gusts of 46 to 57 mph.


Seasonality of High Wind
In Berkeley, high wind events are typically associated with the seasons.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                       B-126
   •   In the winter, high winds come with weather systems and cold fronts, generally
       between November through March.

   •   In the summer, temperature and pressure differences between the Pacific Ocean
       and the interior valleys to Berkeley’s east create stronger afternoon and evening
       winds coming from the west.

   •   Primarily in the fall, dry offshore foehn winds, known as the “Diablo Winds,” occur.
       Diablo Winds are associated with fire weather.

Connection to climate change
Climate change creates more intense and variable weather conditions (both wet and dry),

including high wind.


Connection to wildland urban interface fire
Diablo winds can create significant fire danger. Diablo winds are dry and fast. Fires that

ignites when Diablo winds are blowing will spread more quickly. See the Wildland Urban

Interface Fire Section of this plan for details.


Connection to utility disruption
High wind events can lead to downed trees and/or power lines, causing power disruption.

Sometimes when high wind events coincide with extreme heat and dry conditions, in

some cases the local utility PG&E may initiate a public safety power shutoff (PSPS) event,

temporarily shutting of power in areas of high fire risk to prevent wildfires. Similarly,

Enhanced Powerline Safety Settings (EPSS) allow PG&E power lines to automatically

turn off power within one-tenth of s second. This can happen when there’s a hazard, like

a tree branch falling into a power line, which can cause a fire. These settings are in high-

fire risk and surrounding areas.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-127
B.6.b   Location of High Wind
The location and elevation allow high winds to be felt throughout Berkeley. The westerly

wind carries oceanic moisture toward the city, and as the wind flow hits the Berkeley Hills,

it splits, producing northward and southward winds. The hot and dry Diablo Winds,

particularly common in the spring and fall, affects the Berkeley Hills area more, while the

cold storms, more common in the winter, increase wind speeds in the flats.



B.6.c   Extent of High Wind and Anticipated Intensities

Beaufort Wind Scale
The Beaufort Wind Scale measures wind severity according to visible environmental

impacts, without the use of instruments:


   •    0 is calm, meaning calm wind. Smoke rises vertically with little if any drift.

   •    1 is light air, with speeds of 1 to 3 mph. The direction of wind is shown by smoke
        drift, not by wind vanes. Little if any movement with flags. Wind barely moves tree
        leaves.

   •    2 is light breeze, with speeds of 4 to 7 mph. Wind felt on face. Leaves rustle and
        small twigs move. Ordinary wind vanes move.

   •    3 is gentle breeze, with speeds of 8 to 12 mph. Leaves and small twigs in constant
        motion. Wind blows up dry leaves from the ground. Flags are extended out.

   •    4 is moderate breeze, with speeds of 13 to 18 mph. Wind moves small branches.
        Wind raises dust and loose paper from the ground and drives them along.

   •    5 is fresh breeze with speeds of 19 to 24 mph. Large branches and small trees in
        leaf begin to sway. Crested wavelets form on inland lakes and large rivers.



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                            B-128
    •   6 is strong breeze with speeds of 25 to 31 mph. Large branches in continuous
        motion. Whistling sounds heard in overhead or nearby power and telephone lines.
        Umbrellas used with difficulty.

    •   7 is near gale, with speeds of 32 to 38 mph. Whole trees in motion. Inconvenience
        felt when walking against the wind.

    •   8 is gale, with speeds of 39 to 46 mph. Wind breaks twigs and small branches.
        Wind generally impedes walking.

    •   9 is strong gale, with speeds of 47 to 54 mph. Structural damage occurs, such as
        chimney covers, roofing tiles blown off, and television antennas damaged. Ground
        is littered with many small twigs and broken branches.

    •   10 is whole gale, with speeds of 55 to 63 mph. Considerable structural damage
        occurs, especially on roofs. Small trees may be blown over and uprooted.

    •   11 is storm force, with speeds of 64 to 75 mph. Widespread damage occurs. Larger
        trees blown over and uprooted.

    •   12 is hurricane force, with speeds of over 75 mph. Severe and extensive damage.
        Roofs can be peeled off. Windows broken. Trees uprooted. RVs and small mobile
        homes overturned. Moving automobiles can be pushed off the roadways.

Damage to Trees and Vegetation
The extent of damage caused by a high wind event is related to what meteorologists call

antecedent conditions. Essentially, if previous weather conditions have been wet, the

impacts of high winds on trees, for example, could be higher since the ground is weak

with saturation. Timing can also play a role. If it’s the first high wind event of the season,

there might be more foliage, limbs, or branches that fall as the wind blows for the first time

in a while. 68



B.6.d   Previous High Wind Events
The strong wind can create dangerous conditions, especially when combined with low

humidity and dry fuels. This combination could escalate fires if ignition occurs or damage

Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           B-129
infrastructure and human health. Therefore, wind speed is constantly monitored. Using

data collected by observational instruments placed at the Lawrence Berkeley National

Lab, we identified several days with sustained winds exceeding 25 miles per hour

(Category 6, considered a strong breeze with speeds of 25 to 31 mph). The highest wind

speed recorded was 31 mph on March 21, 2023, and 29 mph on January 26, 2021.

Additionally, there are numerous days with wind gusts surpassing 31 miles per hour, the

highest being 63 mph on March 14, 2013, and 61 mph on March 21, 2023. The winter

months (December, January, February, and March) statistically experience prevailing

strong winds of 20 mph or higher.


The winter months of 2023 had several severe storms that included flooding, high winds,

and landslides. During January to April 2023, there were three federally declared

disasters in Alameda County, including DR-4699, DR-4683, and EM-3591.



B.6.e   Probability of Future Events
As temperatures increase worldwide due to climate change, changes in rising sea levels,

humidity, and storminess are unavoidable as the physical processes are all interlinked.

Given the prevalence of previous high-wind events, it is expected that each year will bring

more. By analyzing past and present weather patterns, scientists predict an increase in

wind speed and wave height in coastal areas, including the Bay Area and Berkeley.



B.6.f   Vulnerabilities

People
High winds can pose significant safety risks to people. Large branches can break off or



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                        B-130
topple trees, putting people outside or inside adjacent buildings at significant risk. Winds

may dislodge other heavy objects, and dust and debris can cause injuries to the eyes,

throat, and mouth.


High winds can be particularly dangerous for people experiencing homelessness, people

who work outside, and people who live in mobile or unanchored homes.


Structures
Downed trees or blowing objects can damage infrastructure, including homes, public and

private buildings, and vehicles.


Systems
High winds can topple trees, which in turn can take down power lines and/or cause other

objects to do the same. Downed power lines pose an immediate risk to people in the area,

and can also have widespread impacts via power outages.


Natural, historic, and cultural resources
High winds can severely damage or kill trees, such as when major limbs fail or the trunk

topples to the ground. For example, in 2022 a redwood tree fell at Willard Park after a

windstorm. In the 2023 storms, the City lost an 80-foot Guadalupe Cypress in Caesar

Chavez Park and UC Berkeley lost a redwood tree in the UC Botanical Garden.


According to the University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management

Program 69, wind can harm gardens, landscapes, and other parts of the natural

environment. Wind can damage bark, flowers, foliage, fruit, and limbs of most trees or




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-131
shrubs.



B.6.g    Potential Impacts and Loss Estimates
Climate change is expected to increase the potential impacts and losses associated with

high wind, as it brings more varied and extreme weather. Changes in population patterns

and in development are not expected to drastically change the potential impacts of high

winds.


Because high wind events are generally associated with either winter storms or fire

weather, the impacts from high winds alone are not tracked specifically.


However, winter storms in 2023 illustrate potential impacts. Berkeley’s Parks, Recreation,

and Waterfront Department estimates that these storms toppled 85 trees on City property,

many of them falling around the Berkeley waterfront. This count does not include trees

that fell on private property. There is not a comprehensive list of damages or estimates

of total damage, but reported damage includes one tree falling onto a house and another

on a pickup truck. 70 From December 2022 to April 2023, there were more than 300 calls

to 311 about broken branches and trees, more than any winter since 2015-2016.


Damage from these storms resulted in three federally-declared disasters in Alameda

County and created a backlog of tree removal work that limited staff capacity and time for

tree planting and maintenance.


GFOA’s High Wind Analysis
High winds can cause damage in the community. High winds can occur relatively

frequently. For example, data from the National Weather Service indicates that there have


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                       B-132
been 118 wind events in the entire San Francisco Bay Shoreline zone since 2011, with

an average speed of 43 miles per hour.


Of course, not every wind event in this zone will impact Berkeley. An examination of wind

data from a local weather station for the last 24 months showed that the average

windspeed of the 10 sustained wind events was about 30 mph. For comparison, FEMA

regards 67 mph as a very strong wind event that would be likely to cause significant

damages. During the same 24-month period, the San Francisco Bay Shoreline Zone

experienced three events over 40 mph. The biggest was on April 11, 2002. On that day

in Berkeley, the maximum sustained wind period was around 40 mph. It should be noted

that sustained winds (customarily measured over ten minutes) are not as strong as short

wind gusts that can happen during the wind event. For example, during a recent two-year

period the top speed of a wind gust was an average of 4.7 mph greater than the speed

measured for the associated sustained wind event.


To estimate the number of wind events per year on average Berkeley can expect to

experience, 24 months of local weather station data was compared to the same period

from the National Weather Service data. The wind events for the San Francisco Bay

Shoreline zone were fully felt in Berkeley in four out of eleven cases (36%). That same

portion was then applied to the entire 12-year period of history to arrive at an assumption

that there will be an average of 3.5 wind events per year, on average.


An assumption was made that there is a 3% chance of a wind event with sustained winds

of 67 mph or greater, which is equivalent to assumptions from FEMA’s estimates of losses

for Berkeley. 50% of wind events were assumed to be 45 mph or less, which is consistent



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                        B-133
with historical data. To estimate damage, estimates were taken from FEMA for damages

from a very strong wind event (67 mph), based on total exposed value and expected rates

of loss, which was $43,200 per event. That loss was then scaled down to expected

damage from a 45mph event. According to the Beaufort Wind Scale, winds at 45 mph

result in damages such as twigs and small branches broken from trees. It was therefore

assumed that damage was minimal at winds of this speed. These assumptions resulted

in the loss exceedance curve shown in Exhibit 14.


Exhibit 15. Loss Exceedance Curve for High Wind, 10 Year and 1 Year Risks (millions

B.7     Rainfall-Triggered Landslide

B.7.a   Description of Rainfall-Triggered Landslide
According to the United States Geologic Survey, a landslide is a movement of a mass of

rock, debris, or earth down a slope. The term “landslide” includes five modes of slope

movement, including falls, topples, slides, spreads, and flows. They are further subdivided

by the type of geologic material (bedrock, debris, or earth).


In the United States, the most frequent and widespread damaging landslides are started

by prolonged or heavy rainfall. The majority of rainfall-triggered landslides are shallow

(less than a few meters deep), small, and move rapidly. Rainfall-trigged landslides often

turn into debris flows (fast moving slurries of water, soil, and rock) as they travel down

steep slopes.


Rainfall, snowfall, changes in water level, erosion, ground water, and human activity can

contribute to landslides. Examples of human activity include grading for roads, home

construction, and landscaping, all of which can decrease hillside stability by adding weight

to the top of a slope, destabilizing the bottom of a slope, and/or increasing water content

of the underlying materials.


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                            B-135
Connection to climate change
Climate change is creating more intense and varied weather conditions, including intense

rainfall, which can contribute to landslides.


Connection to wildland-urban interface fire
Tree roots and vegetation can be important to providing support and preventing erosion.

Fires can burn trees and vegetation, removing that hillside support. Post-fire landslide

hazards include fast-moving, highly destructive debris flows that can occur in the years

immediately after wildfires in response to high intensity rainfall events.



B.7.b   Location of Rainfall-Triggered Landslide
The California Geological Survey has produced two maps that together provide helpful

data on where landslides are most likely to be triggered by winter storms.


The Landslide Inventory is an ongoing project to collect and display current and historical

landslide data for the State of California. Map 23 shows the Landslide Inventory for

Berkeley, focused on the Berkeley hills. Landslide movement could range from a few

inches to tens of feet in any given year, but ground surface displacements as small as a

few inches are enough to break typical foundations.


On Map 23:


   •    Active landslides are shown in brown.

   •    Dormant landslides are shown in orange, yellow, or light yellow. These are deep-
        seated or dormant landslides that are not currently moving, but that may have
        moved in historic time or in recent geologic time. These dormant landslides could
        be reactivated by changing surface or subsurface conditions.



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                        B-136
Generally speaking, in Berkeley, there are active and dormant landslides spread

throughout locations in the Berkeley hills.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                             B-137
Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan   B-138
Map 24 shows the overall susceptibility to deep seated landslides in areas throughout

Berkeley. Rock strength and slope are combined to create classes of landslide

susceptibility. These classes express the generalization that on very low slopes, landslide

susceptibility is low even in weak materials, and that landslide susceptibility increases

with slope and in weaker rocks. Very high landslide susceptibility, classes VIII, IX, and X,

includes very steep slopes in hard rocks, and moderate to very steep slopes in weak

rocks. Generally speaking, these classes in Berkeley are concentrated in northeast

Berkeley and in the Berkeley hills. The further east in the Berkeley hills have greater

susceptibility with steeper slopes and weaker rocks (shown with darker red colors).




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-139
Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan   B-140
B.7.c   Extent of Rainfall-Triggered Landslides and Anticipated Intensities
The most dangerous landslides in terms of life safety are fast-moving, generally shallow

debris flows. These are triggered when intense rainfall follows storms that have already

saturated hillsides. Debris flows initiate in concave slope areas where subsurface water

is concentrated, elevating pore pressure above the natural strength of the soil. Once

initiated, debris flows can travel great distances at relatively high velocities, flowing down

drainages and onto alluvial fans and damaging any structures lying in their paths.

Preexisting and recently-active, larger landslides (such as those shown in Map 23) are

more often triggered by exceptionally long periods of seasonal rainfall, and sometimes do

not start moving until long after the rain has stopped. These types of slides may not move

as rapidly as debris flows, but can damage large areas and many structures, resulting in

extensive landslide losses.



B.7.d   Previous Rainfall-Triggered Landslide Events
The most recent landslide in Berkeley occurred in January 2023 and it was federally

declared disaster DR-4683. In December 2022 and January 2023, six atmospheric river

events brought over 15 inches of rain to Berkeley, along with wind gusts over 55 miles

per hour. A large chunk of hillside located on the eastern edge of Zaytuna College’s Upper

Campus broke loose. The landslide traveled onto the private property immediately

downslope, destroying an outbuilding and damaging the home. In total, residents were

evacuated from one impacted property, along with seven more threatened properties

further downslope). There were no injuries but homes remained evacuated for multiple

weeks while the slide was remediated.


Another landslide occurred in Berkeley in January 2017. At the time, the overall rainfall in

Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           B-141
California was on pace to be the wettest season in over 100 years on record. Rain

saturated the soil in Berkeley and throughout the State. The slide occurred on an

undeveloped lot in the North Berkeley hills and threatened to close the street situated in

the path of the slide. Repairs to the hillside were completed in late 2018. There were no

injuries.


During the winter of 1997-1998, another landslide occurred in North Berkeley, when soils

became oversaturated from heavy rains brought by the El Nino weather system. One

home was significantly damaged and had to be demolished. Residents had to evacuate

two additional homes but were able to reoccupy these homes after the hillside was

stabilized. No one was hurt.


In 1996, a minor slide collapsed the Euclid Avenue retaining wall, blocking the roadway.


At other times over the 20th century, landslides from rainfall-saturated ground in the

Berkeley Hills damaged and sometimes destroyed homes and public infrastructure,

including streets, sewers, and other utilities. Most of the areas damaged were later rebuilt

or built over. 71



B.7.e   Probability of Future Events
Berkeley has a number of active landslides (shown in Map 23), which means they are

currently moving or movements have been recorded in the past. There are a number of

deep-seated landslides that continuously move, with the rate of movement affected by

rainfall and groundwater conditions.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-142
There have been 4 damaging landslides, 1 triggered by rain, in Berkeley since 1982. Using

this rate of three landslides in 41 years, there is a 7% annual chance of a landslide.


However, climate change will likely increase this risk. Climate change results in more

intense rainfall events, creating favorable conditions for more devastating landslides.

There is not currently a way to quantify how climate change increases the probability of

a damaging landslide.



B.7.f   Vulnerabilities

People
People may be hurt or killed during a landslide. Damage to roads and sidewalks may

prevent people from evacuating, and will challenge responders to access the area.


Structures
Landslides are most likely to damage residential or privately-owned structures because

the landslide risk predominately affects residential areas. According to a USGS report

approximately 6,000 structures are located in areas at moderate to high risk of

landslides. 72


Property owners are responsible for mitigating landslide risks to their own properties.

Homeowner’s insurance often excludes landslides, forcing property owners to manage

damage and costs without coverage.


The hazard is greater in steeply-sloped areas, although slides may occur on slopes of 15


1
 By “major and damaging” we simply mean that the damage was large enough to require intervention by City
government and cause City government a significant cost.


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                                    B-143
percent or less if the conditions are right. Slope steepness and underlying soils are the

most important factors affecting the landslide hazard. However, surface and subsurface

drainage patterns also affect the landslide hazard, and vegetation removal can increase

the likelihood of a landslide.


The hazard can be reduced through grading, strengthening, geotechnical engineering,

drainage, and other landscape methods. The City does regulate and inspect new

development activities, but most of the Berkeley hillside development predates current

best practices and codes. Further, mitigation efforts can be costly and out of reach for

many residents on a fixed budget.


Systems
Roads and sidewalks may be damaged as a result of a landslide.


Underground utilities (water, sewer lines, storm drains, natural gas lines, and conduits)

and aboveground utilities (electricity, telecommunications, cable) may be damaged in a

landslide. Damage to underground utilities may pose serious health and environmental

risks. Interruptions in electrical power may require with disabilities and people who

depend on electrical equipment for medical needs to evacuate or to have emergency

power supplies, even if they are not directly impacted by a landslide.


In Berkeley, several collector streets that are critical for emergency access and

evacuation are located in areas susceptible to landslides.


Natural, historic, and cultural resources

The Berkeley hills, where landslide risk is most present, include homes of architectural


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                      B-144
significance. There are also several parks, recreational areas, as well as institutions that

may be impacted by a landslide.


According to Map 24, significant portions of the University of California - Berkeley

campus, as well as the Lawrence Berkeley National Lab, are susceptible to landslide.



B.7.g   Potential Impacts and Losses
Landslides can cause serious injury or death. Fortunately, recent landslides have not

caused any deaths or injuries. There is currently no data on how many deaths or injuries

to expect with a given landslide, but Berkeley’s landslide-exposed areas are densely

populated, meaning that there is significant risk to people.


Climate change is expected to increase the potential impacts and losses associated with

rainfall-triggered landslides. Expected changes in population patterns potentially increase

impacts and losses associated with rainfall-triggered landslides. As the population

steadily increases, if there is additional development in the eastern hills, more people

could be exposed to landslide risk. Changes in land use and development may potentially

increase impacts and losses. New state laws are mandating increased density throughout

the city, including in the eastern hills, which are more exposed to wildland-urban interface

fire and landslides.
