B.8     Tsunami

B.8.a   Description of Tsunami
A tsunami occurs in a body of water when a rapid disturbance vertically displaces the

water, causing a series of surges. These changes can be caused by an underwater fault

rupture (that generates an earthquake) or underwater landslides (typically triggered by

earthquakes).


Tsunamis affecting the Bay Area can result from offshore earthquakes within the Bay

Area, or from very distant events. While it is most common for tsunamis impacting the

Bay Area to be generated by faults in Washington and Alaska, local tsunamis can be

generated from local faults running underwater (such as the small tsunami that was

triggered by the 1906 earthquake). The San Andreas Fault runs along the coast off the

Peninsula and the Hayward fault runs partially through San Pablo Bay.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                            B-147
Connection to climate change
As sea levels and temperatures rise, so does the potential impacts of tsunami. Increases

in sea levels and higher tides may be contributing factors to more frequent and intense

coastal flooding.



B.8.b   Locations of Tsunami
In 2021, the California Geological Survey (CGS) and the California Governor’s Office of

Emergency Services (Cal OES) updated the existing tsunami inundation maps for

Alameda County, shown in Map 25. In this update, the tsunami boundaries have changed

to reflect the best available science as well as local geographic features that impact

evacuation safety.


Map 25 shows in blue shading the area of potential tsunami inundation in Berkeley. It

does not reflect the inundation area from any singular tsunami, but represents what is

possible from large, realistic scenarios primarily from the Alaska and Cascadia subduction

zones. This map is intended to be used to evacuation planning purposes only.


Given Berkeley’s sloping terrain and the Bay’s waters at their current levels, tsunami

inundation will not extend far inland from the shoreline, but the zone has increased slightly

since the last update to reflect new science and local features. According to Map 25 and

shaded in blue, the tsunami inundation zone extends along the entire shoreline of the

Bay. Starting at the city’s northern border, the zone stretches east from the Bay until it

meets Fifth Street. At Page Street, the edge of the zone stretches as far east as Sixth

Street until Delaware Street. At Hearst Street, the edge of the zone runs east to Fifth

Street. At University Avenue, the edge of the zone runs east to Fourth Street. From


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                          B-148
Addison to Heinz Avenue the eastern edge runs to Third Street or to where Union Pacific

Railroad is located. At the far south end of the city after Heinz Avenue, the eastern edge

of the zone runs to Fifth Street for one block and to Seventh Street at Potter and Folger

Avenue.


According to Map 25, the zone captures Golden Gate Fields, the Tom Bates Regional

Sports Complex, Eastshore State Park, the Berkeley Marina, the Dona Spring Animal

B.8.d   Previous Tsunami Events
There have been no federally-declared tsunami disasters in Berkeley since the last

update. But in January 2023, an underwater volcano erupted near Tonga, resulting in a

tsunami advisory for Berkeley. Residents evacuated from boats, docks, and near the

shoreline. While there were some noticeable swells and strong current leading to

entrance of the Berkeley Marina, there wasn’t any reported damage. 73


The most recent tsunami to cause damage in Berkeley was associated with the March

2011 earthquake off the coast of Japan. As a result of the tsunami, a half-meter-tall surge

was observed nearby in Oakland with 4-6 knot current. The tsunami surge entered the

Berkeley Marina, causing $158,000 of damage to docks and boats. 74


Tsunamis generally impact the Pacific Coast of California, and reports of tsunamis

entering the San Francisco Bay are rare. Tsunamis, or seiches as they are called when

they occur within an enclosed body of water, can also be generated within the Bay by the

Hayward fault, which passes under San Pablo Bay. The 1868 Earthquake on the Hayward

fault is reported to have created a seiche within the Bay. It is unknown whether the seiche

impacted the City of Berkeley. The 1964 Alaska earthquake caused extensive tsunami

damage that flooded and heavily damaged coastal northern California near Crescent City;

data is not available regarding impacts to Berkeley.



B.8.e   Probability of Future Events
The probability of a tsunami occurring is typically described in return periods, or the

estimated average amount of time between events. Map 27 shows the extent of

inundation in Berkeley associated with a 100-year, 200-year, 475-year, and 975-year



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                        B-153
events.


   •   A 100-year event has a 1% chance of occurring in a given year.

   •   A 200-year event has a .5% chance of occurring in a given year.

   •   A 475-year event has a .2% chance of occurring in a given year.

   •   A 975-year event has a .1% chance of occurring in a given year. In other words, a
       975-year event has a 5% chance of occurring once in the next 50 years.

B.8.f   Vulnerabilities

People
The people most at risk in any kind of tsunami are those that live on boats at the Berkeley

Marina. This includes 100 liveaboard households, as well as 13 houseboats, for a total of

113 households. The Berkeley Marina has 1,000 boat slips. Approximately 200 residents

live onboard boats in these slips. An additional estimated 13 live onboard houseboats,

and regulations permit all slip holders to spend 12 nights per month on their boats.


Everyone who lives in or visits Berkeley’s tsunami inundation area (Map 25) is exposed

to tsunami. According to ESRI Demographic Data, 1,416 people in 502 households live

in Berkeley’s tsunami inundation zone. Of that population, 58 households include a

member with a disability, 213 include a member who is over 65 years old, and 23

households are below the poverty line. Berkeley’s tsunami inundation area has an

estimated daytime population of 6,840, including employees, visitors, and people

recreating. This data likely undercounts individuals who are unhoused and those that live

at the Berkeley Marina as mentioned above.


According to ESRI Demographic Data, there are 448 businesses with 4,821 employees

in the tsunami inundation zone. These businesses are estimated to have a high visitor

potential, which may make evacuation more challenging, if customers are unfamiliar with

tsunamis and or the geography of the area.


Warning systems typically allow for enough notice for at-risk individuals to evacuate. In

the event of a distant-source tsunami, where the underlying earthquake does not impact

Berkeley, warnings can be issued before the tsunami arrives onshore in Berkeley.


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                          B-156
However, the limited number of egress routes will slow evacuations. Evacuations will also

be slowed by the pinch point created on the stretch of University Avenue between Marina

Boulevard to the west and West Frontage Road to the east. This stretch of roadway is the

only eastward driving option out of the Marina.


Evacuation
The numbers of people and assets exposed to a tsunami are relatively low as compared

with other hazards presented in this Plan. However, evacuation routes for Marina

residents and visitors are limited. Interstate 80 runs north-south along the eastern edge

routes from the Marina into Berkeley:


   1. Via the University Avenue Bridge



   2. Via the frontage road north to Gilman Street



   3. Via the frontage road south to Ashby Avenue/CA-13



   4. Via Interstate 80


   5. Via the I-80 Bicycle/Pedestrian overcrossing 75



An earthquake occurring in the waters close to Berkeley could cause a near-source

tsunami, which would allow for little to no time to provide warning to people in the

inundation area. A near-source tsunami could severely compound evacuation challenges



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                      B-157
for individuals in the Marina. These evacuation challenges will disproportionately impact

people with disabilities and people with access and functional needs. They may not have

immediate transportation options to evacuate quickly. Additionally, in the event of a

tsunami, they may be separated from their caregivers and may need assistance to

evacuate.


Tsunamis can cause the release of pollutants, toxic substances, and other hazardous

materials, threatening public health, water, and the environment. Debris and hazardous

Structures
Of primary concern to the City is the Berkeley waterfront, which is primarily used for

recreational purposes, educational and environmental programming, industrial, non-

profit, and commercial operations.


At the Berkeley Marina, existing docks are a range of ages, with an average age of around

40 years old. Many docks are in significantly deteriorated condition. Broken finger docks,

utilities, and pilings pose a safety risk to Marina customers and their vessels. This

deteriorating infrastructure exacerbates the area’s vulnerability to tsunami. D & E docks

were damaged badly in the Tsunami of 2011 (and are scheduled to be replaced in 2024),

and many finger docks and pilings are still unusable and have not been repaired or

replaced. This results in lost revenue to the Marina, lost capacity, and a reduction in the

recreational resources available to the public.

B.8.g   Potential Impacts and Losses
Climate change is anticipated to increase the potential impacts and losses associated

with tsunamis. With a steadily increasing population, more people will be exposed in the

tsunami inundation area. New state laws are mandating increased density throughout the

city, which may increase development in the tsunami inundation zone. However, any new

development would be required to comply with the applicable regulations to ensure

avoidance of and/or adequate mitigation of hazard-induced risk.


Estimating losses from tsunami inundation is difficult given that the inundation maps do

not represent inundation from a single scenario event. Inundation from any single event

will almost certainly be less severe than depicted in Map 25, which is intended to display

worst-case scenario run-up heights from all potential tsunami sources across the Pacific

Rim.

SAFRR Analysis
The 2013 SAFRR tsunami scenario 78 depicts a hypothetical but plausible tsunami,

created by an earthquake offshore from the Alaska Peninsula. The study projected

impacts on the California coast, which included:


   •   Pilings in the Berkeley Marina will not be overtopped by tsunami waters, but over
       half of the docks in California coastal marinas will be damaged or destroyed

   •   One-third of boats in California coastal marinas will be damaged or sunk

   •   In Alameda County, tsunami inundation will create $20 million in building damage
       and $164.4 million in damage to building contents

   •   Wastewater treatment plants in Alameda County will be inundated and could
       release raw or partially-treated sewage and wastewater-treatment chemicals.

GFOA Analysis
Berkeley is at some risk from tsunami. The worst tsunami that researchers have

commonly contemplated is the 1-in-900-year tsunami. This represents a tsunami so large

that we would expect to see one that large only once in 900 years. Map 25 shows the

area of the City we could expect to be impacted by such a tsunami. A tsunami of this size

is expected to impact about 1,400 residents, a daytime population of 6,800, and 448

buildings.


The damage of less intensive tsunamis is substantially less. A tsunami of sufficient

intensity to occur only once every 475 years is only estimated to impact 125 residents,

1,100 daytime population, and 14 businesses.


Unfortunately, researchers have not produced usable estimates of projected economic

losses from a major tsunami. Further research is needed to fully assess Berkeley’s


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                      B-162
tsunami hazard, including structural assessment of buildings and infrastructure in the

inundation zone, to determine if they are designed and constructed with the strength and

resilience needed to resist the effects of tsunami surges.


The City will leverage ongoing research and coordinate with regional, State and federal

partners to help answer these questions.



B.9     Sea Level Rise and Shallow
        Groundwater Rise

B.9.a   Description of Sea Level Rise and Shallow Groundwater

Sea Level Rise
Sea level rise is an increase in the level of the world’s oceans. Warmer temperatures

associated with climate change are causing global sea levels to rise through two

processes:


   •    Warmer temperatures are increasing the amount of ice melt from the world’s
        glaciers, ice caps and ice sheets. This melted ice increases the volume of water in
        the ocean.

   •    In a process termed “thermal expansion,” warmer temperatures cause ocean water
        to expand, further increasing the ocean’s volume.

Shallow Groundwater Rise
Recent scientific studies have begun to evaluate the impact of the shallow groundwater

rising in low-lying coastal areas (like Berkeley) combined with sea level rise. According to

the San Francisco Estuary Institute and the Pathways Climate Institute 79, as sea levels



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-163
rise in San Francisco Bay, shallow groundwater underneath low-lying coastal

communities will also rise. For this reason, low-lying inland areas could flood from below

by emergent groundwater long before coastal floodwaters overtop the shoreline. As

groundwater rises, it will increasingly infiltrate sewer systems, flood basements, and

damage underground infrastructure. Rising groundwater will also interact with

contaminated lands around the Bay, creating a potential exposure pathway that could

impact the environment and public health. And rising groundwater will increase

liquefaction hazards in response to earthquakes, particularly in former open water,

mudflat, marsh, and floodplain areas that have been filled for development. Liquefaction

occurs when loosely-packed, water-logged sediments at or near the ground surface lose

their strength in response to strong ground shaking.


Connection to climate change
Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide and other heat-trapping gases into

the atmosphere; oceans then absorb the majority of this heat. As water becomes warmer,

it expands. This results in ocean levels rising worldwide.


The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has identified four potential

scenarios that reflect different future scenarios for greenhouse gas concentrations of the

atmosphere. The scenarios are known as Representative Concentration Pathways

(RCPs). They range from:


   •   RCP 2.6: Represents stopping all current greenhouse gas emissions, as well as
       significant carbon sequestration (a negative carbon output), to

   •   RCP 8.5: Represents continuing and increasing carbon emissions.



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                       B-164
Each scenario presents estimates for expected increase in sea level rise as the planet

warms and melting rates increase. Table 11 provides analyses of sea level rise

projections for the State and the Bay Area under these different climate scenarios in the

year 2100. 80

Connection to flooding
Sea level rise increases flooding frequency in the following ways:


   •   Groundwater table and stream water levels rise, increasing areas subject to
       flooding.

   •   Storm surges rise, exposing new areas previously not at risk of flooding.

   •   Coastal erosion increases, expanding areas exposed to flooding and inundation 83.

   •   Levees and storm walls have to endure increasing loads and may be susceptible
       to overtopping, making these traditional measures to address sea level rise no
       longer adequate or financially feasible.

Connection to hazardous materials release
Rising groundwater could push toxic materials stored underground upward, which could


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                      B-165
create major impacts on public health and the environment. The City is planning to expand

on the new science around groundwater rise combining with sea level rise to better

understand specific impacts on hazardous materials in Berkeley.

In these scenarios, emergent groundwater begins to appear in dark blue. Emergent

groundwater is when the groundwater surfaces, making the depth of the groundwater

zero. Emergent groundwater can damage surface infrastructure like roadways and add

groundwater is projected.

B.9.f   Vulnerabilities

People
Sea level rise will have disproportionate impacts on disadvantaged communities in

Berkeley. For example, the areas most likely to experience flooding with increased sea

level rise are in West Berkeley, which has a higher percentage of communities of color

and low-income communities. These are the same neighborhoods that were historically

redlined, have poorer air quality, and experience higher incidents of hospitalization due

to asthma. West Berkeley also has a history of industrial buildings and usage, resulting

in more hazardous materials stored underground. As the groundwater table rises along

with the sea level, these materials can also rise and move, causing environmental and



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           B-175
public health hazards.


Structures
Consideration of storm surge and other compounding flooding risks on structures is

increasingly important, particularly when designing infrastructure with finite effectiveness,

such as sea walls or barriers. Both permanent inundation from sea level rise as well as

more frequent and more extensive flooding events will need to be considered in long-term

planning along Berkeley’s coast.


The 2019 Draft Berkeley Marina Area Sea Level Rise Assessment is a site-specific

analysis for compliance with State requirements in AB 691. The document identifies three

locations in the Berkeley Waterfront that are most susceptible to intermittent inundation

in the future due to sea level rise:


   1. Virginia Street Extension (north shore of McLaughlin Eastshore State Seashore)
      intersection with Marina Boulevard

   2. South Shore of University Avenue

   3. North-East side of the Berkeley Inner Harbor.

The 2019 Draft Berkeley Marina Area Sea Level Rise Assessment is a living document

and will be used to inform future City of Berkeley projects and development at the Marina.


Systems
As sea levels rise, storms could cause key underpasses and roads accessing Highway

80, including Ashby Avenue (State Highway 13), to flood more often or be permanently

inundated, impacting transportation on this major regional artery.



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                          B-176
Berkeley’s stormwater and sanitary sewer pipes are vulnerable to inundation. In addition,

flooding resulting from sea level rise in combination with severe storms may threaten

natural gas pipelines regionally. Prolonged and more frequent inundation from sea level

rise can accelerate structural failures and threaten the functionality of California’s natural

gas distribution system. 87 This infrastructure vulnerability can lead to disrupted service

and the leakage of methane gas from the system. Methane is both a health and safety

hazard as well as a highly potent greenhouse gas, further contributing to climate change.


Cultural and Natural Resources
According to the 2019 Draft Berkeley Marina Area Sea Level Rise Assessment, in

Berkeley the major risk of sea level rise to the shoreline is the loss and/or degradation of

the revetment, which is a structure intended protect the bank from erosion. This could

jeopardize the landfill of César E. Chávez Park, causing erosion and loss of landmass.

There is a potential of erosion and loss of the integrity of both the San Francisco Bay Trail

Spur and University Avenue.


Several trails and access to the Marina viewing points and coastal access will be impacted

by projected sea level rise. Degradation of the trails will make walking and running less

accessible and will also cut off potential for small boat recreation.


Damage to natural resources includes potential damage to the protected natural area

within César E. Chávez Park and the Western Burrowing Owl habitat, both located in the

northeast corner of the park. Because there is significant inundation within the McLaughlin

Eastshore State Seashore, any habitat within the grassland will be significantly impacted

starting in 2030.


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           B-177
Sea level rise will inundate beaches and shoreline habitats. These changes are expected

to substantially alter the Bay ecosystem, reducing wetlands, and adversely affecting water

quality and wildlife. 88


Landfilled areas and areas experiencing drought—both common in the Bay Area—are

particularly susceptible to land subsidence, which is the gradual settling or sudden sinking

of land. 89 In the Bay Area, this includes developed areas that sit on top soft compressible

bay mud. 90 Land subsidence can expand areas susceptible to sea level rise as these

areas sink while sea levels are rising to meet them. 91


Scientists predict that climate change will have many effects on freshwater and marine

environments. These effects, along with nutrient pollution, could increase the frequency,

intensity, and exposure to harmful algal blooms. Algal blooms endanger human health,

the environment, and the economy. Sea level rise would create more shallow and stable

coastal water, conditions that are perfect for algae growth. 92


Activities that have value
The Berkeley Waterfront is a critical community asset for recreation, education, and local

businesses. Recreation activities occur both on land and surrounding waters. Nonprofit

sailing clubs operate out of the Berkeley Waterfront and many boaters and fishers use

the area. Recreation areas on land include César E. Chávez Park, Shorebird Park and

the Shorebird Nature Center, Horseshoe Park, and Adventure Playground. César E.

Chávez Park features a bird habitat, and an off-leash dog area.


Many businesses operate out of the area, including restaurants, the DoubleTree hotel,




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-178
boat repair/storage facilities, and stores. In the Berkeley Marina, there are about 1,100

boat slips including about 100 liveaboard slips. Additionally, two small-scale commuter

ferries operate out of the Berkeley Marina along with fishing charter boats.



B.9.g   Potential Impacts and Losses
Potential financial impacts to the Berkeley Marina caused by projected sea level rise

include damage to commercial and public buildings and infrastructure, loss of public

resources, loss of habitat and natural resources, and loss of berth rental revenue to the

City.


All current and upcoming capital projects in the Berkeley Marina near the shoreline band

will be designed to be resilient to mid-century sea-level rise and be adaptable to end of

century. These projects’ sea level rise mitigation measures will be reviewed and approved

by Bay Conservation Development Commission’s permit review process, ensuring the

latest sea level rise requirements are being met by the design.

B.10   Floods

B.10.a Description of Floods
Floods occur when there is an overflow of water in areas that are normally dry. In

Berkeley, three types of flooding typically occur: coastal flooding, creek flooding, and

storm drain overflow.


Coastal Flooding

Coastal flooding occurs when water inundates or covers normally dry coastal land as a

result of high or rising tides or storm surges. Higher tides and sea level rise reduce creek

and storm drainage flow capacity in the western portions of the City. See the Sea Level

Rise section of this Plan for more information.


Creek Flooding

Like in many urban areas, creeks in Berkeley have been affected by urban development.

Stretches of creeks in Berkeley are completely contained by culverts, and open channel

segments of the creeks are often segmented by shorter culverts that enable streets and

development. 93 Creeks in west Berkeley flow year-round. The upper reaches of creeks

only flow for a short time after rainfall. When the level of runoff exceeds the capacity of a

creek, the flood waters overtop the banks and flood into properties and streets. Creek

flooding in Berkeley generally originates on private property. Blockages can happen in

creeks, thus the City increases cleaning efforts on the right of way ahead of and during

significant rainfall events. Residents are responsible for maintaining creeks and related

infrastructure within their property.


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                          B-181
Storm Drain Overflow

The City’s storm drainage infrastructure collects urban runoff and carries it either directly

to the Bay or to nearby watercourses that discharge to the Bay. Causes for storm drain

overflow are generally rainfall events that exceed the capacity of the storm drainage

facilities, blockages in the storm drainage facilities, or damage to storm drainage

infrastructure that reduces its capacity.


When storm water runoff exceeds the capacity of the storm drain infrastructure, the

excess water flows into city streets. Most of Berkeley’s storm drain infrastructure is

engineered to accommodate a 10-year design storm. 94 Using this 10-year design storm

standard is considered the most cost-effective design practice, and provides guidance

for computing flows and for sizing storm drainage infrastructure. 95 Maintenance helps

preserve the flow capacity of the infrastructure, reducing the frequency of flooding,

however many components of Berkeley’s storm drain infrastructure are over 90 years old

and are past their useful life expectancy. Concrete pipes have eroded or separated and

metal pipes have corroded over the years. In some locations sink holes have formed as

soil enters the storm drain through cracks and other defects.


Connection to Climate Change
Climate change increases the intensity and severity of rainfall events, which leads to more

frequent flooding. Climate change also creates sea level rise, which in turn will lead to

rising groundwater, increasing flood risk. For more information, review the Sea Level Rise

section of this Plan.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                          B-182
Connection to Infectious Diseases
According to the National Institutes of Health, the risk of viral infection increases after a

flood. 96 Floods can increase the transmission of viral diseases, especially waterborne

infections, vector-borne diseases, and respiratory infections.


Connection to Utility Disruption
An unknown number of property owners rely on electric sump pumps to keep their homes

and buildings free from water during the rainy season. A power outage that disables sump

pumps during a storm can lead to flooding inside structures.


Connection to Sea Level and Shallow Groundwater Rise
New studies have linked sea level rise and groundwater rise to increased flood risk in the

San Francisco Bay Area. 97 For more information, review the Sea Level Rise section of

this Plan.



B.10.b Location of Floods
The City maintains approximately 93 miles of storm drain pipelines and appurtenant

structures in the public right-of-way and in easements. The City is responsible for the

maintenance of approximately 0.5 miles of open creeks and nearly 4 miles of creek

culverts running in the right of way or in City owned properties. A majority of the City’s

stormwater assets are nearing or past their expected useful life and others require an

evaluation of hydraulic capacity.

In 2011 the City’s Public Works Department developed the Watershed Management Plan

Creek Flooding: FEMA National Flood Insurance Program
Berkeley’s creek flooding exposure is assessed through the National Flood Insurance

Program (NFIP), which makes federally-backed flood insurance available to

homeowners, renters, and business owners in participating communities. Participants in

the NFIP must regulate development in floodplain areas in accordance with NFIP criteria.


Berkeley has participated in the NFIP since September 1, 1978 and is currently in good

standing with the program. NFIP compliance is monitored by FEMA regional staff and by

the California Department of Water Resources under a contract with FEMA.

Floodplains
The 100-year Floodplain shows the area that has a 1% chance of experiencing creek

flooding in any given year. The 500-year floodplain has a 0.2% chance of experiencing

creek flooding in a given year. Areas in the 100-year floodplain are assumed to also flood

in a 500-year flood scenario. Because floods reaching the level of the 500-year Floodplain

occur so rarely, they are not as well-researched and specific impacts are less known.

Stormwater Master Plan
The City is working with a contractor to develop a comprehensive stormwater master plan

(SWMP), which is expected to be completed at the end of 2025. The SWMP will provide

an updated inventory of system-wide deficiencies and establish a capital stormwater

improvement plan to address these deficiencies based on an equity and risk-based

prioritization model. The SWMP will also provide updated maintenance and inspection

plans for the City’s stormwater assets and identify green infrastructure implementation

opportunities. The SWMP will analyze potential funding mechanisms to supplement

current funding levels for the program as needed to support enhanced operations,

regulatory compliance implementation, and capital improvements identified in the master

plan.



B.10.c Extent of Floods and Anticipated Intensities
Floods can last for a few minutes to a few weeks. This timing often depends on the

duration of the rainfall and the land on which it occurs. In low and flat areas, slow moving

water can linger for days or weeks. Excessive rainfall from winter storms is the most

common cause of flooding between November and March.


The following factors contribute to the frequency and severity of flooding in a given event:


   •    Rainfall intensity and duration

   •    Existing saturation

   •    Features of the watershed

   •    Natural features

   •    Coastal conditions



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-194
For example, an intense rainstorm at the end of a rainy winter when soils are already

saturated is more likely to result in flooding than if the same storm occurs at the beginning

of the rainy season when soils are not as wet.


Depth and velocity are common ways of measuring the severity of a flood. These provide

information on how deep the water is and how fast it is moving. The depth and velocity of

a flood are good predictors of how much damage it may cause.



B.10.d Previous Flood Events
Berkeley’s most recent flooding occurred in December 2022 and January 2023 when a

powerful series of storm systems brought more than 15 inches of rain. This much rain in

a 20-day timeframe occurs only once every 50 years, according to the National Oceanic

Atmospheric Agency (NOAA). The winter months of 2023 had several severe storms that

included flooding, high winds, and landslides. During January to April 2023, there were

three federally declared disasters in Alameda County, including DR-4699, DR-4683, and

EM-3591.


In October 2022, an atmospheric river brought heavy rains and strong winds to Berkeley,

resulting in nuisance flooding as well as many downed trees and powerlines.


In 2004, widespread flooding occurred throughout Berkeley during a 25-year rainfall

event. Flooding also occurred during the 1997 - 1998 El Niño season.


In the early 1960s, the Strawberry and Codornices Creeks overflowed, along with flooding

of streets and intersections. The flooding was of short duration and shallow depth and

occurred in small areas. A few buildings flooded, including some on the University of



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                          B-195
California, Berkeley campus.



B.10.e Probability of Future Events
According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Storm Events

Database, there have been an estimated 45 days with flooding in Alameda County in the

last 20 years. This equates to about 2 days per year, as an estimate. Climate change will

likely bring stronger storms with heavy rains, increasing the number of days per year of

flooding in Alameda County.



B.10.f Vulnerabilities

People
The 100 year and 500 years floodplains are concentrated in west Berkeley along the Bay

and around the Aquatic Park. West Berkeley has historically been the home to

underserved communities and marginalized populations, including people experiencing

homelessness. People in West Berkeley may not have the resources to take household

mitigation measures and or manage the impacts of floods if they occur.


Floods pose a number of risks to people. Serious injury or death can occur when people

do not evacuate areas that are flooded or enter floodwaters. Urban runoff and flooding

can also result in contaminated drinking water and an increase in the transmission of

infectious diseases. Mold and mildew can also grow on any damp surface within 24 to 48

hours, posing additional serious health risks to people and animals.


Structures
Flooding can cause serious damage to buildings. Floods can cause structural damage,


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                      B-196
such as loose floors or foundation cracks. There may also be broken electrical wires,

appliance damage, damage to water and septic systems, and mold and mildew.


Heavy rains can also put stress on culverts. Berkeley is underlain by a patchwork of creek

culverts, most privately constructed and over 100 years old. A culvert failure could be

physically and economically catastrophic in an area such as Downtown Berkeley where

buildings have deep basements, many underground utilities, and streets are congested

with vehicle and pedestrian traffic. Most culverts are located on private property, with

some located beneath private improvements. Failure of a private culvert may cause

significant damage to private property, and require improvements to that property. The

City intends to repair culvert breaks beneath public property as-needed, as it currently

does if there is a break in a storm drain. However, many private property owners are

unaware that improvements on their property may be situated above a culvert.


Flooding can impact utilities, including power, water, and gas. Severe storms and deep

waters can damage power lines and underground infrastructure, impacting buildings and

other infrastructure.


Systems
In past rainfall events, flooding along low-lying roadways has hindered traffic flow. Low-

lying underpasses leading to Interstate 80, as well as highly-trafficked city streets, have

flooded. This creates traffic impacts for community members and first responders.


Natural, historic, and cultural assets
Local gardens face a threat of contamination if they are exposed to urban runoff. Heavy



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                        B-197
storm water runoff can contaminate the ocean, lakes, and other bodies of water with other

bacteria. 99



B.10.g Potential Impacts and Losses
The potential impacts and losses associated with floods are expected to increase due to

climate change. Berkeley’s population continues to steadily increase, adding people

exposed to the area’s hazard and their cascading impacts. The 100 year and 500 years

floodplains are concentrated in west Berkeley along the Bay and around the Aquatic Park.

These areas haven’t changed since the last update, and development in this area of the

City is characterized by industrial and heavy commercial uses, although there is some

residential development. Any new development would be required to comply with the

applicable regulations to ensure avoidance of and/or adequate mitigation of hazard-

induced risk.


GFOA’s Flood Analysis
In 2006, Berkeley, along with 16 other cities in Alameda and Contra Costa counties

experienced a storm that was severe enough to receive assistance from FEMA. This

event was used as a starting point to simulate future storms. Data from severe storms in

early 2023 also inform this model.


Frequency: There have been three severe storms in Alameda and Contra Costa counties

that were received FEMA support since 1998. Berkeley was impacted by two of the

storms. Hence, the model simulated an 12% annual chance of storms, with a 66% chance

that Berkeley would be impacted by any given storm.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                      B-198
To simulate damages, per capita damage from each of the cities impacted by the 2006

storms was assessed, providing a range of potential losses. This range was then used to

simulate Berkeley’s potential losses from future storms: both economic losses to the

community at large and financial losses to the City government.

community from severe storms. Some very large losses seem possible, even if highly

unlikely.

2004 Flood Analysis
A 2004 analysis explored Berkeley’s flood exposure and vulnerabilities to a one percent

annual chance flood occurring in Berkeley. This analysis predicted that:


   •   The maximum flood depth would be two feet deep, mostly near creek channels.


   •   Approximately 675 structures would be impacted to various degrees:


           o The majority would be inundated by one foot or less of water.


           o Approximately 200 structures could flood with up to two feet of water.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-200
A flood depth of one to two feet has the potential to damage structures, first floor and

basement finishes, contents and appliances in exposed buildings.


The 2004 analysis used FEMA’s standard loss curves to determine the percent of

replacement value of damage caused by various heights of creek flooding. These curves

are based on years of data from flood losses on insured properties around the country.

Single-story structures with one foot of floodwater are estimated to have structural

damage equal to 14% of their replacement value and damage to 21% of the structures’

contents. Single-story structures with three feet of water on average experience 27% loss

of their replacement value and 40% loss to their contents.

total $201 million in 2023 dollars. Approximately $90 million is damage to the building

These numbers are likely significant underestimates, because they do not account for the

flooding caused by storm drain overflow, which would occur concurrently with creek

flooding. Berkeley’s exposure to a one percent annual chance flood has likely increased

since 2004 but resources are not available at this time to perform a new analysis.


Few Berkeley property owners are known to carry flood insurance, presumably because

of negligible flood damage in recent decades, so those losses would be borne almost

entirely by building owners.


Some of these losses could be avoided if property owners protected properties through

sandbagging or other activities, particularly in areas expected to receive one foot or less

of flood water. The City offers free sandbags to city occupants, but remediation activities

like sandbagging require property owners to have adequate warning time and manpower.


Due to Berkeley’s small watersheds and paved, urban environment, floodwaters are likely

to both rise and recede quickly. This means residents and business owners may have

only a short warning period for impending floodwaters, but they should be able to begin

the cleanup and repair process quickly. Building cleanup will occur within a handful of

days; repairing and replacing furniture and equipment will take weeks to months.

Repetitive Loss Properties

B.11   Utility Interruption

B.11.a Description of Utility Interruption
Utility interruption is any loss of a public service which includes but is not limited to

electrical service, telecommunications, wastewater and potable water, and natural gas.

Interruption can be planned and include a warning, such as with Power Safety Power

Shutoffs that proactively turn off electricity to mitigate wildfire risk, or interruption can

come as a secondary impact of a natural hazard described in this plan. Interruption can

also occur without a preceding natural hazard, with a variety of causes, for example

maintenance and repair or accidental damage.


In Berkeley, electrical service, telecommunications, potable water, and natural gas

infrastructures are not under the City’s control, but rather are owned and managed by

other quasi-governmental, private, or special district entities.


   •   Most electricity (generation) is provided by Ava Community Energy. Pacific Gas
       and Electric or PG&E provides a small portion of electricity, manages the
       transmission and distribution of electricity, responds to outages, and provides
       billing and customer service. Berkeley’s electricity system is almost entirely
       aboveground, making it vulnerable to earthquake, fire, landslide, and storm
       damage.

   •   Potable water is provided by East Bay Municipal Utility District or EBMUD. EBMUD
       provides drinking water to approximately 1.4 million people and sewer services to
       640,000 in the East Bay. EBMUD was created in 1923, and the age and extent of
       its system makes it particularly vulnerable to damage.


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                          B-203
   •   Telecommunications are managed by a variety of private partners, including
       Verizon, AT&T, and Comcast, among others. Telecommunications infrastructure
       is spread throughout the city, and therefore susceptible to damage from the variety
       of natural hazards mentioned in this plan. Telecommunications also rely on the
       electricity system to function.

   •   Natural gas is managed by PG&E. The natural gas transmission line runs the
       length of Berkeley (north-south direction) under Seventh Street, which is an area
       susceptible to earthquake liquefaction.

The City manages some utility infrastructure, including storm drains and the sanitary

sewer collection system that links to the EBMUD system. The sewer and storm drainage

systems are also old and have weak components, making them vulnerable to damage.


The systems described in this section provide the foundation for day-to-day life in

Berkeley. These systems are also vital to many of the City’s disaster response activities,

and restoration of these systems will be critically important to Berkeley’s recovery.


Utility Poles and Wires
Aboveground utility poles and wires are both vulnerable to natural hazards and when

destabilized can themselves become hazardous and create fires. Utility-caused fires have

become a major contributor California’s fire hazard. Aboveground utility lines are

vulnerable to strong winds, earthquake shaking and ground failure, and to object coming

into contact with wires. When utility poles are destabilized or wires are damaged, the

wires themselves can become hazardous as they continue to conduct electricity, putting

people in harm’s way, creating sparks, and igniting fires. Live wires coming in contact with

combustible fuel, as well as other disruptors like squirrels, rodents, birds, and vehicles

knocking down utility poles, contribute to the fire ignition hazards.


Undergrounding is the process of placing overhead power lines, poles, cables, and other


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           B-204
utility infrastructure underground. Undergrounding reduces the likelihood of a fire ignition

and has been shown to stabilize power and communications reliability, beautify the urban

environment, and enhance public safety by eliminating fire ignition sources and

obstruction of evacuation routes.


According to the 2018 Conceptual Study to Underground Utility Wires in Berkeley

presented by the Public Works, Disaster and Fire Safety, and Transportation

Commissions, Berkeley is comprised of diverse neighborhoods with a mix of commercial

and residential properties. Undergrounding could be a beneficial adjustment in the city,

improving safety, quality of life, and reliability from natural and human-induced disasters.

Currently, approximately 16% (34.6 miles) of utility wires are undergrounded on all streets

in Berkeley.


To reduce risks associated with overhead wires and other utilities, in 2023 the State

adopted SB 884 (McGuire), allowing the use of federal infrastructure funds for

undergrounding utility lines. Following this, PG&E committed to protecting communities

from wildfire threats by undergrounding 10,000 miles of power lines in the Highest Fire

Threat Districts. On January 30, 2024, the Berkeley City Council adopted a resolution to

urge PG&E to underground utility wires in Berkeley’s Very High Fire Hazard Severity Zone

(VHFHSZ) in order to mitigate wildfire risk and limit obstruction of evacuation and ingress.

See the Wildland-Urban Interface Fire section for more details on the WUI fire hazard. 105


Connection to climate change
Climate change is increasing the severity and variability of storms and other natural

hazards. These events pose serious risks to our utilities.


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-205
Connection to hazards of concern
Most of the hazards included in this plan can impact utilities. In the Vulnerabilities Section

of each hazard, there is information about how the hazard can impact Systems, including

utilities.



B.11.b Location of Utility Interruption
Utility interruption is usually localized, as in the event of a damaged power line, water

main, or some other relevant infrastructure. However, the natural hazards covered in this

plan can create more widespread outages that can impact larger portions of the city. All

locations in Berkeley may experience utility interruption. Locations with greater hazard

exposure are more likely to experience utility interruption resulting from the natural

hazard.


Public Safety Power Shutoff
Power Safety Power Shutoffs are planned power outages when there is high risk of

wildfires. When originally begun, PG&E’s Public Safety Power Shutoffs affected large

portions of the Berkeley hills. Since then, PG&E has narrowed the areas affected by

PSPS, but some parts of Berkeley may still experience a Public Safety Power Shutoff,

including:


    •   Along Summit Road at Ajax Place to where it meets Grizzly Peak and Senior
        Avenue.

    •   Around the top of Marin Avenue.

    •   East of Vistamont Avenue to Wildcat Canyon Road.

    •   A portion of the Northeast Berkeley hills that includes roughly around the following
        streets: Santa Barbara Road, Vermont Avenue, Michigan Avenue, Cragmont


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           B-206
       Boulevard, Spruce Street, Northampton Avenue, Acacia Avenue, Montrose Road,
       Euclid Avenue.

B.11.c Extent of Utility Interruption and Anticipated Intensities
The extent and severity of utility interruption depends on many factors, including cause,

location, duration, and time of year. For example, the cause of the interruption directly

impacts how widespread the outage will be. One broken water main will likely on impact

a small geographic area, but a storm with high winds might impact power lines all across

the city. Utility interruption can also range from a small localized event to a larger, regional

outage. The severity of the interruption is much higher if it impacts a large geographic

area, affecting more people and critical infrastructure. Longer interruptions are also more

intense than shorter ones, as people rely on utilities for a variety of basic needs. Time of

year also relates to severity, as losing power on a hot or cold day is more intense,

especially if people need cooling or heating infrastructure.



B.11.d Previous Utility Interruption Events
There have been no federally-declared utility interruption disasters in Berkeley since the

last update. There is not a comprehensive list of all the utility interruption events in the

last five years in Berkeley. However, a few notable events had widespread impacts:


   •   Winter storms in 2023 toppled trees and power lines, resulting in over 10,000
       customers losing power.

   •   A water main broke in 2020 cutting off running water supply to the entire Berkeley
       Marina.

   •   A pole fire in 2020 cut internet service for 5,000 customers in and around Berkeley.

   •   PG&E Public Safety Power Shutoffs in 2019 left thousands without power for
       multiple days.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                             B-207
B.11.e Probability of Future Events
The probability of utility interruption is high, given the number of systems involved, aging

infrastructure, and significant exposure of each system to the many hazards presented in

this plan.



B.11.f Vulnerabilities

People
Berkeley residents, visitors, businesses, institutions, and other partners rely on utilities

for day-to-day life.


Electricity

Electricity powers everything in our daily lives, from essential domestic functions such as

heating, cooling, and lighting, to a wide range of household appliances and technologies,

as well as transportation, including electric cars, scooters, and public transportation.

Electricity is also often used to manage industrial and hazardous materials, which can be

released and cause serious damage if there is a power failure.


Loss of electricity for prolonged periods pose a significant threat to individuals who

depend on specific medical equipment or medications. According to data from the U.S.

Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) emPOWER program, some Berkeley

residents rely on electricity- or power-dependent devices and durable medical equipment

(DME), including 287 electric beds, 111 motorized wheelchairs or scooters, and 340

oxygen concentrators. Prolonged power outages increase the risks for those dependent

on these devices, potentially leading to a surge in vulnerable community members

requiring emergency services and hospital care.


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-208
If the electricity is out during an extreme temperature event, people who are sensitive to

high or low temperatures, including the elderly, children, and people with certain medical

conditions will be even more at risk. Without electricity, people may lose food supplies,

especially impacting people with low incomes and people with various health needs.

Businesses, grocery stores, gas stations, and other services might also have to close,

impacting the local economy and people’s ability to get basic necessities.


Water

The water supply is critical to human safety and survival. People rely on safe running

water for daily activities, including, eating, drinking, bathing, and going to the bathroom.

Consumption of contaminated water can lead to the transmission of diseases and serious

illnesses and even death. While some people have emergency water supplies, many do

not. People would either have leave their home and or purchase water from nearby

suppliers.


The water supply is also crucial to firefighting and emergency response activities. If there

is a widespread water supply interruption, it could negatively impact firefighting

capabilities.


Telecommunications

Telecommunications is a key aspect of daily life. The City government, including our first

responders, use telecommunications for daily operations. Back up options are available,

but may hamper services to the public.


People rely on telecommunications for personal use, work, and to report emergencies.

People rely on their phones to gather information, have entertainment, and to


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-209
communicate with their families. Without this as an option, people may struggle to do

these things, impacting their mental, physical, and emotional health.


Structures
In most cases utility outages do not lead directly to structural damage. However, water

damage is serious, costly, and can occur in association with damage to sewer, drainage,

or wastewater systems. Water damage, if not quickly addressed, can lead to mold, which

is detrimental to public health and makes buildings unsafe for human use.


Systems
The utility systems in Berkeley, including electricity, water, telecommunications, and

natural gas are susceptible to outages, either from day-to-day conditions or natural

hazards mentioned in this plan. Further details about the utility vulnerabilities associated

with the natural hazards in this plan are included in their respective sections.


Natural, historic, and cultural resources
Berkeley is home to a number of natural, historic, and cultural resources that could be

negatively impacted by utility disruption. If there is damage to water systems,

contaminated water could spill into the Bay or into other natural ecosystems, such as

creeks and parks, around Berkeley.


Berkeley is home to many businesses that rely on water, natural gas, and electricity to

operate. Not having these utilities for a long period of time could put them out of business

with lost goods and profit. There are other cultural institutions in Berkeley, such as arts

organizations, theatres, and businesses that cannot operate without utilities and a


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-210
prolonged outage could threaten their existence.


Activities that have meaning
Utilities are a key part of day-to-day life for Berkeley government, residents, businesses,

and visitors. Electricity and internet are crucial to City operations and its ability to serve

the public. Private businesses, employers, UC Berkeley, and schools also rely on utilities

to operate every day and welcome their students, employers, and customers.

Transportation systems rely on electricity too, which would make it difficult for people who

rely on it to reach destinations and activities around the Bay Area.



B.11.g Potential Impacts and Loss Estimates
There is currently no data on the economic impacts from utility disruption for Berkeley.

However, utility disruptions do cause notable economic impacts, including lost income

and food for example if the power is out. There are also added costs to City operations

as well as to businesses, employers, schools, and other local groups.


There may be replacement and content costs for any structures that have water damage.



B.12   Hazardous Materials Release

B.12.a Description of Hazardous Materials Release
Hazardous materials release could harm community members by exposing people to

vapors that are toxic, suffocating, cause burns or are irritating. Hazardous materials

release can threaten not only life and property, but also the environment, in areas such

as creeks, the Aquatic Park lagoons and the San Francisco Bay.


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           B-211
The impacts of a release depend on its chemical characteristics, the amount and rate of

substance spilled, the location, and its dispersion. Flammable and combustible materials

can cause fires in areas that are largely constructed of wood; they may also cause

explosions. Wind speed and direction, as well as topography, can greatly impact the

dispersion plume of a release.


The City’s Toxics Management Division (TMD), within the Department of Planning and

Development, maintains the Hazardous Materials Area Plan, which identifies facilities

that, in the event of a regional disaster, may pose the greatest risk to human health or the

environment.


The Fire Department is the first responder for hazardous materials incidents within the

City, and has access to chemical inventories, locations and emergency planning for all

these facilities. The chemical inventories and facility maps are available electronically to

the Fire Department.


The Department of Public Works manages the City’s hazardous materials emergency

response to spills on the right-of-way and also manages the hazardous materials

emergency response contractor.


Connection to climate change
According to the Environmental Protection Agency, climate change may increase our

exposure to chemicals. Climate change is causing more frequent and intense storms and

varied weather, which can result in more release of hazardous materials.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-212
Connection to hazards of concern
Most of the hazards of concerns in this plan can result hazardous materials release,

including earthquake, flooding, wind, and wildland-urban interface fire.



B.12.b Locations of Hazardous Materials Release
A hazardous materials release can occur throughout the city near where hazardous

materials are manufactured, stored, used, or transported. Hazardous materials release

can occur as a result of a natural hazard, such as earthquake shaking, or can happen

accidentally. In Berkeley, a hazardous material event is more likely to occur in the City’s

industrial area in West Berkeley where there is a concentration of industrial sites and

transportation routes.


Map 37 identifies the locations of Hazard Level 1 Industrial Sites. Level 1 industrial sites

are identified as square red icons on the map.

Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan   B-214

Petrochemical refineries and other large chemical facilities in Contra Costa County could

release hazardous materials that could impact the Berkeley community.


Hazardous materials also travel through Berkeley by truck and rail. Specific routes known

to carry hazardous chemicals are:


   •   Interstate 80

B.12.c Extent of Hazardous Materials Release and Anticipated Intensities
There are 528 facilities 106 within Berkeley that are regulated by TMD. 107 TMD has grouped

these facilities into Hazard Levels 1, 2 and 3:


   •   Level 1: Facilities that have substantial quantities of hazardous materials onsite,
       and/or have hazardous materials that can easily disperse or explode, and are toxic
       or pose other special hazards to human health and the environment.

   •   Level 2: Facilities that have medium to large quantities of hazardous materials
       onsite, and/or materials with known hazards.

   •   Level 3: Facilities for which Berkeley Fire Department engine companies can
       handle incidents without additional facility storage information, because the
       hazards are known or familiar (e.g., gas station without welding cylinders, or a
       facility with motor oil).

The majority of the 528 facilities in Berkeley are Level 3 automotive- or medically- related

facilities with limited quantities of hazardous materials and hazardous waste.



B.12.d Previous Hazardous Materials Release Events
There have been no federally-declared hazardous materials release disasters in Berkeley

since the last update. Berkeley has not recently experienced significant hazardous

materials releases secondary another natural hazard. However, the city has experienced

industrial accidents from both mobile and fixed sources. Truck accidents involving

potentially harmful materials have occurred in the western part of the City, on Interstate

80 and its ramps. Industrial sites have released small amounts of dangerous substances,

such as anhydrous ammonia from an ice rink and a sake brewery. 108 In 2011, an

uncontrolled release of 1,600 gallons of diesel on the UC Berkeley campus resulted in

diesel entering the stormwater system, and discharging into Strawberry Creek. 109 In 2017

a truck accident on Interstate 80 released approximately 200 gallons of diesel fuel on the

roadway next to the estuary. The fuel was contained and the fuel did not release into the


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-217
estuary. After the incident, the roadway barriers have been strengthened and improved.



B.12.e Probability of Future Events
Transportation accidents have occurred with trucks carrying dangerous materials. These

accidents will undoubtedly occur in the future. 110 A release on the freeway or railway

would most immediately impact the western industrial area of the city. Winds typically

blow from the west to the east, meaning that a gaseous release could easily spread to

the City’s eastern residential areas.


The City has completed a Hazardous Materials Commodity Flow Study with a grant from

the California Office of Emergency Services and the federal Department of

Transportation. This study retrieved or collected data on bulk chemicals being transported

on freeways, major city streets, and the railroad and through pipelines.

Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-220
B.13   Infectious Disease Outbreak
The City of Berkeley works in alignment with Alameda County, Bay Area Region, and

California Department of Public Health to plan and respond to infectious disease.



B.13.a Description of Infectious Diseases
Infectious diseases are illnesses caused by germs, such as bacteria, viruses, and fungi;

that enter the body, multiply and cause an infection. Some infectious diseases are

contagious, meaning they can spread from one person to another. These diseases can

be spread many ways, including direct contact, insect bites, food or water contamination,

and airborne transmission. A threat of infectious diseases is an epidemic, which affects a

large number of people in a population, community or region, or pandemic, which affects

several countries or continents.


It should also be noted that bioterrorism can also involve communicable diseases. The

Centers for Disease Control (CDC) has identified high priority biological agents that have

the potential for major public health impact. These include:


   •   Anthrax (Bacillus anthracis)

   •   Botulism (Clostridium botulinum toxin)

   •   Plague (Yersinia pestis)

   •   Smallpox (variola major)

   •   Tularemia (Francisella tularensis)

   •   Viral hemorrhagic fevers (filoviruses [e.g., Ebola, Marburg] and arenaviruses [e.g.,

Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                        B-221
       Lassa, Machupo])

The State of California has a list of over 95 communicable diseases, which must be

reported by health providers or laboratories to local public health officials.


Connection to climate change
According to the Center for Disease Control and Prevention, our risk for infectious

diseases is increasing because of climate change. 113



B.13.b Location of Infectious Diseases
All of Berkeley is susceptible to infectious diseases. The populations at the highest risk

for infectious diseases are the very young, the elderly, or individuals who are

immunocompromised. However, higher-poverty neighborhoods of color are at greater risk

due to the effects of health and social inequalities. In addition, because of the

communicable nature of these diseases, those who are especially at-risk include people

experiencing homelessness and people in congregate settings, such as people in long-

term care facilities or dormitories.



B.13.c Extent of Infectious Diseases and Anticipated Intensities
Infectious diseases vary in their impact and severity depending on the disease. These

complications can range from minor to severe illness or death. The impact of the disease

is also affected by environmental factors and human behavior.



B.13.d Previous Infectious Disease Events
Since the last update, there was a federal declared disaster for the COVID-19 pandemic

(DR-4482). In 2020, the start of the COVID-19 pandemic began. A total of 23,887


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                       B-222
polymerase chain reaction (PCR) cases were confirmed in the City of Berkeley. In

response to the pandemic, City of Berkeley issued several health alerts and protocols to

align with the Bay Area, California Department of Public Health (CDPH), and Centers for

Disease Control (CDC) guidance to limit the spread of infection.


Berkeley residents have been affected by the following other infectious disease

outbreaks, epidemics, and pandemics over the last 15 years.


   •   In 2009, H1N1 caused over 8,917 hospitalizations and 578 deaths in California.
       The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) released stockpiled N95
       respirators for use by health care facilities experiencing shortages. Berkeley Public
       Health Division distributed supplies to Health care facilities experiencing
       shortages. Points of dispensing were set up Bay Area-wide to administer pandemic
       influenza vaccine.

   •   In 2011, there were 24 confirmed cases of mumps in Berkeley, with approximately
       2 additional suspect cases. All confirmed cases were within the UC Berkeley
       campus community, and all persons had received 2 or more doses of the measles,
       mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. In consultation with CDPH, City of Berkeley
       recommended a 3rd dose of MMR for UC Berkeley students living in congregate
       settings such as dormitories to help control the outbreak.

   •   In 2014, more than 54 cases of pertussis were reported in Berkeley. This was a 5-
       fold increase compared to previous years. Berkeley cases ranged from infants to
       teenagers, with most being 10 - 17 years of age. Cases involved at least two
       schools in the Berkeley Unified School District. The state experienced more than
       1,700 cases of pertussis. Clinicians were advised to immunize women with the
       tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis (Tdap) vaccine during every pregnancy between
       27-36 weeks’ gestation to optimize antibody transfer and protection of infants at
       birth, and to immunize young infants promptly with the diphtheria, tetanus, and
       pertussis (DTaP) as young as 6 weeks during a community outbreak.

   •   In 2015, California experienced a measles outbreak with over 100 confirmed cases
       statewide. Berkeley had 1 confirmed case; there were 6 cases in Alameda County
       and many in surrounding Bay Area counties. Berkeley Public Health notified
       schools, preschools and daycare communities recommending staff and students
       be protected against measles with the MMR vaccine.

   •   In 2018, multiple outbreaks and cases of norovirus were reported to the City of


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-223
       Berkeley Public Health Division. A health alert was issued to remind ill persons to
       practice good handwashing and to avoid preparing food for others while they are
       sick and for at least 48 hours after symptoms resolve. Clinicians were advised to
       consider norovirus in patients presenting with diarrhea, vomiting, nausea and
       abdominal pain, and Instruct patients with norovirus/gastrointestinal (GI) illness to
       remain home from work or school until 48 hours after symptoms have resolved.

   •   In 2019, an outbreak in San Diego, Santa Cruz and Los Angeles counties alerted
       Alameda County and the City of Berkeley to take precaution, and provide post-
       exposure prophylaxis and pre-exposure prophylaxis to high-risk populations.
       Groups at highest risk included persons using illicit drugs, men who have sex with
       men, persons with chronic liver disease, and persons experiencing homelessness.

   •   In 2022, multiple clusters of monkeypox (mpox) virus were reported in several
       countries, including the US. Many of the cases involved men who have sex with
       men (MSM) without a history of travel to an endemic country. There were 16
       confirmed cases in the City of Berkeley. As a precaution, multiple Bay Area
       counties provided post-exposure prophylaxis and pre-exposure prophylaxis to
       high-risk populations. City of Berkeley partnered with Alameda County, CDPH,
       East Bay Advance Care, Asian Health Services, and Steamworks to provide mass
       vaccination sites weekly at Steamworks for 5 months.

B.13.e Probability of Future Events
The concern for future events is determined by asking the following questions:


   •   How easily does the disease spread?

   •   How susceptible is the population to this disease?

   •   Has this disease been a recent issue?

   •   These questions were evaluated using the following factors:

   •   How easily does the disease spread?

   •   Mode of Transmission

   •   R0 – Rate of infection in a susceptible population

   •   How susceptible is the population to this disease?



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         B-224
   •   Vaccine Effectiveness

   •   Vaccine Coverage

   •   Has this disease been a recent issue?

   •   Confirmed cases in Berkeley in 2022 alone

   •   Confirmed cases in Berkeley 2010-2022

   •   Year of the last outbreak or epidemic in Berkeley, Alameda County or California

Scores were assigned to the responses or values for each factor. Low scores indicate

less concern, higher scores indicate more concern. The average of the scores for the

factors available were used to determine and overall measure of no, low, medium or high

concern.

Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                                            B-227
B.13.f Vulnerabilities

People
Infectious diseases can be difficult to evaluate due to the wide variation in disease

characteristics. Therefore, they pose difficulties in terms of comprehensive risk

assessments. According to the Alameda County Department of Public Health, “In

Alameda County, communities of color face inequitable conditions that increase the risk

of chronic diseases. Others especially at-risk of infection and disease transmission are

people experiencing homelessness and people in congregate settings.”


As of July 2023, 80 Berkeley residents lost their lives as a result of COVID-19 infections.

The death rate for African Americans residents is four times greater than Latino residents

and nearly six times greater than whites, demonstrating the disproportionate impact on

disease and death on African American residents.



B.13.g Potential Impacts and Losses
In most infectious disease outbreak, the impact is limited, with the majority of illnesses

treatable and the likelihood of fatalities low. Large-scale outbreaks like the onset of

COVID-19 in the spring of 2020 can strain existing health care facilities. As of July 2023,

250 Berkeley residents have been hospitalized as a result of COVID-19 infections and 80

Berkeley residents lost their lives as a result of COVID-19 infections.


The impacts of a pandemic go far beyond positive cases, hospitalizations and deaths.

During the COVID-19 pandemic the stress, collective grief, physical and social distancing

needed to slow the spread of the virus, and the resulting distress from lost wages,



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                        B-228
unemployment, and closures of educational and youth development programs created a

secondary public health crisis.

Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                    B-239
     C.      Mitigation Strategy
Berkeley aims to be a disaster-resilient community that can survive, recover from, and thrive

after a disaster. Berkeley envisions a community in which the people, buildings, and

infrastructure in and serving Berkeley, are resilient to disasters; City government provides

critical services in the immediate aftermath of a devastating event of any kind; and basic

government and commercial functions resume within thirty days of a damaging earthquake or

other significant event.


Disaster mitigation reduces or eliminates long-term risks to people and property from hazards

and their effects, and/or provides passive protection at the time of disaster impact. Disaster

mitigation is a foundational element of disaster resilience.


Element C of this plan outlines Berkeley’s mitigation strategy, and how it connects to

Berkeley’s disaster resilience vision. The strategy identifies and analyzes a comprehensive

range of specific mitigation actions and activities being considered to reduce the effects of

each hazard described in Element B: Risk Assessment. The Strategy is based on existing

authorities, policies, programs, and resources, as well as Berkeley’s ability to expand on and

improve these existing mitigation tools as described in Elements C.1 of this plan.

Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                                         C-15
C.1.a   Guiding Policies and Goals
Many City policies shape Berkeley’s growth. In addition to disaster resilience, City goals

include protecting the environment, promoting sustainable development, providing low-

income housing, preserving historic structures, and maintaining City infrastructure. Key

policies impacting development are detailed below.


Sustainable Development
Berkley promotes sustainable development policies. The General Plan includes policies to

maintain sufficient land zoned for high-and medium-density residential development. These

policies allow for sufficient new construction to meet Berkeley’s fair share of regional housing

needs. Policies are coordinated to ensure that all new development is sensitive to Berkeley’s

unique physical character and scale, and that new housing and future development occur in

areas of the city that are best served by public transportation.


Affordable Housing
Berkeley also promotes affordable, seismically-safe housing. The General Plan includes

policies promoting access to quality housing for people at the lowest income levels, and

inclusion of low-income groups in new housing development. The General Plan also

encourages maintenance and improvements to prepare buildings for a major seismic event,

with the expectation that improvements do not necessitate substantial rent increases for

tenants. In January 2023, City Council adopted the Housing Element, which identifies policies

and programs to provide and preserve healthy, resilient housing at a range of prices, with

special attention given to special needs housing, homelessness prevention, and affirmatively

furthering fair housing (AFFH).




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                          C-16
Restoration of Natural Waterways
The General Plan’s Environmental Management section encourages the restoration of natural

waterways. Many Berkeley streams were culverted in the 1960s as a flood control measure.

Any change in the status of these culverts, already in a weakened state, would alter the

Berkeley’s flood risk.


Climate Mitigation and Adaptation
As outlined in Berkeley’s 2009 Climate Action Plan, Berkeley has community-wide goals to

reduce emissions and mitigate our impact on global anthropogenic climate change. This

includes reducing energy and water usage, moving toward clean energy in our buildings and

transportation, reducing our waste, and ensuring sustainable and equitable development. In

addition, the Berkeley community must adapt to the current impacts the community is already

facing from the changing climate, as well as plan for future impacts projected to occur. Climate

mitigation strategies are outlined in the Climate Action Plan, and continue to be implemented

Citywide. The City’s climate adaptation strategies are included in the Local Hazard Mitigation

Plan and the Resilience Strategy.


Preserving Historic Character
The City values preserving historic character. Any hazard, and earthquakes and fires in

particular, could destroy many historic structures, which tend to be more vulnerable to these

hazards than newly-constructed buildings. The General Plan’s Urban Design and

Preservation Element encourages support of long-term protection of historically- or

architecturally-significant buildings to preserve neighborhood and community character

through maintenance of the historic resources inventory, and use of the State Historical

Building Code, Rehabilitation Tax Credits, and Mills Act contracts preservation incentives.



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                          C-17
Disaster Resilience
The Berkeley community recognizes that disasters have the potential to undercut all of the

City’s goals. As stated in the General Plan:


The city’s healthy environment with its unique character and quality of life based on cultural,

social and economic diversity could be dramatically and enduringly altered by a serious

hazard event. Berkeley must protect what we already have as well as what we build through

employing sound development practices and building and planning code enforcement, and

continuously working to reduce the vulnerability of existing buildings and infrastructure, to

improve emergency response and to prepare for recovery. Without these measures, disasters

will occur and the other goals of the General Plan will be lost.



C.1.b   Public Works
 The City of Berkeley’s Public Works Department is the largest department in the City and

 provides both direct services to the community, as well as critical support services to the

 City organization. Public Works is responsible for maintaining the City’s physical assets

 and infrastructure in a safe and serviceable condition. Public Works provides services

 ranging from refuse and recycling collection, diversion and disposal, to property

 FY 2024 include the replacement of the City’s Transfer Station, developing a Zero Waste
