       cover flooding.

   •   During heavy rains

           o Elevate important items, if possible, during heavy rains, especially from first
             floor/garage.

           o Do not walk, swim or drive through flooded waters. Turn around, don’t
             drown.

           o experienced flooding in the past

After a flood
           o If your home floods, review this Field Guide for Flooded Home Cleanup.

Utility Interruption

Power Outage
   •   Know the location of your circuit breakers and/or fuse boxes and how to check
       them.

   •   Make sure PG&E can reach you and alert you of an outage by calling 1-800-743-
       5000 and updating your contact information.

   •   Make a plan to stay safe and comfortable during power outages.

   •   First, think about your household’s emergency power needs. What will you need
       to stay warm? To keep food cool? To operate any medical devices?

   •   Determine the power draw of the devices that you want to keep operating, and
       how long you want to operate them.

   •   Consider purchasing a power bank or generator to provide the power you need to
       stay safe in your home in short-duration outages.

   •   Make a plan to stay with family, friends, or at a hotel if your home is affected by a
       long-term power outage.

   •   When power outages are planned or likely (for example, severe storms or heat

Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                          C-85
       waves are forecast):

   •   Fully charge your phone and any chargeable devices including battery packs and
       even electric vehicles.

   •   Make sure you have flashlights and fresh batteries close at hand.

   •   Prepare to use your alternate plans for refrigerating medicines or operating power-
       dependent medical devices.

   •   When a power outage occurs:

           o Unplug all electric appliances to avoid overloading circuits or damaging
             devices when the power turns back on.

           o Leave 1 lamp plugged in with the switch “on.” When the lamp turns back on
             you’ll know your home has power again. Turn your appliances back on one
             at a time when power is restored.

           o If you encounter a downed power line, always stay away and call 9-1-1
             immediately. Do not touch anything that touching the lines or drive over
             them.

Water Outage
   •   Each person in your household will need 1-2 gallons of water daily for drinking,
       washing, and cooking. Store as much water as you can. At minimum, store water
       for 3 days (3-6 gallons per person).

   •   Options for storing water include: single gallons of water, water barrels, water
       cubes, or canned water. When choosing the best option for your household,
       consider cost, ease of storage, required maintenance, and how easy it will be to
       access and use during an emergency.

Wastewater Outage
If you don't have water to flush with or your sewage system isn't working:

   •   Modify your own toilet to collect waste without flushing. Turn the water valve to off.
       Flush out any water still in the bowl (the toilet shouldn't refill). Put some kitty litter,
       peat moss, lime, or something similar that will absorb liquid and help reduce odors
       into the inner bag. Go to the bathroom in the inner bag. You may be able to use
       the same bag more than once before replacing. Once the inner bag is full or you

Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                                C-86
       feel it needs to be replaced, tie it up. Insert a new inner bag and add
       absorbent/odor reducer for the next use.

   •   Use a 5-gallon bucket. You can add a toilet seat and set it up as described above.

   •   If sewage from plumbing fixtures backs up into your home, avoid contact with the
       sewage as it may contain harmful pathogens.

Telecommunications Outage
   •   Establish a backup communication with your family. Choose a meeting place and
       time in case you can’t call each other.

   •   Keep a battery-powered AM/FM radio handy to receive emergency alerts if
       internet, phone, and television aren’t working.

   •   Print important documents or save them to a thumb drive in case of internet outage.

   •   During emergencies or large events, high demand for cellular networks can make
       it hard to place a call. A text message may go through when voice calls cannot,
       because text messages require less bandwidth from the cellular network.

   •   If you lose cellular service completely to your phone but the internet is still working,
       you can switch your phone’s settings to turn on “Wi-Fi” calling to make calls through
       the internet.

D.3 Mitigation Plan Integration
The City of Berkeley develops its updated Local Hazard Mitigation Plan every five years.

The planning process brings together staff from every department to develop the risk

assessment, mitigation strategy, and report on progress since the last update. After this

process, staff continue to work closely together on maintaining the LHMP as well as on

new projects. Core Planning Team members bring their knowledge and experience with

the LHMP to their respective departments and ensure its integrated into their other

ongoing work. For example, the 2019 LHMP was incorporated into the 2023 City’s

                                                                                               D-6
Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan
Housing Element.


The Risk Assessment is crucial to the City’s understanding of its hazards, vulnerabilities,

and potential losses. It is used to educate City staff, partners, community members, and

elected officials about the hazards that can occur in Berkley and what is at risk. The Office

of Emergency Services works to maintain the Risk Assessment and ensure that the latest

data, science, and information is used and integrated in educational materials and

planning processes. For example, the 2019 LHMP Risk Assessment informed the City’s

Community Wildfire Preparedness Plan (CWPP) as well as Extreme Heat Workshops for

the City’s Emergency Operations Plan (EOP).


The actions outlined in the Mitigation Strategy are developed and prioritized in

collaboration with every Department that is involved in the work. To ensure that the list of

actions remains manageable, only actions that have a confirmed clear and viable funding

source are included. As a result, the LHMP is closely aligned with the City Budget and

Capital Improvement Plan. Each year, the City assesses potential capital improvement

projects and available funding as it implements its Five-Year Capital Improvement Plan.

Capital improvement actions in the Plan are assessed as part of this annual process.

As with prior LHMP updates, this Plan will be well-integrated into the City’s existing and

future plans. This list of planning mechanisms where the Plan will be integrated are listed

below.

Budget Process
Because the 2024 LHMP will be adopted by the City Council into the General Plan, the

data and information from the Risk Analysis as well as the hazard mitigation goals and

actions in the Mitigation Strategy will help guide the City’s budget process. The budget

process assigns resources to address the goals, objectives, and community priorities set

by the City Council. The budget process is the final step of assigning resources to

implement mitigation actions. The Budget process is described in detail in Element C:

Mitigation Strategy.


Community Outreach
Community outreach is a key component of any planning mechanism. The City’s Office

of Emergency Services has been trying to augment its outreach capacity, in addition to

improving the outreach associated with the LHMP. The 2024 LHMP planning process

inspired a whole suite of new outreach materials designed to educate community

members about hazard risks and the mitigation strategy, including actions they can take

to reduce risk. These materials are designed to be relevant and adjustable so that they

can be used after the 2024 LHMP is adopted.


LHMP as an Appendix to the General Plan
Upon its adoption by the Berkeley City Council, the 2024 LHMP will be incorporated as

an appendix to the Disaster Preparedness and Safety Element of the City’s General Plan.

The Berkeley General Plan is a comprehensive, and long-range statement of community

priorities and values developed to guide public decision-making in future years. The

Plan’s goals, objectives, and policies serve as a guide for day-to-day decisions that are


                                                                                     D-8
Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan
essential for responsive government. Decisions made by Berkeley City Council and

its advisory boards, and commissions about the physical development of the City should

be consistent with the goals, objectives, and policies of the General Plan. The City Council

and Planning Commission will use the General Plan when evaluating land use changes

and making funding and budget decisions. It will be used by the Zoning Adjustments

Board and City staff to help regulate development proposals and make decisions on

projects. The policies of the Plan apply to all property, both public and private, within the

Berkeley city limits.


Upcoming General Plan Updates and Additions
From 2024-2026 the City will be updating the General Plan’s Safety Element, and creating

a new Environmental Justice Element. The data and information in the 2024 LHMP’s Risk

Assessment, as well as the actions in the Mitigation Strategy, will directly inform the

updated goals for both of these critical new documents. Many of the 2024 LHMP’s Core

Planning Team members will continue their collaborative mitigation work by participating

in the process to develop the Safety Element updates and new Environmental Justice

Element.

Resilience Strategy
In 2014 the City of Berkeley was selected to participate in the 100 Resilient Cities (100RC)

Initiative, pioneered by The Rockefeller Foundation. The City conducted extensive

research that included community outreach and engagement as well as review of existing

plans, including the 2014 LHMP, as it developed its Resilience Strategy, which was


                                                                                       D-10
Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan
released in April 2016. Building on existing efforts and with guidance from the Mayor, the

City Council, and the community, the Berkeley Resilience Strategy identifies six long-term

goals and recommends specific short-term actions to help address some of Berkeley’s

most pressing challenges. One of the goals is to adapt to the changing climate, which

integrates information from the LHMP.


The Resilience Strategy is being implemented through projects, programs and plans

across the City, and the LHMP will continue to be a key planning document that influences

these processes. The City continues to have a Chief Resilience Officer (CRO) and

participates in organizations such as the Resilient Cities Network and the Bay Area

Climate Adaptation Network (BayCAN). As an example of a current resilience project, the

City is working to implement solar photovoltaic arrays and backup batteries at critical

municipal facilities to provide clean, reliable energy assurance in the face of a disaster

and/or power outage.


Waterfront Specific Plan
The Waterfront Specific Plan is a four-year planning project (formerly “Berkeley Marina

Specific Area Plan”) that will provide a path for achieving a financially self-sustainable,

publicly owned marina that preserves and enhances infrastructure to support current and

future community needs, while adapting to climate change and promoting environmental

stewardship. Key to this goal is consideration of the waterfront-specific hazards, including

sea level rise and flooding. The 2024 LHMP’s data, information, and mitigation strategies

are being developed hand-in-hand with the Waterfront Specific Plan (WSP), which will

designate areas for commercial redevelopment and recreation opportunities and provide


                                                                                       D-11
Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan
design guidelines for future projects.


Climate Action Plan
The 2019 and 2024 updates to the LHMP support concepts outlined in the Berkeley

Climate Action Plan, which was developed through a community-wide process and was

adopted by City Council on June 2, 2009. The Climate Action Plan outlines a vision, goals

and policies to reduce community-wide greenhouse gas emissions by 33 percent below

2000 levels. Further, in 2018, then-Governor Brown committed California to carbon

neutrality by 2045, the Berkeley City Council resolved to become a “Fossil Fuel-Free

City,” and the Council declared a Climate Emergency, all steps to signal the urgency of

these ambitious goals and the need to act on climate threats in an equitable manner.


Because climate change impacts can cause or exacerbate many of Berkeley’s hazards

of concern, in 2014 the LHMP was updated to include climate change as a hazard of

concern. Historically, the City of Berkeley has used the Climate Action Plan to present

activities to mitigate climate change itself by addressing ways to reduce greenhouse gas

emissions, and the LHMP to present climate adaptation actions, which would better

prepare the community to adapt to the changes in climate we are already seeing. In this

way both plans reflect and support one another. The City continues to implement the

initiatives set forth in the Climate Action Plan through other plans such as the Electric

Mobility Roadmap (adopted in 2020) and Existing Buildings Electrification Strategy

(adopted in 2021), and this and future updates to the LHMP will continue to inform these

implementation plans and include actionable climate adaptation strategies. For example,

the City is implementing the Pilot Climate Equity Fund and Just Transition Pilot Programs,


                                                                                     D-12
Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan
both of which address transitioning away from gas in buildings, which can be hazardous

as described in the LHMP’s Risk Assessment.


In the 2024 LHMP, climate change has been more thoroughly integrated into each hazard

of concern rather than as a standalone hazard. As a result, there are more actions in this

plan that relate to reducing emissions and mitigating climate change as a way of reducing

the impacts of various natural hazards.

     E.    Plan Update
E.1 Changes in Development
The people and structures in Berkeley are continually changing. Since 2000, the City’s

population has grown steadily, increasing approximately nine percent each decade. The

Department of Finance estimates that the City’s population was 122,580 in 2020.

Berkeley’s population is anticipated to continue to grow steadily between 2020 and 2040

according to the Association of Bay Area Government’s Plan Bay Area 2040 projections.

The City’s population is anticipated to reach about 136,000 by 2030 and 141,000 by 2040.


According to the Department of Finance, there were 51,523 housing units in Berkeley in

2020. This represents a four percent increase from 2010 and a 10 percent increase since

2000. Due to the built-out nature of the city’s development pattern, the majority of new

units constructed in the last ten years are part of multi-family buildings containing five or

more units, and are located on in-fill sites, mostly along existing commercial corridors.

Overall, the number of multi-family units in the City increased by seven percent while the

number of single-family units increased by less than one percent.


The University of California, Berkeley is expanding its facilities both on and off the

campus. UC Berkeley’s 2021 Long Range Development Plan projects that the campus

population will increase 22% in the next 15 years. To accommodate this growth, UC

Berkeley is planning to add over 2 million gross square feet to the campus footprint, an

additional 11,000 student housing units, and over 1,000 new parking spaces in the vicinity

Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                            E-1
of the existing campus, which is located at the eastern portion of the city.


Residents ages 15 to 24 comprise the largest age group in Berkeley, followed by people

ages 25 to 34, likely due to the presence of UC Berkeley. The majority of households are

renter-occupied (57%), and there is a sizeable proportion of the population residing in

group quarters (about 11%) due to dormitories and other student housing associated with

the University. The senior population (ages 64 to 84) represents about 12% of the

residents in Berkeley, and has increased by 40% since 2010. Overall, 42 percent of

Berkeley’s households are considered lower income, earning less than 80 percent of the

area median income (AMI). Special needs populations in Berkeley include senior-headed

households (27% of total households), extremely low-income households earning up to

30% of AMI (21%), seniors living alone (12%), persons with a disability (8%), single-

parent households, including those with children (8%), and large family households over

five of more persons (4%). Additionally, about 1,100 persons (1%) are experiencing

homelessness in Berkeley as of February 2022.


Housing cost burden is a prevalent issue in Berkeley, impacting over half of lower income

households, and one third of moderate-income households. As of 2017, about 40 percent

of Berkeley households are cost burdened with 23 percent experiencing a severe cost

burden. Cost burden is notably more prevalent among renter households, with over half

of renter households paying more than 30 percent of their income to housing expenses.

Building new housing is one way to reduce housing cost burden in the city. As of

December 2023, approximately 4,600 new housing units were in the pipeline for

development, representing almost 9% of the existing housing stock in Berkeley. Due in

part to the City’s inclusionary housing ordinance, approximately 13% (620 units) of those

Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                        E-2
units are deed-restricted affordable according to federal and State statutory limits on

household size and income.


City plans and policies guide decision-making to address the housing needs of Berkeley’s

residents. City resources should focus on housing affordability for people at the lowest

income levels, and maintain and improve existing housing that will prepare buildings for

a major seismic event. The City is working to expand the supply of housing for all

residents through zoning amendments to increase the production of accessory dwelling

units and infill ‘middle housing’ in high resource neighborhoods. Further, the City is

focusing on housing for special needs groups through numerous programs and actions

that prevent homelessness, seek solutions for those who are experiencing

homelessness, and encouraging housing projects that include affordable units and those

suitable for households with children and large families.


Effects on Berkeley’s Risks and Vulnerabilities
As more people join the Berkeley community, the city will have more people who are

exposed to the area’s hazards. Additionally, as density and population increase, the

demand for fire and emergency services also increases. For example, 911 calls will

increase, with each call having an impact on the system, including the availability of

resources. In 2023, the City completed a Standards of Coverage and Community Risk

Assessment (SOC) to define appropriate levels of service based on a comprehensive

analysis which included the impacts of increased density and vertical growth. The SOC

determined that fire and emergency resources need to be enhanced to meet current and

future demand.


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                        E-3
Since the last plan was approved, because of Berkeley’s built-out nature, new

development tends not to add new geographic areas of hazard exposure. But with

increased density, more people will be exposed to the area’s hazards. All of Berkeley is

exposed to earthquake shaking. All of Berkeley is exposed to wildland-urban interface

fire, but the areas of heightened exposure are in the eastern hills. New state laws are

mandating increased density throughout the city, including in the eastern hills, which are

more exposed to wildland-urban interface fire and landslides.


The 100 year and 500 years floodplains are concentrated in west Berkeley along the Bay

and around the Aquatic Park. These areas haven’t changed since the last update, and

development in this area of the City is characterized by industrial and heavy commercial

uses. Any new development would be required to comply with the applicable regulations

to ensure avoidance of and/or adequate mitigation of hazard-induced risk.


The city’s western edge is also exposed to tsunami inundation and sea level rise from

climate change. The tsunami inundation has increased slightly since the last update to

reflect new science and local features. New science has also emerged evaluating the

impact of shallow groundwater rising in low-lying coastal areas. Ultimately, low-lying

inland areas could flood from below by emergent groundwater long before coastal

floodwaters overtop the shoreline. Data shows that Berkeley already faces high

groundwater in multiple areas in the west, meaning that the scenarios for sea level rise

impacts are likely worse than previously thought. However, the actual areas of sea-level

rise exposure, as well as the impacts of sea-level rise on the area’s liquefaction and

flooding hazards, are not yet clear, as it depends on carbon emissions.



Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         E-4
New development in part reduces Berkeley’s vulnerability to natural hazards. New

construction adheres to modern design codes, including regulations for structural

resistance to earthquakes, landslide mitigation efforts, fire-resistant materials, fire

mitigation measures, and elevation above flood levels. Replacing or significantly

renovating older structures significantly increases the Berkeley community’s protection

from natural hazards.



E.2 Changes in Priorities and
Progress on Local Mitigation
Efforts
While the City’s goals and objectives have remained very similar to the 2019 plan, the

2024 LHMP reflects thorough revisions from the 2019 document. The 2024 Risk

Assessment accounts for newly available science and research and emerging hazards.

As a result of significant hazard events since the 2019 update, Poor Air Quality, Infectious

Disease, Wind, and Utility Disruption have their own sections in the Risk Assessment.

Climate change has been thoroughly integrated into each hazard, instead of having its

own section, inspired by community outreach that overwhelming suggested that it

shouldn’t stand alone. The 2024 mitigation actions account for progress made on

mitigation actions since 2019, changes in development in Berkeley, and our new

understanding of the hazards we face. There are several new actions related to mitigating

the risk of Wildland Urban Interface Fire, resulting from the creation of a new WUI Division

in the Fire Department and the development of the Community Wildfire Protection Plan


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           E-5
(CWPP).


There are also new actions associated with mitigating the risks associated with Sea Level

Rise and Flooding near the waterfront, especially in light of new data about the risks of

rising groundwater.


The Mitigation Strategy also includes new actions associated with abiding by new state

laws around evacuation and the upcoming process to update the City’s General Plan,

Environmental Justice and Safety Element.


For the first time, this Mitigation Strategy highlights the work that community members do

to reduce risk in Berkeley. There are Actions listed for individuals and households to take

to reduce their risks and contribute to collective mitigation efforts.



Status of 2019 Mitigation Actions
This Plan was last adopted on December 20, 2019. Since that date, Berkeley has made

steady progress on implementing 2019 plan actions and supporting activities.


The following categories are used to describe the progress made since 2019:


   •   Completed: Activity has been completed as written.

   •   Completed with modifications: Over the course of completing this action, the City
       modified the activity to better meet the associated objective.

   •   In Progress: Progress has been made since 2019, but the activity is still ongoing.

   •   Deferred: Progress has not been made since 2019, but the activity is still relevant.

   •   Deferred with Modifications: Progress has not been made since 2019, but the
       activity is still relevant, and the City modified the activity to better meet the


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                          E-6
        associated objective.

    •   Deleted: Progress has not been made since 2019, and the activity is no longer
        relevant.

In Progress activities are incorporated into the 2024 LHMP’s mitigation strategy.


The Progress on the 2019 Actions are detailed in the Appendix in Status of 2019 Actions

Spreadsheet.



Integration of Information
As with previous updates, the 2019 LHMP was well integrated into other planning

mechanisms.


LHMP as an Appendix to the General Plan
Upon its adoption by the Berkeley City Council, the 2019 LHMP was incorporated as an

appendix to the Disaster Preparedness and Safety Element of the City’s General Plan.

The Plan’s goals, objectives, and policies serve as a guide for day-to-day decisions that

are essential for responsive government. Decisions made by Berkeley City Council and

its advisory boards, and commissions about the physical development of the City should

be consistent with the goals, objectives, and policies of the General Plan. The City Council

and Planning Commission use the General Plan when evaluating land use changes and

making funding and budget decisions. It will be used by the Zoning Adjustments Board

and City staff to help regulate development proposals and make decisions on projects.

The policies of the Plan apply to all property, both public and private, within the Berkeley

city limits.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                           E-7
Budget Process
Because the 2019 LHMP was by the City Council into the General Plan, the data and

information from the Risk Assessment as well as the hazard mitigation goals and actions

in the Mitigation Strategy influenced the City’s budget process. The budget process

assigns resources to address the goals, objectives, and community priorities set by the

City Council. The budget process is the final step of assigning resources to implement

mitigation actions.


In 2022 and 2023, the City of Berkeley considered the implication that extreme events,

like natural disasters, could have on the City government’s financial condition, particularly

its reserve levels for the general fund. In this plan for the first time, some hazard sections

Risk and Loss Estimates include analysis from the GFOA. The City engaged the GFOA

to produce a recommendation to help it decide the appropriate reserve level for the

general fund, given the risks from extreme events. GFOA is a non-profit association of

more than 23,000 state and local government finance professionals and elected officials

from across North America. A key part of GFOA’s mission is to promote best practices in

public finance, including reserve policies. The analysis by GFOA also shed light on the

potential broader economic losses to the community from the risks posed by extreme

events and created additional analysis incorporated into the 2024 LHMP.


Community Wildfire Protection Plan
The Community Wildfire Protection Plan approved in 2023 integrates information from the

2019 LHMP, expanding upon the 2019 Hazard Analysis and Mitigation Strategy. The

Community Wildfire Protection Plan is a roadmap for fire hazard mitigation and


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                             E-8
preparedness at both the City of Berkeley and neighborhood level and offers ways to

mitigate the risks posed by wildfires, including goals for improving wildfire response,

community preparedness, fuel management, infrastructure, ignition reduction, home

hardening, and more. Demonstrating the connection between these documents, the

Community Wildfire Protection Plan provided additional data, information, and hazard

mitigation goals related to wildland-urban interface fires


Vision 2050
Berkeley’s Mayor Arreguin launched Vision 2050, an initiative to encourage long-term

planning to meet the serious challenges to our infrastructure, including climate change,

inequality, population increases, and obsolescence. The Berkeley community voiced their

support for Vision 2050 with the passage of Measure R in the November 2018 election.

The Vision 2050 Task Force was formed in Spring 2018 and included over 40 Berkeley

community members with technical expertise and in-depth knowledge. The task force

was organized into four working groups: quality of life, environment, technology, and

finance/ management. The LHMP was one of the key plans reviewed and incorporated

into the Vision 2050 Framework, particularly on the topics of earthquakes and landslides.


Housing Element
In 2023, the City of Berkeley adopted a 2023-2031 Housing Element, deemed in

compliance with State Housing Element Law by the California Department of Housing

and Community Development on February 28, 2023. This Housing Element Update,

incorporated into Berkeley’s General Plan, contains goals, policies, and programs to

guide the City’s decision-making around the development and rehabilitation of housing,


Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                        E-9
to meet the City’s Regional Housing Needs Determination target of 8,934 new units of

housing, across income levels, in Berkeley over 8 years.


The 2019 LHMP was used as a background document in the development of the 2023-

2031 Housing Element and was referenced in regards to environmental constraints to

housing production. Specifically, the comprehensive strategy from the 2019 LHMP used

to mitigate Berkeley’s WUI fire hazard, including annual property inspections, more

restrictive local building code amendments, and vegetation management and defensible

space, was used to determine safe housing development and rehabilitation in this area

within the 2023-2031 Housing Element.




Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                    E-10
     F.    Plan Adoption
The public review process is considered a key step in the City Council’s adoption of the

2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan. To that end, City staff has engaged with City

Commissions and the City Council and throughout the process to develop this plan. Two

City Commissions play a key role in plan review and adoption:


Disaster and Fire Safety Commission
       The Disaster and Fire Safety Commission (DFSC) is made up of nine members

       appointed by the City Council, per the guidance of a local ordinance. This

       Commission meets in public monthly, and advises the City Council on all matters

       affecting fire safety and/or disaster resilience within Berkeley. For this reason,

       following FEMA’s issuance of Approval Pending Adoption for the Final Draft 2024

       LHMP, staff will request the Commission’s recommendation to Council on the Final

       Draft 2024 LHMP.


Planning Commission
       The Planning Commission oversees and reviews the planning process and

       planning issues. Revisions to the General Plan come before the Planning

       Commission, which meets twice each month in public. Because the Local Hazard

       Mitigation Plan is an appendix to the City of Berkeley’s General Plan, following

       FEMA’s issuance of Approval Pending Adoption for the Final Draft 2024 LHMP,

       staff will request the Commission’s recommendation to Council on the Final Draft

       2024 LHMP.
Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         F-1
Additional Commissions
       Concerned citizens staff nearly forty Berkeley commissions, boards and

       committees addressing a wide range of issues important to the community. All of

       these commissions meet in public.


Because of the wide scope of issues covered in the mitigation plan, the City invited all

Commissions to review the First Draft Plan during the public comment period from May

24 to August 8, 2024.


Following the public feedback deadline, City staff reviewed feedback from Commissions

and community members, and incorporated appropriate changes into the Final Draft Plan.


Following FEMA’s issuance of approval pending adoption, City staff will bring the Final

Draft 2024 LHMP to the City’s Disaster and Fire Safety Commission and Planning

Commission for their recommendations to City Council to adopt the Final Draft Plan.

Following those meetings, staff will bring the Final Draft 2024 LHMP to the Berkeley City

Council for adoption.

Final Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan                                         F-3
     G.    Community Education
In the 2024 LHMP Planning Process, the City endeavored to make the Risk Assessment

more applicable and accessible to individuals and households. First, to help the

community understand the hazards and associated risks, the City of Berkeley Office of

Emergency Services made videos available on YouTube that describe each hazard in

this Plan. The videos also include a list of Community Actions to reduce risk as well as

City Actions in the 2024 LHMP Mitigation Strategy. Additional videos related to mitigating

wildfire risk are available on www.BerkeleyFire.Com.


Traditionally, this Plan has focused on the Actions that the City takes, with partner

support, to mitigate risks. This plan recognizes that individuals and households also take

actions to reduce risk and contribute to the community’s collective mitigation efforts. To

support this work further, the end of Element C: Mitigation Strategy has a list of individual

and household actions to reduce risks associate with that hazard. The Appendix also

includes the list of Community Actions for individuals and households in a spreadsheet

format that also includes how much time, money, and effort each Action might take.

                                  What is Mitigation?




City of Berkeley Local Hazard Mitigation Plan ▪ Core Planning Team ▪ June 20, 2023   3
                                                                  Internal




What is Mitigation?
• Two ways to deal with hazards:
      - Increase emergency response capability
      - Increase actions taken to reduce or eliminate the impacts of future
        incidents


• Mitigation is sustained actions:
      - To reduce or eliminate long-term risks to people and property from
        hazards and their effects
      - That provide passive protection at the time of disaster impact




City of Berkeley Local Hazard Mitigation Plan ▪ Core Planning Team ▪ June 20, 2023   4
                                                                  Internal




What is Mitigation?
• Mitigation is:
      - Strengthening structures
      - Making land use decisions that will minimize damage
      - Reducing vegetation in high-fire areas
      - Strapping down water heaters


• Mitigation is not:
      - Purchasing equipment to use in emergency response
      - Conducting drills
      - Disaster awareness programs
      - Storage of disaster supplies for post-disaster relief

Why does this plan matter to Berkeley?
• Now: FEMA Grant Funding
      - Pre- and post-disaster
      - City has grant-funded projects completed, underway, and proposed


• In the next disaster: may reduce Berkeley’s disaster recovery
  costs
      - Can eliminate the 6.25% local match requirement for the City of Berkeley
        to receive post-disaster public assistance from FEMA

                                       Mitigation Goals




City of Berkeley Local Hazard Mitigation Plan ▪ Core Planning Team ▪ June 20, 2023   13
                                                                  Internal




2019 LHMP
 A.      Reduce the potential for loss of life, injury and economic damage to Berkeley
         residents and businesses from earthquakes, wildfires, landslides, floods,
         tsunamis, climate change, extreme heat, and their secondary impacts.
 B.      Increase City government’s ability to serve the community during and after
         hazardous events by mitigating risk to key City functions.
 C.      Connect with residents, community-based organizations, institutions,
         businesses, and essential lifeline systems in order to increase mitigation
         actions and disaster resilience in the community.
 D.      Preserve Berkeley’s unique character and values from being compromised by
         hazardous events.
 E.      Protect Berkeley’s historically underserved populations from the impacts of
         hazardous events by applying an equity lens, including equal access to
         mitigation efforts.

      - Prioritize actions in 2024 Mitigation Strategy (August)
      - Following initial public outreach process, re-prioritize actions as
        appropriate (September/October)

                                       Mitigation Goals
                                        (Second Draft)




City of Berkeley Local Hazard Mitigation Plan ▪ Core Planning Team ▪ August 2, 2023   3
                                                                   Internal




2024 Draft Mitigation Goals
A.    Reduce the potential for loss of life, injury, environmental and economic
      damage to Berkeley residents and businesses from earthquakes, wildfires,
      landslides, floods, tsunamis, climate change, heat waves, poor air quality,
      infectious disease, utility disruption, and their secondary impacts.
B.    Increase City government’s ability to serve the community during and after
      hazard events by mitigating risk to key City functions.
C.    Preserve Berkeley’s unique character and values from being compromised
      by hazard events.
D.    Connect with residents, community-based organizations, institutions,
      businesses, and essential lifeline systems in order to increase mitigation
      actions and disaster resilience in the community.
E.    Protect Berkeley’s historically underserved populations from the impacts of
      hazardous events by applying an equity focus to mitigation efforts.
     A.     Protect Berkeley’s underserved communities from the impacts of climate change and natural
            hazards by incorporating their needs and voices into mitigation planning and decision-
            making.

                                          Public Process

                                                                   Internal




Public Outreach Activities and Timeline
August through October
• Surveys and short conversations at in-person popular events (National Night Out, Solano Stroll, 1923
  Fire Anniversary, Farmer’s Markets, etc.).
• Short online survey, distributed via flyers, social media, website.
• Presentations and conversations with neighborhood groups
October – February (around/post First Draft Plan release)
• Presentations at Planning and Disaster and Fire Safety Commissions.
• Council Work Session
• Continued presentations and conversations with neighborhood groups, or hosted by local partners
• Short online videos that explore the Plan in bite sized chunks and provide a way for people to
  comment.
• Open email address for people to write in comments
• Drafts at each Library
• Flyers and social media encouraging responses

City of Berkeley Local Hazard Mitigation Plan ▪ Core Planning Team ▪ August 29, 2023   2
                                                                  Internal




                                       Mitigation Goals
                                         (Third Draft)




City of Berkeley Local Hazard Mitigation Plan ▪ Core Planning Team ▪ August 29, 2023   3
                                                                  Internal




2024 Draft Mitigation Goals
A.    Reduce the potential for loss of life, injury, environmental and economic
      damage to Berkeley residents and businesses from earthquakes, wildfires,
      landslides, floods, tsunamis, climate change, heat waves, poor air quality,
      infectious disease, sea level rise, wind, utility disruption, and their
      secondary impacts.
B.    Increase City government’s ability to serve the community during and after
      hazard events by mitigating risk to key City functions.
C.    Protect and enhance quality of life in Berkeley.
D.    Connect with residents, community-based organizations, institutions,
      businesses, and essential lifeline systems in order to increase mitigation
      actions and disaster resilience in the community.
E.    Protect Berkeley’s historically underserved populations from the impacts of
      hazardous events by applying an equity focus to mitigation efforts.
     - Co-create mitigation plans, policies, and programs with Berkeley’s underserved communities,
       elevating the voices of these community members and prioritizing their needs to prepare for
       and adapt to climate change and natural hazards.


City of Berkeley Local Hazard Mitigation Plan ▪ Core Planning Team ▪ August 29, 2023                 4

         Hazards addressed              Addresses hazards of            Addresses hazards of       Does not address

                                        multiple hazards

What can you do about flooding?




                                  23
 Protect your neighborhood
• Flooding often occurs due to storm drain blockage. Keep
  water flowing by participating in the adopt a drain
  program.




                                                            24
Protect your home
• Direct water away from your building.
• Watch how water flows or accumulates around your
  home to identify potential trouble spots.




                                                     25
Flood Insurance
                  • Consider flood insurance, since
                    typical homeowners insurance
                    policies do not cover flooding.

During heavy rains

                     • Elevate important items,
                       if possible, especially
                       from first floor/garage.
                     • Do not walk, swim or
                       drive through flooded
                       waters. Turn around,
                       don’t drown.
                     • Be ready for
                       power/internet outage
                     • If your home floods, be
                       ready for cleanup.

High Wind Events




                   32
How is Wind formed?

Wind is air in motion, traveling
   between areas of high
  pressure to low pressure

The steeper the difference in
air pressure, the stronger the
           wind is




                              33
                                        Wind in Berkeley

In Berkeley, high wind events are associated with
the seasons

o Winter: weather systems and cold fronts


o Summer: temperature and pressure differences
  between the Pacific Ocean and the interior
  valleys to the east create strong winds from the
  west


o Spring & Fall: warm, dry offshore winds from
  the northeast, known as “Diablo Winds”
                                                      34
                                     Related Hazards

Climate Change:
• More extreme storms and weather conditions are
  expected

Wildland Urban Interface Fire:
• The Fall “Diablo Winds” and dry vegetation could result
  in a high fire danger




                                                       35
                         What is “high wind”?



• Sustained wind of 40 mph or
  more, lasting for 1 hour or more
                 or
• Wind gust (usually 20-30
  seconds) of 58 mph or higher

Recap
• Creek flooding and storm drain issues cause most
  flooding in Berkeley
• Infrastructure improvements can reduce risks
• Residents can protect their neighborhoods and homes
• High winds can create dangerous situations – get ready
  and then stay out of the way if you can!

What is a Tsunami?
• Tsunamis affecting the Bay
  Area can result from
  offshore earthquakes
  within the Bay Area, or
  from very distant events.
• Tsunamis impacting the Bay
  Area are usually generated
  by faults in Washington and
  Alaska.




                                           8
                                             Internal




               Where is it in
                 Berkeley?
Tsunamis would mostly impact the areas
      of Berkeley near the Bay. From the
 coast to about sixth street is considered
     the tsunami zone. The area that we
   watch the most is the marina and the
                     maritime community.

Maritime Community




                     23
                               Internal




Keep Your Boat Tsunami Ready!
Make sure your boat is secured and ready. Keep in mind
that the City will shut down the dock 1 hour before the
tsunami’s anticipated arrival time.
  • Secure your boat to the dock and tie down any loose gear.
  • Check your dock line condition and replace any worn dock
    lines.
  • Remove as much loose boating gear onboard as possible,
    especially electronics and important documents. Any gear that
    will remain on your boat should be secured.
  • Turn off and disconnect shore power cords, water supply hoses
    and propane or other gas valves.
  • Secure and lock all hatches and port holes. Check for leaks,
    and seal them as necessary.

                                                                    24
                                     Internal




Maritime Community
The City of Berkeley will evacuate docks and shut them down within 1 hour of a
tsunami’s estimated arrival.

Dear Jenn,

My name is Jamie Albrecht, and I am an Emergency Services Coordinator with the City of Berkeley.
First, I want to thank you for all that you do to serve the Berkeley community. Second, I’d like to
invite you to contribute to our 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan.

The City of Berkeley is currently updating its 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan. The LHMP is a public
document that addresses Berkeley’s natural hazards and establishes a 5-year mitigation strategy to
better protect the community in the next disaster. As a key partner to the City of Berkeley, you are
invited to participate in the plan development process.

We’re interested in hearing from you:
  1. Description of your main functions and any disaster related work your organization does
  2. Any key vulnerabilities or concerns you have related to natural hazards in Berkeley. In the
      2024 update to the LHMP, we are considering the following natural hazards: earthquake,
      wildfire, tsunami, landslide, poor air quality, extreme heat, utility disruption, sea level rise,
      high wind events, and flooding.
  3. What actions do you recommend the City take to reduce disaster risk?
  4. What work in reducing disaster risk in Berkeley does your organization want to highlight or
      share from the last five years?

We hope you will take this as a great opportunity to inform the community about your concerns and
all your hard work to keep Berkeley safe. With this information, we can take better and more
informed actions as City and as a Berkeley community.

Please provide your feedback before September 18. I will follow up a few times between now and
then to provide a reminder. Please let me know if you have any questions or want to hop on a call.

Thank you again for your help with this Plan and for all that you do for Berkeley!

Warmly,

Jamie

Hi Trevor and Bruce,

I hope that you both have been doing well! It’s been nice to get to know you both a little bit more
through the luncheon and the recent meetings. I wanted to reach out about something a bit
different that I am currently working on, which is updating our 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan.
The linked website has the 2019 Plan.

The Local Hazard Mitigation Plan is a big, public document with strict requirements provided by the
Federal Emergency Management Agency that addresses Berkeley’s natural hazards, like
earthquakes, extreme heat, and wildfires. It also establishes a 5-year mitigation strategy to better
protect the community in the next disaster, focused on actions that reduce risk before a disaster
happens, like retrofitting buildings. As a key part of the Berkeley Community and partner to the City,
I hope you will considering contributing to the plan development process by sharing the following:

    1. Your role in the Berkeley community, and any functions you have before, during, or after a
       disaster
    2. Any key vulnerabilities or concerns you have related to natural hazards in Berkeley. In the
       2024 update to the LHMP, we are considering the following natural hazards: earthquake,
       wildfire, tsunami, landslide, poor air quality, extreme heat, utility disruption, sea level rise,
       high wind events, and flooding.
    3. What actions do you recommend the City take to reduce disaster risk?
    4. What work in reducing disaster risk does your organization want to highlight or share from
       the last five years?

We hope you will take this as a great opportunity to share your concerns as well all that you do to
keep Berkeley safe. With this information, we can take better and more informed actions as City and
as a Berkeley community.

Please provide your feedback by replying to this email before September 12. I will follow up a few
times between now and then to provide a reminder. Please let me know if you have any questions or
want to hop on a call.

Thank you again for your help with this Plan and for all that you do for Berkeley!

Warmly,
Jamie

document that addresses Berkeley’s natural hazards and establishes a 5-year mitigation strategy to
better protect the community in the next disaster. As a key partner to the City of Berkeley, you are
invited to participate in the plan development process.

We like to include the following information from key partners in our plan:
  1. Description of your main functions and any disaster related work you do
  2. Any key vulnerabilities or concerns you have related to natural hazards in Berkeley. In the
      2024 update to the LHMP, we are including sections on the following hazards: earthquake,
      wildfire, tsunami, landslide, poor air quality, extreme heat, utility disruption, sea level rise,
      high wind events, and flooding.
  3. Any actions you recommend the City take to reduce disaster risk? Or actions you want to or
      are currently working on with the City on to reduce risk? (I know you’re collaborating quite a
      bit with our Parks, Recreation, and Waterfront Department on some exciting grant
      opportunities, so we will definitely be highlight those, but feel free to share anything you want
      related to that work!)
  4. What work in reducing disaster risk in Berkeley does PG&E want to highlight or share from the
      last five years?

We hope you will take this as a great opportunity to inform the community about your concerns and

informed actions as City and as a Berkeley community.

1. ROLL CALL:
   Commissioners Present: Blaine Merker, Jeff Vincent, John E. Moore, Christina Oatfield,
   Emily Marthinsen, Elisa Mikiten, Alfred Twu, Savlan Hauser, and Barnali Ghosh.

   Commissioner Absent: None.

   Staff Present: Secretary Alisa Shen, Clerk Zoe Covello, Grace Wu, Justin Horner, Sarah
   Lana, and Eleanor Hollander.

2. LAND ACKNOWLEDGEMENT.

   Commissioner Ghosh shared that Indigenous Peoples Day Powwow and Indian Market will
   be held at Civic Center Park on Saturday, October 7th from 10am to 6pm.

   The City of Berkeley recognizes that the community we live in was built on the territory of
   xučyun (Huchiun (Hooch-yoon)), the ancestral and unceded land of the Chochenyo (Cho-
   chen-yo)-speaking Ohlone (Oh-low-nee) people, the ancestors and descendants of the
   sovereign Verona Band of Alameda County. This land was and continues to be of great
   importance to all of the Ohlone Tribes and descendants of the Verona Band. As we begin
   our meeting tonight, we acknowledge and honor the original inhabitants of Berkeley, the
   documented 5,000-year history of a vibrant community at the West Berkeley Shellmound,
   and the Ohlone people who continue to reside in the East Bay. We recognize that Berkeley’s
   residents have and continue to benefit from the use and occupation of this unceded stolen
   land since the City of Berkeley’s incorporation in 1878. As stewards of the laws regulating
   the City of Berkeley, it is not only vital that we recognize the history of this land, but also
   recognize that the Ohlone people are present members of Berkeley and other East Bay
   communities today. The City of Berkeley will continue to build relationships with the Lisjan
   Tribe and to create meaningful actions that uphold the intention of this land
   acknowledgement.

Mitigation Strategy Summary
• 33 Actions
• Focus:
      - Current work with funding secured
      - Improvements to buildings, infrastructure, and wildfire mitigation (aligning with
        the Community Wildfire Protection Plan)
• New actions
      - Mitigating poor air quality, infectious disease, high winds, and utility interruption
      - New WUI fire mitigation measures
      - Action to improve the way we communicate hazard information to marginalized
        populations
      - Climate Equity Collaborative work to engage community partners in resilience
        work
      - Evacuation Time Study

Local Hazard Mitigation Plan Update ▪ First Draft 2024 LHMP ▪ Commission Presentation       13
Land Use Planning Actions
• Maintaining City participation in National Flood Insurance Program
• Ensuring new and existing developments and infrastructure are protected
  from floods due to sea level rise through the permitting process for new
  development and conditions
• Use development standards to ensure new development does not
  contribute to an increase in flood potential
• Streamline the rebuilding process: Give priority to project applications that
  would rebuild to current standards following disasters.
• Complete implementation of the Evacuation and Response Time Study to
  identify necessary roadway safety improvements, along with prioritized
  roadways, to facilitate safe evacuation during emergency scenarios.
      - Land Use Planning is involved by providing guidance on current and potential
        development that might impact evacuation
      - The results of this Study will be included in the update to the Safety Element

                   What is Hazard Mitigation?




Local Hazard Mitigation Plan Update ▪ First Draft 2024 LHMP ▪ Commission Presentation   4
    Hazard mitigation breaks the cycle of
    damage, by taking action now to reduce
    impacts later.

Examples of mitigation activities
 • Home hardening (like in top photo)
 • Strengthening structures (like
   earthquake retrofits)
 • Making land use decisions that will
   minimize damage
 • Reducing vegetation in high-fire
   areas (like in bottom photo)
 • Strapping down water heaters

Local Hazard Mitigation Plan Update ▪ First Draft 2024 LHMP ▪ Commission Presentation   19
Tsunami
Mitigation Actions
• Continue to replace and repaid damaged
  finger docks
• Collaborate with the California Office of
  Emergency Services, the California
  Geological Survey, and the Federal
  Emergency Management Agency to
  document and explore additional tsunami
  hazard mitigation measures for Berkeley’s
  maritime communities.




Local Hazard Mitigation Plan Update ▪ First Draft 2024 LHMP ▪ Commission Presentation   20
Sea Level Rise
Mitigation Actions
• Mitigate the impacts of sea level rise in
  Berkeley.
   - Continue to ensure new and existing
      public and private developments and
      infrastructure are protected from floods
      due to sea-level rise through the
      permitting process for new
      development and conditions.
   - Identify funding and nature based
      solutions to adapt to sea level rise at
      Berkeley Waterfront areas at risk of
      future inundation




 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan Update ▪ First Draft 2024 LHMP ▪ Commission Presentation   21
                                                                                                     Berkeley Floodplains




Flood
Mitigation Actions
• Maintain City participation in the National
  Flood Insurance Program
• Use development standards to ensure that
  new development does not contribute to
  an increase in flood potential                                                     Storm Drain Issues

• Complete a Stormwater Master Plan for all
  City stormwater infrastructure
• Renovate the tide tubes that remove storm
  water from Berkeley Aquatic Park and
  Potter Street to the Bay
• Design public improvements such as
  streets, parks, and plaza for retention and
  infiltration of stormwater by diverting urban
  runoff to bio-filtration systems

 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan Update ▪ First Draft 2024 LHMP ▪ Commission Presentation                                 22
Utility Interruption
Mitigation Actions
• Urge PG&E to perform utility undergrounding in Berkeley's Very High Fire Hazard Severity
  Zone (VHFHSZ) to mitigate wildfire risk and limit evacuation and ingress obstruction.
• Coordinate undergrounding efforts with the State of CA Public Utilities Commission, and
  elected officials.
• Provide key hazard information and best practices to Berkeley's business and arts community
  through established networks, for example by exploring opportunities for local business to
  share best practices and resources during utility interruptions.
• Identify potential actions to mitigate energy assurance vulnerabilities at critical City facilities
  during planning/conceptual design of both retrofits and new construction.
• Provide guidance to help the City consider opportunities to design, finance and implement
  clean energy assurance strategies (e.g., photovoltaic-supplemented generation, energy
  efficiency activities, and/or mobile charging stations).
• Work with partners to identify additional non-City critical facilities and develop strategies to
  provide clean backup power at these sites.
• Create new formats and user friendly guidance to educate the public, especially underserved
  populations, on Berkeley hazards.

Pursuant to the City Council Rules of Procedure and State Law, the presiding officer may remove,
or cause the removal of, an individual for disrupting the meeting. Prior to removing an individual,
the presiding officer shall warn the individual that their behavior is disrupting the meeting and that
their failure to cease their behavior may result in their removal. The presiding officer may then
remove the individual if they do not promptly cease their disruptive behavior. “Disrupting” means
engaging in behavior during a meeting of a legislative body that actually disrupts, disturbs,
impedes, or renders infeasible the orderly conduct of the meeting and includes, but is not limited
to, a failure to comply with reasonable and lawful regulations adopted by a legislative body, or
engaging in behavior that constitutes use of force or a true threat of force.

Local Hazard Mitigation Plan Update
Share your ideas for actions the City of Berkeley and its residents can take to
reduce risks from natural hazards, such as earthquakes and wildfires.

Help inform the City of Berkeley’s updated First Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan. The Plan
outlines the hazards that can occur in Berkeley and what actions the City is taking to reduce risk. It also
lists actions that you can take to reduce personal risk and help our collective mitigation efforts.

The First Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan is available for review and comment until August 8.
The Plan Elements are linked below:

     Executive Summary (updated on 06/04/2024 to fix page numbers)

     Element A Planning Process

     Element B Risk Assessment (updated on 06/04/2024 to correct Berkeley Fire Zone map and to fix page
     numbers)

     Element C Mitigation Strategy

     Element D Plan Maintenance

     Element E Plan Update

     Element F Plan Adoption (only for Final Draft Plan)

     Element G Community Education

     Appendix


          Status of 2019 Actions Spreadsheet

          2024 Mitigation Strategy Actions Spreadsheet

          2024 Community Actions Spreadsheet


Help us by engaging with the first draft of the Plan, learning about the natural hazards that can occur in
Berkeley, like earthquakes and wildfires, and commenting on the lists of actions to reduce our risks.

To learn more about the hazards that can occur in Berkeley, watch our videos.

To be involved in the planning process:
     Attend one of our community presentations, which will be posted under ‘upcoming events’ at the bottom of
     this page

     Email mitigation@berkeleyca.gov with your comments by August 8

     Attend the Planning Commission meeting on June 5

     Attend the Disaster and Fire Safety Commission meeting on June 26




PROJECT OVERVIEW
All local governments are required to update their Local Hazard Mitigation Plans every five years. This
update provides an opportunity to assess any changes to the hazards Berkeley faces and to recommend
projects to reduce risk.

Natural hazards, like earthquakes and wildfires, can cause loss of life and damage property and
infrastructure. Mitigation is an investment in future safety and sustainability. By taking actions to reduce
risk now, we can reduce losses later.

Having an updated Local Hazard Mitigation Plan increases community safety by providing a roadmap of
actionable projects to reduce risks. An updated Plan also ensures the City is eligible for state and federal
disaster assistance and mitigation grants, like the ones that fund our seismic retrofit programs.



PROJECT TIMELINE
The 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan effort began in April 2023 and is estimated to be complete in
December 2024.

     First Draft Released (May 2024)

     Public Comment Period (May 24 – August 8, 2024)


          The Public Comment period was extended from July 31 as of June 26.

     California Office of Emergency Services and Federal Emergency Management Agency Approval (August –
     October 2024)

     Public Hearing at Planning Commission to Recommend Adoption of Plan (October 2024)

     Adoption of Final Plan (December 2024)

            The First Draft of the City’s 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (LHMP) update has been
            released on the City’s website (www.BerkeleyCA.gov/Mitigation). The document’s
            Executive Summary and Actions are attached to this letter.

            As a Commission Secretary, please:
               • Include the attached material as an Information Item in your next Commission
                  meeting packet
               • If your Commission wishes to provide feedback on the plan, please send
                  comments to mitigation@berkeleyca.gov by July 31.

            Plan Content
            The LHMP identifies natural hazards in Berkeley and outlines a five-year strategy to
            further protect Berkeley’s people, buildings, infrastructure, and environment from those
            hazards. The City began updating the LHMP in early 2023. This update effort will allow
            Berkeley to apply for federal mitigation grant programs and State funding, and is
            anticipated to be complete at the end of 2024.

            The content of the LHMP is dictated by State and federal requirements and focuses on
            City actions to reduce risks. In an effort to make the LHMP more relevant and
            accessible to community members, staff created a new section called “Berkeley
            Household Risk Reduction” to offer clear steps people can take to mitigate risks in their
            own households. Staff also wants to acknowledge all the work community members do
            to contribute to collective risk reduction in Berkeley by taking these actions.

            Commission Review
            All City Commissions are welcome to review the First Draft Plan. Commissions
            interested in providing feedback must submit it to mitigation@berkeleyca.gov by July

            meeting, staff will request the Commission’s recommendation to Council on the Final
            Draft Plan. Because the LHMP will be an amendment to the City’s General Plan, the
            Planning Commission must make a recommendation to Council on the Final Draft Plan.

            Staff will also present the Final Draft Plan to the Disaster and Fire Safety Commission.
            Because the Disaster and Fire Safety Commission closely monitors the City’s
            preparedness and mitigation efforts, staff will request that the Commission make a
            recommendation to Council on the Final Draft Plan at this meeting.

Subject:          Draft 2024 Local Hazard Mitigation Plan Posted for Public Comment
Date:             Thursday, May 30, 2024 4:38:00 PM


Dear Berkeley Parent Teacher Association,

The City of Berkeley is updating its Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, and the First Draft has been posted
for public review at http://www.berkeleyca.gov/mitigation. The Mitigation Plan identifies Berkeley’s
natural hazards of concern and outlines a five-year strategy to further protect Berkeley’s people,
buildings, infrastructure and environment from these hazards. Schools are a key part of our
collective disaster resilience – from the buildings they occupy to the services they provide to the
connections they create. We are interested in hearing from you and how we can help you feel ready
for the natural hazards in Berkeley.

We invite you to engage with the Plan, by either:

        Attending one of our public review workshops on June 3 or July 20
        Watching our detailed videos on Berkeley’s natural hazards
        Emailing your comments to mitigation@berkeleyca.gov
        Providing feedback in-person or via mail to the Berkeley Fire Department (2100 Martin Luther
        King Jr. Way)
        Attending our presentations at the Planning Commission on June 5 or Disaster and Fire Safety
        Commission on June 26

Members of the public are invited to provide written feedback on the First Draft Plan until July 31,
2021. If engaging with the Plan feels like too much, we understand that. If you’re interested in
connecting more in general with the Office of Emergency Services, please email me at
jalbrecht@berkeleyca.gov – I am very interested in connecting with schools, learning what you all
need, and seeing how we can work together.

Thank you so much for considering and for your dedication to the Berkeley community.

In service,
Jamie Albrecht

From:              rachel bradley

Subject:           Re: Public meetings re plan
Date:              Tuesday, June 4, 2024 5:50:32 PM



Thanks Jamie.

I have a couple of thoughts about WUI Fires (since I live in the Berkeley hills north of campus).

The first is the importance of protecting evacuation routes for residents (and incoming fire
trucks) by restricting parking on the narrow roads in the hills to make sure two cars can pass.
This is essential to keep residents safe. It should be enforced at all times by citations, and
especially on high fire risk days, when cars in violation should be towed. This is just the most
basic common sense, based on how people have died in previous fires. People act like they
have the right to park as many giant vehicles as they want on the public street in front of their
house, but this should not trump public safety. They may have to park elsewhere, or use their
driveways or garages. It's time to get serious about this in my opinion, and I know many
neighbors agree.

The second thing is the importance of having homeowners clear dead and dangerous
vegetation on their properties. This needs to be taken more seriously, and quick clean up
required (or else the city should clean and charge homeowners). I have called to report
dangerous conditions on neighborhood properties, and it usually takes many calls over many
weeks to get any results. Given the high risk of fire, this should be a priority.

Thanks for taking my comments into consideration.

Hello
I am a 50 year resident of Berkeley, a homeowner in South Berkeley.
I do not have the bandwidth to read your incredibly long proposals, but I would like to suggest an area of attention if
it is not already included:
Many of our street trees are in abysmal condition and they present a variety of hazards to people and property.
During natural disasters which may include heavy rain and winds, wildfires and earthquakes they can be the source
of danger and damage. As an example, I will discuss the camphor trees on my block, the 2200 block of Stuart St.
Many of them have been pruned by the city to avoid problems with power lines. Pruning in this manner only leaves
them extremely lopsided, prone to toppling in high winds and heavy rains. A number of the trees on my block have
huge dead limbs, and when the city has pruned some of these limbs (leaving other hazardous ones), again they have
dealt with one problem and caused others, more lopsided trees with potential to fall. We even have one camphor tree
where the entire crown is dead, but the city ignores it. I have been in touch with the Dept. of Forestry about this,
been added to waiting lists and seen the city come out and do a very minor and unbalanced job of pruning. And this
is just one block. Our street trees are important and valuable to us in so many ways - but the city must maintain them
and plant additional ones as the old ones die. Here is something the city can do that is an integral part of disaster
mitigation and which does not involve figuring out new ways to deal with difficult problems. The answers are
obvious, but not put into effect. I understand that there is limited money for the Forestry Dept., but perhaps some
funds for disaster mitigation could be correctly added to to street tree maintenance to mitigate these hazards.
Sabina McMurtry

From:               kelly hammargren
To:                 Mitigation
Subject:            LHMP Comments -
Date:               Thursday, August 8, 2024 10:22:53 PM


  WARNING: This is not a City of Berkeley email. Do not click links or attachments unless you trust the sender and
                                              know the content is safe.
The Local Hazard Mitigation Plan Update (LHMP) is very well done and as comprehensive as it is, listed here are a
few additions that need to be addressed regardless of the required LHMP Update timeline.

1) Berkeley should be aggressively moving toward Passive Houses and using Passive House Principles in multi-unit
buildings. This would increase living and working comfort and reduce energy load on the grid.
https://www.phius.org/passive-building/what-passive-building/passive-building-principles

In the Strategy Action chart #49 encourage passive and energy efficient strategies are listed as is the word
"ongoing." Since I have attended every public meeting on new project approvals for nearly 10 years, I can tell you
this is not happening.

2) Passive house principles locate operable windows for the best exposure to cooling breezes. Currently new
construction is designed with no consideration to cooling breezes.

3) The Zoning Adjustment Board (ZAB) and Design Review Committee (DRC) focus on the exterior design not the
interior. There is no current regulation/ordinance in Berkeley that requires operable windows in bedrooms which
means that multi-unit buildings have been approved with multiple bedrooms with no windows. In the situation
where there is an extreme heat event and a power failure these rooms and units become a heat trap / a death trap.

4) The Zoning Ordinances before the City Council establish setbacks between buildings without consideration to air
current, air circulation. This will be increasingly important as the climate continues to warm and heat events become
more frequent. Lining San Pablo with wall to wall taller buildings will impact air flow, increase heat island effect
and create micro climates of sustained heat.

5) Tree canopy is listed as a mitigation in heat events under 51, however, the problem is Berkeley's Urban Forestry
selections are small trees in inadequate spaces instead native trees with large canopies as on California between
Dwight and Allston. The city is being filled through the forestry program with none native trees that do not support
local habitat and ecosystems besides being inadequate to provide shading in heat events.

6) Permeable paving is not listed as a mitigation to stormwater in 53. Permeable paving can easily be incorporated
into street design as was done on the north side of Channing between MLK Jr Way and Milvia. It has also been used
on the north side of San Pablo Park. Permeable paving is not the same as bioswales. Permeable paving could be used
throughout the city instead of hardscape, impermeable concrete, or asphalt in driveways, sidewalks, etc.

5) A large gas pipeline runs up Allston through neighborhoods, past the high school (with over 3000 students) and
by city hall. There is no reporting on inspections and status. A leak and explosion of this gas pipeline like what
happened in 2010 in San Bruno at Milvia and Allston during a work day and school day has the potential to wipe
out much of city government and the high school student body. Not only does there need to be reporting by PG&E,
but in addition electrification needs to be accelerated to remove this kind of hazard.

6) Just like there are notifications of asbestos in buildings, there needs to be notifications to renters when units being
considered for renting and to occupants of rented units that are in fire zones, hillside slide areas, within proximity to
the Hayward fault and when rental housing is in soft story buildings at risk of collapse.

kelly hammargren

effect on the health of our community. The video emphasizes that the health threats of air
contaminants fall mainly on seniors and
pregnant and nursing women, two groups many of whose members lack the financial
resources to protect themselves, at the same time
those most likely to be outside walking.

I have lived in Berkeley since 1987, first on the east side of the city and, since 2005, on the far
west side. I have experienced an extreme
difference in air quality in the two locations and the lack of attention the City has given to this
problem. On the far west side of the city,
there is constant infiltration of our homes and bodies by dangerous particulate matter. We
sweep it up and wash it off our faces every
night. My house dust is dark grey. My lungs feel constricted and only when I make it to the
Marina can I breathe deeply.

Berkeley’s proposals for dealing with these problems are, to me, inadequate. The city proposes
planting trees, providing more convenient parking spaces and encouraging residents to walk
and use bikes, scooters and EV cars.

It seems the City government is trying to delegate responsibility for dealing with these toxic
problems to the general citizenry while failing to take concerted City actions.

Must we wear a mask every day for the rest of our lives?
Install and maintain expensive air filtration systems?
Buy a very costly electric car?
Consult a ‘Spare the Air’ website to find out just how bad our air is on any given day?

Can we really expect our senior population to get around Berkeley on bicycles and scooters in
increasing traffic, trying to be safe as cars
and cyclists alike fail to stop at stop signs and red lights, or even use their signals, drivers and
pedestrians often lost on their phones?

The City wants to encourage walking to reduce auto pollution. But uneven sidewalks, broken
surface streets and poor lighting are
endemic in Berkeley and hardly invite anyone, let alone older residents, to walk outside. I
myself have fallen twice on city streets and many seniors I know have fallen similarly with
resulting sprains, bruising and broken bones.

I’m aware the City has planted some trees on the southwest side of Berkeley and has bought
electric buses. However, our City must do
much better than this.

An important line of attack would be building highway barriers to shield residents from the
roads’ harmful air pollution. There is no barrier at all along 580/80 through Berkeley. In other
cities along the 80 and 580 corridor, there are trees, berms, plantings and walls absorbing a
significant amount of the particulate matter along the roadway. In Berkeley, there is basically
nothing. Increased traffic including
trucks (and freight trains) along the 580/80 make this a worsening problem.

Apartment building developers also have had a continuously deleterious effect on how our
City looks and how it feels to walk down a
street. On Berkeley’s streets, buildings are being built to the last permitted inch, forcing
pedestrians ever closer to truck and car exhaust
containing these particulates.

Imagine walking in the new shoreline park at the end of University Avenue, and not breathing
in the toxic particulate-filled air of 580/80.

Imagine trees and bushes planted along the highway, train way and City commercial/major
streets, providing an environment friendly to
people and birds besides pigeons and seagulls. Imagine tree-lined streets providing cooling
protection from the heat,
cleaning the air and uplifting our spirits.

Imagine shady, spacious, accessible streets working to make life healthier and happier.

Thank you for your attention.

Denah S. Bookstein

2430 Fifth St., Studio L
Berkeley, CA 94710
District Two
