Friends of Five Creek appreciates the opportunity to comment on
Berkeley's Local Hazards Mitigation Plan, May 2024 draft.
We are a 28-year-old, all-volunteer group working for creeks, watersheds,
and local nature from Berkeley to Richmond. We have dealt with risks of
erosion and flooding on local creeks for many years and seen the collapse
of aging culverts. As climate changes, we are increasingly concerned with
the likely effects of sea-level rise and groundwater infiltration, as well as
increased probability of deluges.


This plan is an excellent start. Ongoing improvements and
collaborations will be vital.
The plan's focus and highest level of detail are on wildfire and earthquake.
Development in other areas will be needed. The examples below
regarding collaboration come from our water-related interests. We believe
they apply to other areas as well, with many potential win-wins. For
example, without claiming expertise, increased subsidies for heat pumps
might benefit low-income residents, reduce greenhouse-gas emissions,
lessen air pollution, and reduce dangers from heat waves, leading to a
high cost-benefit ratio.
1. We are delighted that the plan builds in frequent opportunities
for updates as well as ongoing input via a dedicated web site, to be
reviewed by a specific commission.
We have already recommended this model to another city! We look
forward to its use in other Berkeley planning processes. (From the July 31
meeting of the Council Policy Committee on Facilities, Transportation,
Infrastructure, and Sustainability (FITES), we believe that a similar web
site will be used in developing the coming Stormwater Plan).
2. Collaboration among departments and commissions will be
essential to flesh out this plan. Here are examples from F5C's areas of
interest:
       In the area of sea-level rise, the draft recognizes that groundwater
       infiltration due to sea-level rise is a serious threat, with research new
       and ongoing. This should be developed in the coming stormwater
       plan, whose scope is being amended to incorporate these effects. The
     Disaster and Fire Safety Commission should be aware of, and have
     input into, these aspects as they develop.
     Similarly, from the FITES meeting, we understand that the
     stormwater plan's scope is being expanded to include modeling of the
     increasing probability of deluges, as these will affect severity and
     length of flooding (p. B204). This should be collaboratively
     incorporated into the Local Hazards Mitigation Plan as soon as
     possible.
     The current draft refers only in passing to the effects of higher tides
     on flooding in West Berkeley, and tides' and storms' interplay with
     Aquatic Park, which serves as a safety outlet for the city's largest
     storm drains, Strawberry/University and Potter. These threats should
     be explored as part of the stormwater plan.
     The maps and comments in Section B are highly informative, but they
     also show data gaps. For example, the storm drain overflow map on B
     195 shows locations of service calls -- but not which sites get
     preventive maintenance or repeat calls. The stormwater plan should
     remedy this, and thus strengthen this plan.
3. Planning should move rapidly toward exploring and advocating
collaboration with agencies other than the city.
For example, the East Bay Regional Park District is beginning plans for the
North Basin Strip -- much of northwest Berkeley's waterfront -- in
September. Berkeley should be involved in this process, because
decisions will affect flood potential in Northwest Berkeley. In a
simple example, "daylighting" the mouth of Schoolhouse Creek would
decrease flood risk in residential areas east of the freeway (by, in effect,
shortening the constricted "hose" that water needs to pass through).
Collaboration is important with tate Parks and East Bay Regional Park
District for most of the waterfront, CalTrans and the railroad near the
waterfront, and UC Berkeley, Albany, and El Cerrito for creeks, which are
now recognized as being possible wildfire conduits as well [possible areas
of floods and slides.
The plan's collection of low-cost recommendations for
preparedness looks valuable. We hope to find ways to publicize
those dealing with flooding and urban runoff. Perhaps there could be
brainstorming for ways to remind people repeatedly, without too heavy a
hand? Could nonprofits help? An interesting project for a student intern?
These comments are not criticisms. They look to the near future and
the promise of frequent improvements to this plan.
Susan Schwartz, President

To:              City of Berkeley Office of Emergency Services
From:            Disaster and Fire Safety Commission
Submitted by: Weldon Bradstreet, Chair
Subject:         Commission Comments and Questions about the 2024 Local Hazard
                   Mitigation Plan

The Disaster and Fire Safety Commission presents the following comments on the
Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (“LHMP”) The Commissioners are referring these
comments to the OES for their consideration and inclusion, where appropriate, into the
LHMP.

                                 General Comments on the LHMP

A key point we would like to raise in the hazard mitigation work is pointing out that
Berkeley’s continuing efforts to implement Vision Zero by installing protected bike lanes
and pedestrian improvements represents a mitigation strategy for the Extreme Heat,
Sea Level Rise and Air Pollution scenarios because it is the key ingredient in motivating
people to ride or walk in Berkeley, rather than drive. Vehicle emissions are of course a
key driver of carbon emissions and climate change.
Many other cities are ignoring this approach to creating a transportation mode shift, so
Berkeley should get credit for this. We know from the City’s transportation survey, cited
in the attached, that over 70% of Berkeley residents have indicated that they would use
a bike rather than a vehicle for most needs, but only about 10% do this because the
streets are unsafe for cycling.
Creating a transportation infrastructure that’s safe for cycling is essential to reducing
vehicle emissions and the environment problems they produce, including extreme heat,
sea level rise and air pollution events.

"Vapor Pressure Deficit" should be added to our metrics in determining when to warn
residents of potential fire hazard. Vapor Pressure Deficit measures the dryness in the
atmosphere that has the propensity to suck moisture out of all vegetation. A spike in the
Vapor Pressure Deficit signals dangerous fire conditions. This index should be
monitored.




    2180 Milvia Street, Berkeley, CA 94704 ● Tel: (510) 981-7000 ● TDD: (510) 981-6903 ● Fax: (510) 981-7099
              E-mail: manager@CityofBerkeley.info Website: http://www.CityofBerkeley.info/Manager
The Planning Department should not announce zoning or planning changes without first
consulting with the Fire Department and the Disaster and Fire Safety Commission,
including changes in planning codes and ordinances. Berkeley is a densely populated
town, one of the densest places in California. Increased density may play an important
role in our emergency response capability, and thus impact the safety of our citizens.
City streets need to be considered when planning or approving multi‐story
developments. The spate of plans on the two lane section of Shattuck between Derby
and the border with Oakland would seem to strain our ability to move people and
equipment on that narrow stretch. There are numerous retail operations on this street ‐
most importantly the Berkeley Bowl grocery store, What will be the impact if several
multi‐story buildings go up? A fire or earthquake in the late afternoon could be
calamitous if fire trucks had to access these blocks.

In terms of climate resilience Berkeley needs to take measures to protect roof top solar
panels, especially those attached to batteries. Right now, solar arrays have little or no
value in the planning process. Solar access must be prioritized in planning. In power
blackouts, these roof top arrays, attached to batteries could be our main source of
power, apart from emergency generators attached to buildings. But, these arrays do not
require any fuel.
Berkeley should research and adopt measures to establish "micro‐grids" based on solar
panels in neighborhoods. This could be vital to power medical equipment, cooling,
communication, and water pumps.
With the increased impacts of climate change Berkeley should heed the UN scientists
who have determined that any structure over five stories is not carbon neutral and
cannot generate adequate power to keep itself going. The UN panel does say this will
have an impact on urban density, but that it is more important that density.
With more intense storms, Berkeley needs to review its flood and water flow rules,
ordinances and regulations. Right now, the Planning Department says that there are no
rules regulating run‐off from one property onto another. If true, this needs to be
addressed, given that we have stronger storms, the water table is rising, and the sea
level is rising. New or old developments may start to cause problems with how their
water does or does not drain from their property. This is especially important along
historic creeks, storm drains, hillsides, and new developments with excavations deeper
than five feet.

Re: 2024 First Draft Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (LHMP)

Dear LHMP Project Managers,

The Berkeley FireSafe Council (FireSafe Council) is pleased to provide comments on the 2024
First Draft Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (LHMP).

About the FireSafe Council

The FireSafe Council is a community not-for-profit 501(c)(3) organization with the primary mission
of preventing the next catastrophic wildfire in Berkeley. Our principal focus since 2019 has been
reducing hazardous vegetation in and around the city, focusing on the 100+ tons of eucalyptus
debris in the understory of nine eucalyptus groves among the homes in the City’s Fire Zone 2. We
have developed a volunteer-led model, conducting 37 debris-clearing events to date involving over
50 residents and approximately 1,000 UC Berkeley student workdays. The City of Berkeley has
supported this effort by providing Zero Waste green bins and Parks Department trucks to remove
the debris to the City’s green waste site at no charge.

The FireSafe Council estimates that we have removed 75 tons of highly flammable bark, branches,
and leaves from the understory of six of the nine eucalyptus groves on private property, more than
half of the accumulated fuel. These clean ups have been funded by community donations and
grants. Although highly efficient, this model cannot be sustained by the FireSafe Council and, at the
pace we have been able to work, the groves we cleared in 2021 will need to be cleaned up again
before we complete the process. For this reason, the FireSafe Council strongly supported the City
Council’s recent resolution in support of using up to $1 million of Measure FF funds to conduct a one-
time, voluntary eucalyptus understory clean-up on select private properties within the city, with
subsequent maintenance by the property owners. The one-time clean-up of eucalyptus debris by the
City will also enable property access to Fire Department inspectors, an obstacle that has been
particularly problematic for inspecting the eucalyptus groves.

In addition to the above direct action to remove fuel, we have supported Chief Sprague in his
development and implementation of the city’s residential inspection program, participated in
essentially all the Disaster and Fire Safety Commission meetings, and taken numerous other steps
to point out wildfire safety needs and to support public officials in pursuing wildfire safety.
Berkeley FireSafe Council
p. 2

Comments on Draft LHMP

Discuss hazardous vegetation in Element B (Risk Assessment). Element B mentions dense
fuel loads as a compounding factor in the WUI risk, but while the section elaborates, for example, on
existing structure density (which is not mitigatable), it does not elaborate on vegetative fuel loads
(which the city is addressing, as noted, through various vegetation management programs). The
vegetative fuel load – particularly hazardous, fire-prone vegetation such as eucalyptus, Monterey
Pine, and juniper – should be characterized in terms of the WUI risk it presents.

As the FireSafe Council has documented, there are approximately 1,000 eucalyptus trees in
northeast Berkeley, most of which are concentrated in 9 groves on private property. Should these
tall groves ignite in a wind-driven canopy fire, embers and firebrands would ignite additional ground
fires miles ahead of the leading edge of the fire. Including this information in Element B would
provide some context for the statement in Element C, p. C-44, that “Since 2019, Berkeley has
removed nearly 300 hazardous trees (mostly eucalyptus and Monterey Pine) from City parks, paths,
and street rights-of-way” and the recently approved eucalyptus debris-clearing program that should
be mentioned in Element C, as noted below.

Junipers and other fire-prone vegetation commonly seen adjacent to homes are more prone to ignite
homes and other structures, particularly in structure-dense areas, leading to the “structure-to-
structure ignition” discussed on pp. B-65 and B-66.

Re-locate the Element B section on Berkeley Household Risk Reduction to Element C.
Element B is focused on risk assessment but includes a section on “Berkeley Household Risk
Reduction” (p. B-87) that lists numerous steps that individual community members and households
can take to reduce their fire risk. This section is better suited for Element C as part of the mitigation
strategy.

Placing the household action section in Element C will also allow it to be paired with the City’s efforts
to encourage or require individuals and households to act to reduce the community’s risk, and how
the City is complementing those efforts. This will better describe “how the whole community can
work together to mitigate Berkeley’s wildland-urban interface fire hazards” (p. B-87).

Element C should state an intention to develop specific planning goals and metrics on
several topics. Element C:

        “outlines Berkeley’s mitigation strategy, and how it connects to Berkeley’s disaster
        resilience vision. The strategy identifies and analyzes a comprehensive range of
        specific mitigation actions and activities being considered to reduce the effects of
        each hazard described in Element B: Risk Assessment. The Strategy is based on
        existing authorities, policies, programs, and resources, as well as Berkeley’s ability
        to expand on and improve these existing mitigation tools …”

Thus, it is intended to include forward-looking actions as well as descriptions of current
programs. However, the section mostly lists or describes existing programs with little to no
discussion of what the goals of these programs are, when they will be accomplished,

and where funding or additional policies are needed. In short, it is missing a plan for how
Berkeley intends to measurably reduce WUI fire risk. The document should reference the
city’s intentions to develop such a plan.

                                                    2
Berkeley FireSafe Council
p. 3

We are pleased to see the statement on p. C-43 that the BFD’s WUI Division is:

        “working to develop a comprehensive WUI work plan that will provide strategic
        guidance for related work for the next five years. Plans are to expand existing
        programs and extend some services citywide, including fuel reduction on public
        lands and roadsides, private land incentives, debris bins, and citywide chipping
        services.”

While we strongly support such planning, the stated intention to plan should be extended to include
risk-reduction goals, timelines, funding, policy needs, and metrics.

Similarly, the LHMP should state an intention to develop a plan with goals and metrics to improve
WUI evacuation routes through the Safe Passages and other programs, following the completion of
the evacuation studies now underway (noted on pp. C-52 and C-53). The draft LHMP includes very
little discussion of evacuation issues, and the Safe Passages program is not noted.

Related and more broadly, the LHMP should state an intention to develop a spending plan for
Measure FF funds, with goals, timelines, funding, and metrics for WUI and other LHMP-related
issues. The section on Measure FF (p. C-20) summarizes the measure and includes only backward-
looking achievements without any forward-looking goals. For example, the long-range plan could
include removal of all fire-prone vegetation in Fire Zones 2 & 3, with special emphasis on any
hazardous vegetation near structures and all hazardous trees, primarily eucalyptus. The section
should mention that the funding measure is indefinite, and that wildfire prevention and preparedness
activities is one of three categories of allowed purposes for the use of Measure FF funds.

These items should be included in the list of action items.

Element C should indicate the importance of land use planning in reducing exposure to
wildfire risks. The document notes the importance of planning and zoning in reducing Berkeley’s
vulnerability to landslide and flood hazards (Table 5, PDF-p. 61). The document should similarly
note (in the text and the table) the importance of planning and zoning – as well as building codes
and property transfer requirements – in reducing Berkeley’s vulnerability to wildfire, e.g., by studying
the wildfire risks associated with additional population and street parking in Berkeley’s fire zone 2
and 3.

Specific additional suggestions.

    Executive Summary

    •   The compounding impact of climate change on WUI fire should be noted in the Executive
        Summary. The FireSafe Council supports the change in this updated LHMP to incorporate
        climate change into every hazard of concern, rather than addressing it as a separate item.
        The compounding impact of climate change on WUI fire is discussed in

        Element B but is not mentioned in the WUI fire section of the Executive Summary, as it is in
        the “high wind” and “extreme heat” sections of Executive Summary.




                                                   3
Berkeley FireSafe Council
p. 4


   Element B

   •   The architectural significance of Berkeley’s Zone 2 should be noted in the “Natural, historical,
       and culture assets” section of Element B (p. B-82), in addition to the features
       in Zones 1 and 3. Many of the Berkeley Architectural Heritage Association’s “41 Berkeley
       Walking Tours” are in Zone 2.

   •   Exhibit 11 (p. B-86) is difficult to understand. The y-axis should be redrawn to end at $20
       billion (so the trend lines are visible) and the increments relabeled as billions of dollars,
       rather than millions. Otherwise, it’s easy to misread $40,000 million as $40 million, instead of
       $40 billion, which we assume is what is intended.

   Element C

   •   The statement (p. C-20) that the Disaster and Fire Safety Commission reviews and approves
       projects to receive Measure FF funding should be modified. The Commission can only
       recommend budgets and expenditures to Council and, to date, has not been able to do that
       due to lack of sufficient and timely information.

   •   To the list of vegetation management programs listed on p. C-43, add the new
       program to use Measure FF funds to conduct one-time, voluntary eucalyptus
       understory clean-ups on select private properties within the City, prioritized based on
       assessed wildfire risk. On May 7, 2024, the City Council adopted the supportive
       “Resolution to Mitigate Hazardous Eucalyptus Understory on Participating Properties,”
       stating that “hazardous fuel mitigation is the safest and most effective method to
       reducing wildfire risk.”

   •   In Table 4 on High Priority Actions, add the underlined text to this action item: “Coordinating
       regional wildfire mitigation strategies with key partners and stakeholders in adjacent
       municipal jurisdictions.” Consider naming the regional partners in subsection C.1.m.

   General

       The document should be proofread for typos.


The FireSafe Council appreciates the opportunity to comment on the draft LHMP.

On behalf of the Berkeley FireSafe Council

From:               kelly hammargren
To:                 Mitigation
Subject:            LHMP Comments -
Date:               Thursday, August 8, 2024 10:22:53 PM


  WARNING: This is not a City of Berkeley email. Do not click links or attachments unless you trust the sender and
                                              know the content is safe.
The Local Hazard Mitigation Plan Update (LHMP) is very well done and as comprehensive as it is, listed here are a
few additions that need to be addressed regardless of the required LHMP Update timeline.

1) Berkeley should be aggressively moving toward Passive Houses and using Passive House Principles in multi-unit
buildings. This would increase living and working comfort and reduce energy load on the grid.
https://www.phius.org/passive-building/what-passive-building/passive-building-principles

In the Strategy Action chart #49 encourage passive and energy efficient strategies are listed as is the word
"ongoing." Since I have attended every public meeting on new project approvals for nearly 10 years, I can tell you
this is not happening.

2) Passive house principles locate operable windows for the best exposure to cooling breezes. Currently new
construction is designed with no consideration to cooling breezes.

3) The Zoning Adjustment Board (ZAB) and Design Review Committee (DRC) focus on the exterior design not the
interior. There is no current regulation/ordinance in Berkeley that requires operable windows in bedrooms which
means that multi-unit buildings have been approved with multiple bedrooms with no windows. In the situation
where there is an extreme heat event and a power failure these rooms and units become a heat trap / a death trap.

4) The Zoning Ordinances before the City Council establish setbacks between buildings without consideration to air
current, air circulation. This will be increasingly important as the climate continues to warm and heat events become
more frequent. Lining San Pablo with wall to wall taller buildings will impact air flow, increase heat island effect
and create micro climates of sustained heat.

5) Tree canopy is listed as a mitigation in heat events under 51, however, the problem is Berkeley's Urban Forestry
selections are small trees in inadequate spaces instead native trees with large canopies as on California between
Dwight and Allston. The city is being filled through the forestry program with none native trees that do not support
local habitat and ecosystems besides being inadequate to provide shading in heat events.

6) Permeable paving is not listed as a mitigation to stormwater in 53. Permeable paving can easily be incorporated
into street design as was done on the north side of Channing between MLK Jr Way and Milvia. It has also been used
on the north side of San Pablo Park. Permeable paving is not the same as bioswales. Permeable paving could be used
throughout the city instead of hardscape, impermeable concrete, or asphalt in driveways, sidewalks, etc.

5) A large gas pipeline runs up Allston through neighborhoods, past the high school (with over 3000 students) and
by city hall. There is no reporting on inspections and status. A leak and explosion of this gas pipeline like what
happened in 2010 in San Bruno at Milvia and Allston during a work day and school day has the potential to wipe
out much of city government and the high school student body. Not only does there need to be reporting by PG&E,
but in addition electrification needs to be accelerated to remove this kind of hazard.

6) Just like there are notifications of asbestos in buildings, there needs to be notifications to renters when units being
considered for renting and to occupants of rented units that are in fire zones, hillside slide areas, within proximity to
the Hayward fault and when rental housing is in soft story buildings at risk of collapse.

kelly hammargren

Extreme Heat

Slide: Extreme Heat Events

There are multiple factors that identify an extreme heat as a hazard and they include:

- Extreme heat days: days when temperatures reach the 98th percentile of historic maximum
temperature. In Berkeley, an extreme heat day is a day above 88.3 degrees F.

- Warm nights: Nights that do not allow people to cool down and recover, which can increase health
risks. Tn Berkeley, nights are considered warm when temperatures do not cool below 61.7 degrees F.

- Heat wave: happens when there are five or more days of extreme heat days.

- Extreme heat during unexpected times of year: occurs outside of historically hotter months.

- And the last factor is the duration of a heat wave. The longer heat waves have proportionally more
negative impacts on human health and infrastructure than shorter heat waves.

Slide: Urban Heat Island Effect

Extreme heat events can be further exacerbated by the urban heat island (UHI) effect, through which
densely-built cities like Berkeley experience higher temperatures in comparison to surrounding more
rural areas. Factors contributing to the UHI effect include:

- A relative lack of vegetation;

- Reduced air flow because of structures;

- An abundance of hard, dark surfaces—such as buildings, streets, cars and sidewalks— which absorb
heat rather than reflect it. These surfaces also slowly release that absorbed heat throughout the night,
contributing to warmer nighttime temperatures as well.

UHI Connections to…

UHI effect could also be connected to climate change, wildfires, and the air quality.

Due to climate change, projections indicate that the number of extreme heat days, warm nights, and
heat waves will increase exponentially in the next few decades. In addition to this increased frequency
and duration, heat waves are also expected to occur in months not typically associated with extreme
heat.

While hot temperatures do not necessarily start fires, they can decrease moisture in vegetation,
increasing its flammability and the duration and severity of the fire season. Warming temperatures
combined with increased development in the wildland-urban interface are projected to increase fire risk
in most of the Bay Area.

While naturally-occurring ozone that exists higher in the Earth’s atmosphere is beneficial to the climate,
ground-level ozone can be extremely harmful to human health. Extreme heat can contribute to the
formation of ground-level ozone, also known as smog, and other secondary air pollutants, when
                                                    Internal



emissions from industrial facilities, power utilities, cars, trucks and other sources chemically react in the
presence of heat and sunlight. Extreme heat can also cause stagnant air conditions, causing the smog to
stay low longer, and increase community exposure.

Slide: Map of the Tree Coverage

The two main factors that influence how hot it is in certain parts of Berkeley are the urban heat island
effect and thermal belting.

We know that the urban heat island effect often makes temperatures hotter in the urban, more dense
parts of a city. This map of the percentage of tree coverage visualizes what parts of Berkeley might be
more likely to suffer from the urban heat island effect. In Berkeley, The areas shaded in darker green,
predominately in the hills in east Berkeley, have the greatest percentage of tree canopy, while west and
south Berkeley have the smallest percentage of tree canopy.

Urban tree canopy directly reduces the available for heat absorption surfaces and creates shading
beneficial to individuals and buildings. Trees also improve air quality that often worsens during extreme
heat events.

Slide Thermal Belting

Another factor that influences how hot it is in certain parts of Berkeley is thermal benting.

Although the Berkeley hills have a greater tree canopy, temperatures are often higher there than the
rest of the city. The thermal belt phenomenon occurs in areas where there is a hillside and a valley
below. Heat is absorbed by the ground during the day, and the heat energy radiates up from the soil at
night. As the warm air rises, the radiation of the heat causes the air closest to the ground to cool. Since
cold air is heavier than warm air, cooler air sinks down the hillside into the valley. As the cooler air fills
the valley, the warm air heads upwards. This warm air becomes trapped on the hilltop and is referred to
as a thermal belt. For Berkeley, this means that the hills are likely to be way hotter at night than the rest
of the city. The map below shows temperature differentials between the Berkeley hills, flats, and coast
at 11:30 pm at night on Monday, September 5. The Berkeley hills have temperature readings in the 90s
while the flats and waterfront have temperatures in the 60s and 70s.

Heat Index Table

The National Weather Service uses a Heat Index to measure how hot it really feels when relative
humidity is factored in with actual air temperature. The National Weather Service will initiate alert
procedures when the heat index is expected to exceed 105 degrees to 110 degrees Fahrenheit (which is
the orange section of the table marked as dangerous).

Heat Risk Table

 Another National Weather Service HeatRisk index provides a forecast of heat-related impacts to occur
after a 24-hours of exposure to heat. HeatRisk takes into consideration how unusual the heat is for the
time of year, the duration of the heat including daytime and nighttime temperatures, and if those
temperatures pose an elevated risk of heat-related impacts.

Map of ER visits
                                                   Internal



According to the University of California, Los Angeles, across the entire state of California, on an average
heat day, there are a total of 8,222 excess emergency room visits. Alameda County has, on average, 3.5
excess visits to the emergency room for heat related problems per 10,000 persons. This map shows the
rate of the excess emergency room visits in Berkeley, with the darker colors in West and South Berkeley,
indicating higher rates of emergency room visits. Both, West and South Berkeley, have higher
concentrations of low income individuals and people of color, due to historic patterns of disinvestment,
resulting in higher risk and worse outcomes on hot days.

Slide Reducing Vulnerabilities

One of the main strategies to mitigate extreme heat is to reduce Berkeley’s vulnerabilities. This could be
accomplished by expanding the urban forestry team and their activities, encouraging passive and
energy-efficient strategies to cool down buildings, and implementing programs and projects to reduce
emissions. The departments that work on reducing vulnerabilities, such as lack of vegetation, abundance
of dark-absorbing surfaces and poor air quality, are Parks, Recreation, and Waterfront Department,
Office of Energy and Sustainable Development, and Public Works Department.

Few of the implemented strategies include usage of natural ventilation, building of green/cool roofs and
cool pavements, and increase in vegetation, via tree planting projects.

The existing City programs and projects to reduce emissions that contribute to poor air are

- Implement the traffic safety capital construction projects identified and prioritized in the Berkeley
Pedestrian Plan (2021), Berkeley Bicycle Plan (2017), Berkeley - Vision Zero Action Plan (2020), and
Berkeley Transit-First Implementation Plan; these projects are intended to encourage non-driving modes

    -   Implementing the City’s Electric Mobility Road Map which includes electric shared mobility
        (bikes and scooters) as well as electric and hybrid car-sharing, and the installation of public
        charging stations

    -   Manage on-street parking and maintain parking garages to reduce emissions by making it easier
        to find a parking space more quickly (and thus reduce the time spent circling around looking for
        parking)

Cooling Centers

Another extreme heat mitigation strategy consists of operating cooling centers in Berkeley.

As extreme heat becomes more frequent and severe, Berkeley buildings, including City facilities, will
need to increase cooling capacity. This effort must be undertaken strategically over the coming decades
to find solutions that are clean, efficient, and functional during electrical grid outages. Approaches will
include natural ventilation and passive cooling techniques such as shading and orientation, particularly
in new building design. For existing buildings and new construction, consideration may also be given to
heat pump technology, a highly-efficient electric system (up to 400% efficient in energy-efficient
buildings) with both heating and cooling capabilities.

Cooling centers are necessary, particularly for those individuals who cannot escape the heat: they either
lack cooling in their homes, work outside, or are homeless. Citizens of Berkeley and others can utilize
one of the five cooling centers currently operating in the City during heatwaves. Cooling centers are
                                                    Internal



located in the North Berkeley Senior Center, South Berkeley Senior Center, Central Library, Claremont
Branch Library, and Tarea Hall Pittman South Branch Library. The dangers of heat have been proven in
studies that have found links between rising temperatures and a range of mental health issues, including
mental fatigue, aggression, and even higher rates of suicide, as well as physical health issues such as
premature death, cardiovascular stress, and failure of major organs such as the heart and kidneys.

Vulnerable People

    -   The cooling centers are particularly important for vulnerable community members, including:
    -   Elderly and children
    -   People with access and functional needs
    -   Underprivileged areas that lack tree canopy for shading, air conditioning and insulation in
        buildings, or car
    -   People that work outdoors and homeless populations

Prepare to be safe at home:

How can you prepare to be safe at home

Gather supplies to keep yourself cool, including:

Ice – fill up all your ice trays and freeze them and any ice packs overnight

Spray bottle – to spray mist on yourself to keep cool

Personal fan – fan to point at yourself

Towel – to wet and put on your body

Plan to keep your home cool on hot days without air conditioning, using:

A larger fan – to move hot air out of your home

An indoor/outdoor thermometer – set this up to know when to let cooler outside air into your home

Be ready to block sunlight and heat, using blackout curtains, reflective film, solar blankets or cardboard.
Blocking your windows with a light-colored sheet facing out, followed by a dark-colored sheet facing in,
can help to reflect light away and keep your home cooler.

Prepare for potential power outages (or see power outage section)

Keep Pet Safe

How to keep pets safe on hot days:

NEVER LEAVE YOUR PETS IN A PARKED CAR

Not even for a minute! Not even with the car running and air conditioner on. On a warm day,
temperatures inside a vehicle can rise rapidly to dangerous levels. On an 85-degree day, for example,
the temperature inside a car with the windows opened slightly can reach 102 degrees within 10
minutes. After 30 minutes, the temperature will reach 120 degrees. Your pet may suffer irreversible
                                                   Internal



organ damage or die. Learn how to help a pet left inside a hot car by taking action or calling for help.
Local law enforcement can follow this handy guide [PDF] on how to proceed.

Limit exercise on hot days

Take care when exercising your pet. Adjust intensity and duration of exercise in accordance with the
temperature. On very hot days, limit exercise to early morning or evening hours, and be especially
careful with pets with white-colored ears, who are more susceptible to skin cancer, and short-nosed
pets, who typically have difficulty breathing. Asphalt gets very hot and can burn your pet's paws, so walk
your dog on the grass if possible. Always carry water with you to keep your dog from dehydrating.

Don't rely on a fan

Pets respond differently to heat than humans do. (Dogs, for instance, sweat primarily through their
feet.) And fans don't cool off pets as effectively as they do people.

Provide ample shade and water

Any time your pet is outside, make sure they have protection from heat and sun and plenty of fresh,
cold water. In heat waves, add ice to water when possible. Tree shade and tarps are ideal because they
don't obstruct air flow. A doghouse does not provide relief from heat—in fact, it makes it worse.

Cool your pet inside and out

Whip up a batch of quick and easy DIY pupsicles for dogs. And always provide water, whether your pets
are inside or out with you.

Keep your pet from overheating indoors or out with a cooling body wrap, vest or mat. Soak these
products in cool water, and they'll stay cool (but usually dry) for up to three days. If your dog doesn't
find baths stressful, see if they enjoy a cooling soak.

Watch for signs of heatstroke

Extreme temperatures can cause heatstroke. Some signs of heatstroke are heavy panting, glazed eyes, a
rapid heartbeat, difficulty breathing, excessive thirst, lethargy, fever, dizziness, lack of coordination,
profuse salivation, vomiting, a deep red or purple tongue, seizure and unconsciousness.

Animals are at particular risk for heat stroke if they are very old, very young, overweight, not
conditioned to prolonged exercise, or have heart or respiratory disease. Some breeds of dogs—like
boxers, pugs, shih tzus and other dogs and cats with short muzzles—will have a much harder time
breathing in extreme heat.

Make a Plan

Make a plan for where to go (and how to get there) if your home gets too hot.

Consider locations you could visit that have air conditioning, like malls, stores, or community cooling
centers.

Make a transportation plan – consider using friends and family, public transit, carpooling, or using a taxi
or rideshare service.
                                                  Internal



If you use a wheelchair or other mobility device, you may also consider:

Pre-scheduling a paratransit trip to a cool location before the hottest hours of the day

Using Easy Does It for a Rescue Ride or Routine Transportation (BRSD members only)

Buddy up with your friends, family, and neighbors:

Make a plan to check on each other at least twice a day during a heat wave. Check to see if people are
developing signs of heat exhaustion or heat stroke. Remember that people who live alone are at the
greatest risk in a heat wave because no one will notice if they develop heat stroke.

Think about how you can work together to get to a location with air conditioning or a community
cooling center if someone’s home gets too hot.

                                        High Wind Events
How is wind formed?
Wind is the movement of air, traveling from areas of high pressure to low pressure. The greater
the difference in air pressure, the stronger the wind becomes. High- and low-pressure systems
are formed by ascending and descending air, primarily influenced by variations in temperature.
Wind is characterized by its horizontal speed and the direction from which it originates.


Wind in Berkeley
In Berkeley, high wind events are typically associated with the seasons. During winter, generally
spanning November through March, high winds are linked to weather systems and cold fronts.
In the summer months, temperature and pressure disparities between the Pacific Ocean and the
interior valleys to the east result in stronger afternoon and evening winds from the west. In spring
and fall, Berkeley experiences dry, offshore winds from the northeast, commonly known as the
“Diablo Winds.” These winds are most prevalent in the fall when the jet stream shifts southward,
impacting California with alternating areas of high and low pressure.
High wind events are could be felt throughout the city, with different areas experiencing varying
wind strengths based on the type of wind event. For instance, the westerly wind carries oceanic
moisture toward the city, and as the wind flow hits the Berkeley Hills, it splits, producing
northward and southward winds. The hot and dry Diablo wind, particularly common in the spring
and fall, affects the Berkeley Hills area more, while the cold storms, more common in the winter,
increase wind speeds in the flats.


Connections with wind
Climate change is contributing to the escalation of extreme storms and weather conditions,
frequently accompanied by high winds. Considering the increased frequency of high wind events
in recent years, it is anticipated that each subsequent year will bring more of these occurrences.
Climate change is projected to instigate additional severe storms, further intensifying the
frequency of damaging wind events.
Among these wind events, Diablo winds in the fall are particularly worrisome. This is due to the
wildlands and vegetation being at their driest during this season. The combination of Diablo
winds and dry conditions poses a significant risk of a high fire danger.
                                              Internal



Extent of high wind and anticipated intensities
The National Weather Service (NWS) defines “high winds” as sustained wind speeds of 40 miles
per hour (mph) or greater lasting for one hour or longer, or wind gusts 58 mph or greater for any
duration. The NWS issues a wind advisory when there are sustained winds of 31 to 39 mph, or
gusts to 46 to 57 mph. Sustained wind speed is different than a wind gust. A wind gust is a brief
increase in the wind speed typically around 20-30 seconds.


Wind scale
This Beaufort Wind Scale measures wind severity according to visible environmental impacts,
without the use of instruments. For example, when wind speeds is between 1 to 3 mph, the
direction of wind could be determined by looking at the smoke drift. In these conditions there
will be little if any movement with flags or tree leaves. When wind speed is between 32-38 mph,
people should be careful walking under and around trees because in these conditions they get in
motion. And at the higher wind speeds we could expect damages to trees and some structures.

Timing of the wind event could also play a role. If it’s the first high wind event of the season,
there might be more foliage, limbs, or branches that fall as the wind blows for the first time in a
while.



Vulnerabilities
High winds could pose risks to people, structures and systems.
High winds could pose significant safety risks to people. Large branches can break off trees, heavy
objects may blow around, and dust and debris can get into the eyes, throat, and mouth. High
winds can be particularly dangerous for people experiencing homelessness, people who work
outside, and people who live in mobile or unanchored homes, like RVs that may dislodge.
Downed tree or blowing objects can result in significant damage to public and private
infrastructure, including residential homes, public and private buildings, and vehicles.
Wind can take down power lines and or cause other objects to do the same. Damage to power
lines can result in power outages.


How to reduce risk from high winds?
How the whole community can work together to mitigate Berkeley’s high wind hazard? The
following steps are key for individual community members and households to reduce their risk
from high winds.
                                                Internal



Keep trees maintained
           -   City trees are located between the sidewalk and the street, in street medians,
               public parks, or on other properties owned by the City of Berkeley. If you notice a
               tree near your home that requires attention from the forestry team, please submit
               a request by calling 311 or emailing trees@berkeleyca.gov.
           -   Privately owned trees fall under the responsibility of the owner. It is advisable to
               obtain a professional arborist assessment to identify signs of decay, dead
               branches, or other structural issues that could lead to future problems. Ensure the
               maintenance of your trees by regular trimming and pruning every few years.
Before a wind event
           -   Bring in any loose outdoor items, such as holiday decorations and chairs, or
               securely tie them down. Aside from the risk of these items being blown away or
               damaged, airborne debris can pose a safety hazard.
           -   Be prepared for potential power outages. During winter months, consider raising
               the temperature on your thermostat in case you lose power for a few hours or
               longer. This ensures that your living space remains comfortable during unforeseen
               electrical disruptions.
During high winds
           -   If you need to be outdoors, keep a safe distance from trees. This precaution
               reduces the risk of injury in case of falling branches or trees during strong winds.
           -   Avoid driving, particularly in high-profile vehicles, during the most intense winds.
               Strong gusts could potentially blow your vehicle off the road. Additionally, falling
               trees may obstruct the road ahead, posing a hazard that can be challenging to
               discern at night until it's directly in front of you. Exercise caution to ensure your
               safety on the road.
Stay in a safe space until it’s safe to come out.
           -   If you come across downed power lines, promptly report them to the appropriate
               authorities.
           -   Stay away from downed power lines to ensure your safety.
           -   Refrain from walking under trees, especially if there's a possibility they have been
               damaged by winds and could fall. This precaution minimizes the risk of injury due
               to falling branches or trees.

What is a Landslide?
                                                                                                                      •   The most dangerous landslides in
                                                                                                                          terms of life safety are fast-moving,
                                                                                                                          generally shallow debris flows.
                                                                                                                            • These are triggered when
                                                                                                                               intense rainfall follows storms
                                                                                                                               that have already saturated
                                                                                                                               hillsides.
                                                                                                                            • Once initiated, debris flows can
                                                                                                                               travel great distances at
                                                                                                                               relatively high velocities, flowing
                                                                                                                               down drainages and onto
                                                                                                                               alluvial fans and damaging any
                                                                                                                               structures lying in their paths.


The debris flow landslide hit a home on Middlefield Road on its way down the hill from The Spiral on Jan. 16, 2023.
                                               Credit: Kelly Sullivan

High Wind Events




                   32
How is Wind formed?

Wind is air in motion, traveling
   between areas of high
  pressure to low pressure

The steeper the difference in
air pressure, the stronger the
           wind is




                              33
                                        Wind in Berkeley

In Berkeley, high wind events are associated with
the seasons

o Winter: weather systems and cold fronts


o Summer: temperature and pressure differences
  between the Pacific Ocean and the interior
  valleys to the east create strong winds from the
  west


o Spring & Fall: warm, dry offshore winds from
  the northeast, known as “Diablo Winds”
                                                      34
                                     Related Hazards

Climate Change:
• More extreme storms and weather conditions are
  expected

Wildland Urban Interface Fire:
• The Fall “Diablo Winds” and dry vegetation could result
  in a high fire danger

  seconds) of 58 mph or higher

What is Sea Level Rise?
                         • Sea level rise is an increase in the level
                           of the world’s oceans.
                         • Warmer temperatures associated with
                           climate change are causing global sea
                           levels to rise through two processes.
                             - Ice Melt
                             - Thermal Expansion




                                                                        3
                                       Internal




Where is it in
Berkeley?
• Low-lying inland areas could flood
  from below by emergent
  groundwater long before coastal
  floodwaters overtop the shoreline
• Emergent groundwater is when the
  groundwater surfaces and the depth
  is less than zero.




                                                  4
                                       Internal




Where is it in
Berkeley?
• At 24” sea-level rise, we begin to
  see “emergent” groundwater.
    ‒ As the sea-level rises, the
       more emergent groundwater
       is projected.
• At 96” sea-level rise a large
  portion of West Berkeley is
  covered by emergent
  groundwater.




                                                  5
                     Internal




What could be affected by Sea Level Rise?

                 •     Increased infiltration rates into sewer systems,
                       flooding of basements, and damage to
                       underground infrastructure.
                 •     Increased risk that toxic materials could be
                       raised and moved
                 •     Rising groundwater will increase liquefaction
                       hazards in response to earthquakes, particularly
                       in former open water, mudflat, marsh, and
                       floodplain areas that have been filled for
                       development.

What is a Tsunami?
• Tsunamis affecting the Bay
  Area can result from
  offshore earthquakes
  within the Bay Area, or
  from very distant events.
• Tsunamis impacting the Bay
  Area are usually generated
  by faults in Washington and
  Alaska.

Maritime Community

                                     Internal




Maritime Community
The City of Berkeley will evacuate docks and shut them down within 1 hour of a
tsunami’s estimated arrival.




                                                                             22
Internal




           23
                                         Internal




Maritime Community
Make sure your boat is secured and
ready. Keep in mind that the City will
shut down the dock 1 hour before the
tsunami’s anticipated arrival time.




                                                    24
                               Internal




Maritime Community
Make sure your boat is secured and ready. Keep in mind
that the City will shut down the dock 1 hour before the
tsunami’s anticipated arrival time.
  • Secure your boat to the dock and tie down any loose gear.
  • Check your dock line condition and replace any worn dock
    lines.
  • Do not install fendering to the dock.
  • Remove as much loose boating gear onboard as possible,
    especially electronics and important documents. Any gear that
    will remain on your boat should be secured.
  • Turn off and disconnect shore power cords, water supply hoses
    and propane or other gas valves.
  • Secure and lock all hatches and port holes. Check for leaks,
    and seal them as necessary.

    if you suspect a gas leak (smell or sound)

Local Hazard Mitigation Plan Update ▪ First Draft 2024 LHMP         8
                                             Gas (PG&E)
                                 How to secure your home?
1. Locate and clearly label the gas shutoff valve(s)

2. Know how to shut off the gas

3. Have proper non-sparking tools for shutting off gas

4. Have your building and appliances inspected to make sure they

can withstand an earthquake

5. If you are unsure of how to shut off the gas properly and safely,

you should never attempt to do so!!

• Remember to always shut off all the individual circuits
  before shutting off the main circuit breaker




Local Hazard Mitigation Plan Update ▪ First Draft 2024 LHMP                     14
                                                               Electrical Emergency

During and right after the disaster…
• Unplug major appliances

• Locate the circuit breakers or fuses and know how to shut off
 the power

• Turn on the main switch or breaker first, then screw in the fuses
 or switch on the smaller breakers, one at a time

• Never step in water to turn off the

 electricity, call a professional

                                                              Water Storage Options

 Option 1: Gallons of Water from the Dollar Store
• Very low cost
• Easy storage/moving
      o Store this water in a cool, dark place
• Frequent refreshing required
      o Has an expiration date (12 - 18 months)
      o After expiration is still good for handwashing and other sanitation
• Easy to use in an emergency

              Summary of Changes to the City of Berkeley’s
              2024 First Draft Local Hazard Mitigation Plan
This document outlines the revisions made to Berkeley’s 2024 First Draft Local Hazard
Mitigation Plan (2024 First Draft) that are present in the 2024 Final Draft Local Hazard
Mitigation Plan.

   1. In the Executive Summary, on page ES-5, the following information has been added
      about the link between growing WUI fire risk and climate change:

      Climate change is resulting in longer and drier summer conditions leading to wildfires of
      greater frequency and duration. Increased drought conditions cause fuels to become
      extremely dry and more fire prone. Additionally, climate change causes more frequent
      bouts of extreme weather, including low humidity and high winds associated with fire
      weather.

   2. In the Executive Summary, on page ES-6, the following information has been added:

      The fire risk facing the people and properties in the eastern hills is compounded by the
      area’s mountainous topography, hazardous vegetation, minimal access and egress
      routes, and location, overlaid upon the Hayward Fault. Berkeley’s flatlands are also
      exposed to a fire that spreads west from the hills.


   3. In Element A: Planning Process, on page A-3 the following information has been added
      about the Public Review of the First Draft Plan:

      In response to this offer, Council Members suggested a presentation to the Safety
      Committee, which staff gave in July 2024.


   4. In Element B: Risk Assessment, on page B-57 the following text was added:

      Locations of WUI Fires and Related Hazards.

   5. In Element B: Risk Assessment, on page B-68, the following text was added:


      Hazardous Vegetation
      Certain plant species, including native and non-native species, have
      characteristics that make them ignite readily and burn intensely contributing to
      wildfire risk. Characteristics may include being biologically prone to burn due to
      chemical composition, being difficult to maintain in a fire-resistant state, presenting
      challenges to routine maintenance, having high surface area to volume ratio, or
      being prone to rapid changes in moisture content in response to environmental
      conditions. While these characteristics make some plants more fire-hazardous, all
      plants can burn if they are dead, poorly maintained, or drought stressed. i
                                        Internal



   Historically, the East Bay Hills ecosystem burned regularly. Researchers have
   proposed that under indigenous land management, fires due to both natural and
   anthropogenic ignitions occurred every 5-15 years. ii Fire is this ecosystem’s
   natural way of clearing dead vegetation and maintaining forest health. Many
   California native plant species present in the East Bay Hills also need fire in order
   to reproduce.

   Living in a fire-prone area means taking steps to mitigate risks while also
   recognizing that it’s infeasible to remove all of our vegetation. The mere presence
   of a certain fire hazardous species does not always mean it must be removed.
   Other factors, such as maintenance and placement, are more important than the
   plant itself. For property owners thinking about their own landscaping, it’s great to
   focus on California native or other pollinator friendly plants that require little water
   and are easy to maintain. However, “There are no published fire-wise or fire-
   resistant plant lists that are science based or peer reviewed. Design and
   maintenance are more important than plant selection.” iii

   To protect life and property, the Berkeley Fire Department inspects all properties
   in the Very High Fire Danger Severity Zone for Defensible Space, which is the
   buffer created between a structure on your property and the grass, trees,
   shrubs, or other vegetation that surrounds it. This may include the removal of
   certain vegetation within 100 feet from any structure. These mitigation measures,
   along with home hardening, are the scientifically validated actions that have the
   most impact on reducing the ignition potential of homes. Failure to comply with
   recommendations results in citations and fines.

   The City, often in collaboration with regional partners, works to remove and or
   clean up the understory of hazardous trees that are likely to burn and potentially
   impact people and infrastructure. For more information on these programs, review
   Element C: Mitigation Strategy.


6. In Element B: Risk Assessment, on page B-87, the following section was deleted and
   added to Element C: Mitigation Strategy, C.5 Household Mitigation Actions (see # below
   for what was added):

   B.3.i Berkeley Household Risk Reduction

14. In Element C: Mitigation Strategy, on page C-5, the following text was added:

   Measure T1 provides $100 million of funding from bond revenue to pay for
   improvements to City infrastructure and facilities. Berkeley voters passed
   Measure T1 in November 2016. Measure T1 funds are used for a variety of
   infrastructure improvements, including upgrading Senior Centers and Community
   Centers to immediate occupancy and increase their ability to serve the community
   regularly and during disasters. Future mitigation actions could include upgrading
   additional buildings and or building new ones.


15. In Element C: Mitigation Strategy, on page C-10 for Expanded Inventory of Potentially
    Seismically Vulnerable Buildings, the following text was added:


   With the launch of the Retrofit Grants Program, staff conducted extensive research to
   update and refine the City’s inventory of potentially seismically vulnerable buildings. In
                                           Internal



   addition to soft story buildings not currently subject to mandatory retrofit such as those
   with 3-4 residential units or commercial uses, Berkeley has numerous non-ductile
   concrete and tilt-up or other rigid wall-flexible diaphragm (RWFD) buildings. Future
   expansion includes conducting research to determine other hazardous buildings that
   should be inventoried and exploring additional mandatory retrofit ordinances.


16. In Element C: Mitigation Strategy, on page C-12 for Fire Department: WUI Division, the
    following text was added:

   City of Berkeley Fire Department instituted a WUI division in 2021 supported with
   funding from Measure FF. The WUI Division is primarily responsible for the coordination
   of wildland mitigation efforts and related inspection activities. The ability for the Division
   to expand on mitigation activities is outlined in the Action Plan of the Community Wildfire
   Protection Plan (CWPP).

17. In Element C: Mitigation Strategy, on page C-26 the following text was deleted:

   Currently, the City is identifying funding to upgrade the MLK Junior Youth Services
   Center, the Willard Clubhouse, the African American Holistic Resources Center, and the
   South Berkeley Senior Center.

   This text was replaced with:

   Currently, the City is using T1 Funds on the MLK Jr. Youth Services Center Retrofit
   and Renovation project and the Willard Park Clubhouse and Restroom
   Replacement Project. Both of these facilities will be upgraded to immediate
   occupancy status, meaning that post earthquake, only limited structural damage
   will have occurred. The Willard Park Clubhouse is currently under construction and
   the MLK Jr. Youth Services Center is in the design part of the process. Using T1
   and General Funds, the African American Holistic Resource Center is currently in
   the design part of the process. The African American Holistic Resource Center
   (AAHRC) will be a facility to house culturally relevant services to help eliminate
   inequities within Berkeley's African American Community. The vision for
   the African American Holistic Resource Center is to host services to benefit the
   community with education, employment, health, mental health, and housing
   advocacy and supports. It will be built to immediate occupancy status.

   Using funds from Measure T1 and funding from a FEMA grant, the South Berkeley
   Senior Center is being renovated to include disaster preparedness, electrification,
   energy efficient building systems, and other enhancements to the community
   building. It’s in the design phase.

   The City is currently seeking opportunities for funding and grants to develop the design
   and complete construction for the Frances Albrier Community Center.
